THE pessimist is a man who look upon sunshine only as a thir••• that cast ahadaws. A hypocrite is like a tack—he can do the most mischief when pointing to heaven. EXAMPLE is stronger than precept ; but precept is expected to do a great deal of example's work. VERY LADY LlEE.—First Domestic:—" Me new mistress is very lady-like." Second Domestic: "What do you mean by lady-like?" First Domestic: "Sure, Oi mane she's different from most ladies." STILL HE WASN'T SATTSFIED.—Agent : "I hope the new he ter works alright." Tenant: "It makes my blood boil !" IN HAR.D Luca. Jones: " How' -i Wheeler get- ting along since he bought a bicycle?" Brown: " On crutches, I belive.' FATHER : " Harry, what time was it when you got in last night? Harry (vaguely) : "Bed- time." ". SAY, Bill, is your guv'nor a Conservative or a Liberal?" Btll: "Id unno whetheee's a Conserva- tive or not, but'e ain't werry MR. INGLESBY : "Is MISS Gayburd really such a charming girl ? Mrs. Maynewright : "She must be. All her girl friends hate her furiously." THE FATHEP. : "If you marry him, you'll have to live on the wind." The (WTl:ter: "Then, papa, perhaps you'll raise the wind for us." LATENT ENERGY. —FilaßtT : "Is there any life at all in your office-boy Barb r: " Any life? He's only resting for a sport. Wait ten minutes, and you'll see him cl-se the Office." WHERE MONEY TALl{S.—BinkerS : "Look at that shabby millionaire. You can't judge a man by his dress." Winkers : ' No; but you can judge him by his wife's." Little May was showing the pictures in the album to the visit •r, and on coming to the picture of her father's first wife, she said :—"That's my elder mother." THE girl of the period now carries her hands in her pockets like a man—partly because it is fashionable, and partly, doubtless, because there are holes in her gloves. " IlEne's my photograph, Alice, taken lasb week," said Helen. " Isn't it good ? " " Very nice, indeed," said Alice ; " but how you've

changed " MAGISTRATE (to "drunk and disorderly ") : " What are your means of support ? " Prisoner (facetiously : " Well, last night the policeman was, your worship !" FIN-DE-SIECLE YOUNG LADIES. —Fond Mother: " My daug •ters have received a thoroughly prac. tical education; each of them is capable of making work for ten servants." MUCH ALIKE. - Clara : "Isn't this strange This book says that in France a woman has to marry in order to be ree." Dora : " It's the same way here. We must obey papa until we go to the altar and solemnly- promise to love, honour, and obey a husband—and after that we needn't obey anybody." • Too MANY AlRS.—First Politician: "No use talkin'. Quick as we elect a feller to a high office, he begins ter put on airs an' make hisself disagree- able. I'll never vote fur Lightweight ag'in." Second Politician " He's a good feller." Ffrst .Politician :•' Huh ! ‘V here you been livin' ? Only last Sunday I saw 'im all spruced up an' a-goin' tc church."

AN UNLUCKY GIRL No sooner had the pilgrim set foot in the Elysian Fields, than a shade accosted him. "1 am the girl who wouldn't let the curfew ring that night," it hurriedly explaine'd. "Am I well spoken of on ear •h ?" "Well, ' answered th* pilgrim, "I don't profess to be a judge of elocution, but I should say not." ONE WAY OUT—Sweet Girl: "Oh, papa, I have found a way for you to escape the income- tax." Father: "Uuess not." Sweet Girl : "Yes, I have. You give half your stocks to Mr. Slim. purse, and tien 11l marry Mr. Slimpurse, and so all the money will be kept in the family, and the Government won't get a cent." DURING THE CHOLERA SEASON. —Dialogue between two lathe.; : " Have you taken any pre- cautions against the epidemic?" "Certainly." "Well, what have you done? "Got my hus- band to make his will." Losu-Wl.:DED.—Ovcrheard at the Salle des Capucines du ing the delivery of a lecture by the famous X---. " How Rill he is of his subject I" said one of the hearers. "Yes, but how slow he is in emptying himself !" was the reply. A LOST OPPORTUNITY. A lady told a party of friends that she had quarrelled with her husband, and had planted a tree in memory of this their first falling•out "What a splendid idea," whis- pered another lady in her husband's ear; "if we had adopted that plan, we might have had by now a fine avenue of trees in our garden." "I DON'T see what birds build nests for," said "To sleep ia," said his mother. "Ho !" retorted Willie. " Why don t they just lie down on their own feathers?' NOT RIPE FOR AN OPERATION. —Se : "The roof is leaking again. We ought to send for the man to see to it." He : "It might be better to wait until it gets so that he can't possibly make it any worse." LEARNING GOLF—First Yonng Lady (learning golf) : "Der me! What shall Ido now? This ball is in a hole." Second Young Lady (looking over book of instructions) : "Let—me—see. I presu.z e you will have to take a stick of the right shape to get it out." First Young Lady: "Oh, yes, of course. See if you can find one shaped like a dustpan and brush." A TRICK OF THE TRADE.—Newsboy (a novice) " Extry speci-all ! Collision of two men-of-war: Four hundred kihlel !" Bigger Newsboy: "What an ass you are 1 If you go and tell folks all about it, nobody will want to buy the paper. Let me show you what you've got to shout; this is it; Extry speci-all ! Avv, aw !—oh, oh !—wah, wah I —wow ! ho !—wah, wah, wah l—hoy I MRS. FANGLE : "Why, I'm so glad to see you, Mrs. Wallace! I had a presentiment that you would call this evening.' Mrs. Wallace: " In- deed !" Mrs. Fangio : "Yes. Whenever Henry and I sit down to have a nice, quiet evening to our. ves, somebody is sure to call." A ‘VOifAN rushed downstairs the other night, flung her arms round a burglar, and held him while her ho band ran several streets away for a policeman. All of which goes to show the husband was not of a jealous disposition.

LADIES' LETTER.
Mr DEAREST NKLLIE.

I may tell you that tailor jackets are likely to be more general than they have been for a long time. As the sleeves of dress bodices are still made in enormous proportions it would be impossible to wear tailor coats such as used to be in vogue some time back over them. Our tailors have found this out at last, and now they have brought out some smart coats, both in tight and half-fitting shapes ; but instead of being finished like masculine gar- ments with coat sleeves, they have sleeves which even exceed those of dress bodices in width, so that they can be worn over any style of bodice. Redin- gotes are always smart-looking garments, both for ladies and children. They will be worn again this season made in loose and fitting shapes. Some are almost like dressing gowns in style when they have yokes and straight flowing skirts. It is a long time since sealskin, which is to be one of the furs of the season, has been the rage. Tile rich dark brown tint of seal fur is most effective when it is used to trim either dresses, redingotes, or pelisses of coloured cloth; moreover, it blends perfectly with all the fashionable colours. Beaver makes a charming finish for babies' white pelisses; but some prefer white fox or the long silky hair of the Mongolian goat. Most expensive is alaska, but it

looks awfully well. I saw a lady last week wear- ing one of these, and it really became her im- mensely. The garment—a mantle—had the yoke and front of velvet and lace brocade, and it was trimmed with Russian sable tails. The lining was cream satin.

Did you ask me about hats? Straw shapes are almost entirely discarded now in favour of felt and velvet-covered buckram. Flat low crowned hats are still trimmed with rosettes of ribbon on either side of the front, a bunch of quills or a full osprey rises out of the rosette on the left side. Beefeater hats are one of the novelties of the season. These will be largely adopted by children. The hats have a medium flat brim covered with black velvet, while the crown has a full circle of coloured velvet drawn round it, so that it falls over on the brim. The full part is slightly raised on one side by a group of feathers, wing; or rosettes of black ribbon. Toque-shaped hats are considered very smart, both for ladies and little girls. Some of these in colotn•ed velvet have a border of fur to

match the muff and trimmings of the jacket. These are finished with posies of velvet flowers on either side of the front and a short-tied bow of wide satin ribbon at the back of the crown, which stands out well at the sides. One of the prettiest hats I have seen lately was one of those large ones guiltless of feathers, and this is made of felt, with the ruche round the crown of a pink and white glac4 silk fringed. On either side of this ruche Ind at the back are rosettes of black gauze ribbon, while just at one side waves a curled osprey.

A frock which might be worn by a girl from seven to 12 is of shot tweed in two shades of brown. The skirt is plain; the bodice has three box-pleats in front and a deep pointed belt of brown velvet with a bow at the left side, a little muslin and lace collar turning over a velvet band finishing off the neck. Tweeds, too, are being largely made up with velvet yokes edged with fur, while many of the plain cloths have braided eouave fronts and full vests of Paisley patterned velvet. Velveteen is not much used for entire gowns this season save for very little girls, but velveteen bodices with serge, tweed or mohair (a fabric which resembles coarse alpaca) skirts are most fashionable. A simple full bodice of blue-

green velveteen, for instance, with a skirt of deeper green cloth or soft serge, looks exceedingly nice on a fair-haired girl of 12 or 13, and with the addition of a pretty cream lace and muslin fichu would make a dainty party dress, while for a brunette a bodice of red velveteen with a wide collar of white muslin and embroidery, a skirt of black and red shot tweed and a long-ended sash of red velvet, would be extremely stylish. Another costume for girls of the same age is in fancy cheviot, trimmed with velvet and ribbon, either to match or con- trast, suitable for girls from eight to 14 years of age. Your loving JENNIE.

Madame Sarah Bernhardt holds that an actor or actress should retire from the stage at the age of fifty, although she confesses that she has seen many who should have disappeared at the age of five-and-twenty. Miss Clarice Terry, who recently won in New York • thousand-dollar prize as being "the handsomest woman in America," is now appearing in a series of living pic- tures in the transatlantic music halts. Her manager proudly styles Miss Clarice Terry "the modern Venus." The wealth of the new Duchess will, of course, make for her popularity at Blenheim—a popularity which her own personal qualities will enhance. The new Duchess has no bounce about her. She is simple and natural in all her ways. Without being a woman of exceptional talent, she is particularly intelligent; and in art and literature her taste will do her credit. That she will be- come the mistress of the greatest salon in the coining generation—such a salon, says the "New Budget," as the Princess Louise, bad she wealth, longs to create—is the prophecy of those who know the new Duchess best. The "Lady's Pictorial " tells us that Princess Maud always looks well dressed, despite the frequent sim- plicity of her toilettes, and has been known to "sport" a single eyeglass with very chic effect. Latterly, the Princess and her sister have been more smartly costumed than was the case even two or three years ago, when, if Dame Gossip may be believed, Princess Maud once got so tired of a particular dress that one day she took her courage in both hands, a wax match in her fingers, and —the garment in question came to a most inconsistently brilliant end. The "Gentlewoman" thinks that Prince Carl of Den- mark should be three years younger than Princess Maud is of no moment whatever. The Princesses of Wales have never been brought forward. It was the desire of their tether, indeed, that they stesuld be kept back as much as possible, and this very wise bringing up has contributed to their being, all three, unusually naive and youthful, both in bearing and character. Even to this ' day the unmarried Princesses are not allowed, by their parents' wish, to read any novel which has not firat been digested by a pastor or master.

In the rural districts of France various wild creatures are rate' which in England are never put to ouch a use. Squirrels are considered very good food, and, as they are easily shot, they have become rare in some districts. In Lorraine, when there has been a successful wolf-hunt, it is by no means uncommon for the peasants to divide the flesh of the hated beast and feast upon it. Badger; are also used for food, but very rarely. There is scarcely a bird, however, that is not eaten. Nightingales, mag- pies, tomtits—almost everything that flies, big or small, goes on the spit or into the saucepan. It may be truly said of the French that they are the least wasteful people in Europe. Dr. Mafadyen'and Mr. Colwell have, says the " West- minister Gazette," been inquiring into the composition of the " ices" sold in the streets by Italians in London. The analysts tell us that " microscopical examination revealed the following delectables : Bed bugs, bugs' legs, fleas, straw (bed) ?, human hair, cats' and dogs' hairs coal dust, woollen and linen fibre, tobacco, scales of epi- thelium, and muscular tissue." The diet is varied, and you appear to get a good many courses for your money, but for all that there will doubtless be found many who will grumble at the menu. Vegeterians especially should on principle, avoid street ices. The marriage of the Duke of Marlborough to Miss Vanderbilt ham induced a statistical American ' journalist to compile a list of American heiresses who have married foreigners of rank during the last twenty- five years. The total of such marriages is one hundred and thirty-four, and the amount the American girls have taken to their husbands le one hundred and sixty- one million dollars, or about thirty-four millions sterl- ing. The biggest figure was the fifteen million dollars which Miss Anna Gould took to Count Bonniface de Castellane. The next dot was the twelve millon dollars Colonel Ralph Vivian had with Miss Emily Roberts. Mr. Secretary Chamberlain. who is included in a group be- cause he is a Privy Councillor, had a modest hundred thousand dollars with the daughter of Mr. Secretary Endicott. The late Duke of Marlborough and Lord Wil- liam Beresford are bracketed as having been successors in the enjoyment of the seven million dollars attached to the name of Mrs. Hammeraley. It will surprise most people to learn that Sir William Elarcourt's wife, ale Mrs. P. J. Ives,had a fortune of five million dollars—say a million sterling. Lady Randolph Churchill. however, brought her husband only a quarter of a million dollars, while Mr. George Curzon stands on a level with Sir Wil- liam Harcoin t as a husband of a wife with a dot of five million dollars.

The county magistrates at Burnley were occupied several hours on Thursday in hearing a charge preferred against William Marsden, weaver of 24,Shallespeare.st„ PAiham, of inflicting grevious bodily harm upon his wife on Sunday morning, the 29'h September, by strik- ing her several times with a hatchet.—Mrs. Marsden had been unable to appear until Thursday in consequence of the injuries she received. She appeared with 'Pr head bandaged up. and in her evidence stated that though, during the night of the 28th September, her husband was restless, she never apprehended any attack, and after getting out of bed at ten minutes to six, she re- turned again and went to sleep. About half-past six she was awakesed by a terific blow on the face with a hatchet, and found•her husband kneel- ing on her chest, and holding her by the left hand whilst in his right hand he had the hatchet' (produced) raised above her head. She struggled with him, and they both rolled on to the floor, he havin ghi her several times on the hack of her head. She managed to snatch the hatchet away from him, and to throw it outside the room, but it struck the door and fell back into the room. Pe seized it again, and gave her more serious blows. Her niece and nephew were in the same house,hegrd her cries of murder, and altlinivzh they came a few yards int, the room they ran hack again into the street, gioinK the alarm to the neighbours.—Richard Shutt. a neigh- bour, stated that as he was going to the prisoner's house he met Mrs. Marsden coming out in her nightdress with bl,nd flowing from htl. face and head. She had a hatchet with her in her hand, and he took it from her and assisted her into his house, here she was medically attended.—Dr. Grant, who attended the injured woman, gave evidence as to the extent of the injuries.—Other witnesses called stated that the prisoner had suffered from melancholy. and it was stated that he had been medically attended forthis disorder.—Rs was committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizee.

div.head: HIDDEN HAND;
div.p: THE HIDDEN HAND;
CAPITOLA THE MADCAP. BY MRS. E. D. E. N. SOUTHWORTH.
CHAPTER VII. METAMORPHOSIS OF TIIE NEWS-BOY. With caution judge of probability. Things deemed unlikely, e'en impossible, Experience oft hath proved to be true.
7 SHAKESPEARE.

" What shall we do with her!" inquired she Recorder, so/Jo yore, of a brother magistrate who appeared to be associated with him on the bench. "Send her to the Refuge," replied the other, in the same tone.

"What are they consulting about ?" asked Old Hurricane, whose ears were not of the best. "They are talking of sending her to the Refuge," answered a by-stander. " Refuge ? Is there a Refuge for destitute chil- dren in New York. Then Babylon is not so bad as I thooght it. What is this Refuge !" "It is a prison where juvenile delinquents are trained to habits of="

" A prison ! send her to a prison ! never !" burst forth Old Hurricane, rising and marching up to the Recorder. He stood hat in hand before him, and said: "Your Honour, if a pro' legal guardian appears to claim this young person, and holds himself in all respects responsible for her, may she not be at once delivered into, his hands 1"

" Assuredly," answered the magistrate, with the manner of one glad to be rid of the charge. " Then, sir, I, Ira Warfield, of Hurricane Hall, in Virginia, present myself as the guardian of this Capitola Black, whom I claim as my ward. And I will enter into a recognisance for any sum to appear and prove my right, if it should be disputed. For my personal responsibility, sir, I refer you to the proprietors of the Astor, who have known me many years," " It is not necessary, Major Warfield ; we assume the fact of your responsibility and deliver up the young girl to your charge." "I thank you, sir," said Old Hurricane, bowing low.

Then hurrying across the room where sat the reporters for the press, he said : " Gentlemen, I have a favour to ask of you—it is that you will altogether drop this case of the boy in girl's clothes—l mean girl in girl's clothes —I declare, I don't know what I mean ! nor I shan't neither, until I see the creature in its proper dress ; but this I wish to request of you, gehtle- !nen, that you will drop that item from your re- port, or if you must mention it, treat it with delicacy, as the good name of a young lady is in- volved."

. -..—. The reporters with sidelong glances, winks, and smiles, gave him the required promise, and Old Hurricane returned to the side of his protegee. "Capitola, are you willing to go with me?" "Jolly willing, governor. "Then come along, my coach is waiting," said Old Hurricane. And, bowing to the Court, he took the hand of his charge, and led her forth amid the ill-suppressed jibes of the crowd.

- - - There's a hoary-headed old signor," said. one. "She's as like him as two peas," quoth another. "Wonder if there's any more belonging to him of that same sort," inquired a third. Leaving all this sarcasm behind him, Old Hurricane handed his protegee into the coach, took the seat beside her, and gave orders to be driven out towards Harlem.

As soon as they were seated in the coach, the old man turned to his charge and said: " Capitola, I shall have to trust to your girl's wit, to get yourself into your proper clothes again without exciting farther notice." "Yes, governor." "My boy, girl, I mean! lam not the governor of Virginia, though if every one had his rights I don't know but I should be! However, I am only Major Warfield," said the old man, naively, for he had not the most distant idea that the title be- stowed on him by Capitola, was a mere remnant of her newsboys' slang. "Now, my lad—pshaw ! my lass, I mean, how shall we get you metamorphosed again?" "I know, gov—major, I mean. There is a shop of ready-made clothing at the 'Needle Woman's Aid,' corner of the next square. I can get out there and buy a full suit." " Very well ! stop at the next corner, driver," called Old Hurricane.

The next minute the coach drew up before a warehouse of ready-made garments. Old Hurricane jumped out, and leading his charge, entered the shop. Luckily, there was behind the counter only one person—a staid, elderly, kind-looking woman.

"Here, madam," said Old Hurricane, stooping confidentially to her ear—" I am in a little embar- rassment that I hope you will be willing to help me out of for a consideration. I came to New York in pursuit of my ward—this young girl here, whom I found in boy's clothes. I now wish to restore her to her proper dress, before presenting her to my friends, of course. Therefore, I wish you to furnish her with half a dozen complete suits of female attire, of the very best you have that will fit her. And also to give her the use of a room and of your own aid in changing her dress. I will pay you liberally." Half suspicious and half scandalised, the worthy woman gazed with scrutiny first into the face of the guardian, and then into that of the ward ; but find- ing in the extreme youth of the one and the ad- vance age of the other, and in the honest expres- sion of both, something to allay her fears, if not to inspire her confidence, she said :

" Very well, sir. Come after me, young gentle- man—young lady, I should say." And calling in a boy to mind the shop,, she conducted Capitola to an inner apartment. Old Hurricane went out and dismissed his coach. When it was entirely out of sight, he hailed another that was passing by empty, and en- gaged it to take himself and a young lady to the Wasnington House. When he re-entered the shop he found the shopwoman and Capitols returned and waiting for

Capitola was indeed transfigured. Her bright black hair, parted in the middle, fell in ringlets each side her blushing cheeks ; her dark grey eyes were east down in modesty at the very same instant that her ripe red lips were puckered up with mis- chief. She was well and properly attired in a grey silk dress, crimson merino shawl, and a black velvet bonnet.

The other clothing that had been purchased was done up in packages and put into the coach. And after paying the shopwoman handsomely, Old Hurricane took the hand of his ward, handed her into the coach, and gave the order: " To the Washington House." The ride was performed in silence. Capitola sat deeply blushing at the recollection of her nude attire, and profoundly cogitating as to what could be the relationship between herself and the grey old man whose claim the Recorder had so promptly admitted. There seemed but one way of accounting for the great interest he took in her fate. Capitola came to the conclusion that the grim old lion before her was no more nor less than —her own father! Poor Cap. had been too long tossed about New York not to know more of life than at her age she should have known. She had indeed the innocence of youth, but not its sim- plicity. Old Hurricane, on his part, sat with his thick cane grasped in his two knobby hands, standing between his knees, his grizzled chin resting upon it, and his eyes cast down as in deep thought. And so in silence they reached the Washington House. Major Warfield then conducted his ward into the ladies' parlour, and went and entered his own and her name upon the books as "Major Warfield and his ward Miss Black," for whom he engaged two bedrooms and a private parlour.

Then leaving Capitola to be shown to her apart- ment by a chambermaid, he went out and ordered her luggage up to her room, and dismissed the coach. Next he walked to the Aston House, paid his bill, collected his baggage, took another carriage and drove back to the Washington Hotel. All this trouble Old Hurricane took to break the links of his action and prevent scandal. This filled up a long forenoon. He dined alone with his ward in their private parlour. Such a dinner poor Cap. had never even smelt before! How intensely she enjoyed it with all its surroundings I—the comfortable room the glowing fire, the clean table, the rich food, the obsequious attendance, her own genteel and becoming dress, the company of a highly respectable guardian—all, all, so different from anything she had ever been accustomed to, and so highly appreciated. - How ham she felt 1 how much hauDier from

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.p: thi -c73iitritTA —6l her previous wretchedifelii3 T tiT suddenly freed from want, toil, fear, and all the evils of destitute orphanage, and to find herself blest with wealth, leisure, and safety, under the care of a rich, good, and kind father ! (for such Capitola continued to believe her guardian to be). It was an incredible thing! It was like a fairy tale ! Something of what was passing in her mind was perceived by Old Hurricane, who frequently burst into uproarious fits of laughter, as he watched her. At last, when the dinner and dessert were re- moved, and the nuts, raisins, and wine placed upon the table, and the waiters had retired from the room and left them alone, sitting one on each side of the fire, with the table and its luxuries between them, Major Warfield suddenly looked up and asked:
" Capitola, whom do you think that I am !" "Old Hurricane, to be sure ! I knew you from Granny's description, the moment you broke out so in the police office," answered Cap.
" Humph ! yes, you're right ; and it was your granny that bequeathed you to me, Capitola." "Then she is really dead ?"
"Yes. There—dOn't cry about her. She was very old, and she died happy. Now, Capitola, if you please me, I mean to adopt you as my own daughter." "Yes father." , .
" No, no—you needn't call me father, you know, because it isn't true. Call me uncle I uncle uncle "

"Is that true, sir ?" asked Cap. demurely. "No, no, no; but it will do! it will do! Now, Cap. how much do you know anything? Ignorant as a horse, I am afraid." "Yes sir, even as a colt." "Can you read at all ?" "Yes, sir. I learned at the Sunday-school" "Cast accounts and write ?" "I can keep your books at a pitch, sir." " Humph ! who taught you these accomplish- ments ?" •

" Herbert Greyson, sir." "Herbert Greyson! I've heard that name before! here it is again. Who is that Herbert Greyson ?" "He's second mate on the Susan, sir, that is expected in every day." " Urnph ! Umph I—take a glass of wine, Capi- tola ?"
_ "No, sir; I never touch a single drop." " Why ? why? good wine after dinner, my child, is a good thing, let me tell you."

" Ah, sir, my life has shown me too much misery that has come of drinking wine." "Well, well, as you please. Why, where has the girl run off to ?" exclaimed the old man, break- ing off, and looking with amazement at Capitols, who had suddenly started up and rushed out of the MOM.
In an instant she rushed in again, exclaiming: •" Oh he's come! he's come I I heard his voice !" . . _ _
"Who's come, you madcap?" inquired the old man.

"Oh, Herbert Greyson ! Herbert Greyson ! His ship is in, and he has come here! he always comes here—most of the sea-officers do !" exclaimed Cap, dancing around until all her black ringlets flew up and down. Then suddenly pausing, she came quietly to his side, and said, solemnly : " Uncle ! Herbert has been at sea three years ! he knows nothing of my past misery and destitu- tion, nor of my ever wearing boy's clothes. Uncle, please don't tell him, especially of the boy's clothes 1" And in the earnestness of her appeal, Capitola clasped her hands and raised her eyes to the old man's face. How soft those grey eyes looked when praying! but for all that, the very spirit of mischief still lurked about the corners of the plump, arch lips. "Of course I shall tell no one. I am not so proud of your masquerading as to publish it. And as for this young fellow, I shall probably never see him 1" exclaimed Old Hurricane.
CHAPTER VIII. HERBERT GREYSON. "A kind, true heart, a spirit high, That cannot fear and will not bow, Is flashing in his manly eye And stamped upon his brow."
-HALLAVN.

In a few minutes Capitola came bounaii;i-iii.The stairs again, exclaiming joyously— " Here he is uncle ! here is Herbert Greyson ! Come along Herbert! You must come in and see my new uncle ! " And she broke into the room, dragging before her astonished guardian a hand- some, dark-eyed young sailor, who bowed, and then stood blushing at his enforced intrusion. "I beg your pardon, sir," he said, "for bursting in upon you in this way; but—" "I dragged him here willy-nilly," said Capitols. "Still, if I had had time to think, I should not have intruded."

"Oh, say no more, sir! You are heartily welcome ! " exclaimed the old man, thrusting out his rugged hand and seizing the bronzed one of the youth. "Sit down, sir—sit down ! Good Lord, how like!" he added, mentally. Then, seeing the young sailor still standing blushing and hesitating, he struck his cane upon the floor and roared out:

" DEMMY, SIT DOWN, sm I When Ira Warfield says sit down, he MEANS Sit down !" "Ira Warfield !" exclaimed the young man, starting back in astonishment—one might almost say in consternation. "Aye, sir ! Ira Warfield ! that's my name ! Never heard any ill of it, did you?" The young man did not answer, but continued gazing in amazement upon the speaker. "Nor any good of it either, perhaps,—.eh, uncle ? " archly put in Capitola. " Silence, you monkey! Well, young man! well, what is the meaning of all this?" exclaimed Old Hurricane, impatiently. "Oh, your pardon, sir! this was sudden. But you must know I had once a relation of that name —an uncle."

"And have still, Herbert! and have still, lad ! Come, come, boy ! I am not sentimental, nor romantic, nor melo-dramatic, nor anything of that sort. I don't know how to strike an attitude and exclaim—' Come to my bosom, sole remaining off- spring of a dear, departed sister,' or any of the like stage-playing. But I tell you, lad, that I like your looks; and I like what I have heard of you from this girl and another old woman, now dead; and so —but sit down, sit down demmy, SIR, SIT DOWN, and we'll talk over the walnuts and the wine! Capitols' take your seat, too !" ordered the old ' man ' throwing himself into his chair. Herbert also drew his chair up. Capitola resumed her seat, saying to herself, "Well, well, I am determined not to be surprised at anything that happens, being perfectly clear in my own mind that this is all nothing but a dream. But how pleasant it is to dream that I have found a rich uncle and he has found a nephew, and that nephew is Herbert Greyson ! I do believe that I had rather die in my sleep than wake from this dream I" "Herbert !" said Old Hurricane, as soon as they had gathered around the table, "Herbert, this is my ward, Miss Black, the daughter of a deceased friend. Capitola, this is the only son of my de- parted sister." " Hem-m•m ! we have had the pleasure of being acquainted with each other before ! " said Cap, pinching up her lips, and looking demure. "But not of really knowing who each other' was, you monkey! Herbert, fill your glass! Here's to our better acquaintance !" "I thank you, sir. I never touch wine," said the young man. "'Never touch wine ! ' here's another I here's a young prig! I don't believe you ! yes, r do too! Demmy, sir,—if you never touch wine it's because you prefer brandy !--Waiter !" "I thank you, sir. Order no brandy for me. If I never use intoxicating liquors, it is because Igaye a promise to that effect to my dying mother!" Say no more—say no more, lad! Drink water, if you like. It won't hurt you " exclaimed the old man, filling and quaffing a glass of champagne. Then he said : "I quarrelled with your mothor, Herbert, for marrying a man that I hated—yes, hated, Herbert ! for he differed with me about the tariff and—the Trinity! Oh, how I hated him, boy, until he died! and then I wondered in my soul, as I wonder even now, how I ever could have been so infuriated against a poor fellow now cold in his grave—as I shall be in time ! I wrote to my sister, and expressed my feelings; but somehow or other, Herbert, we never came to a right understanding again. She answered my letter affectionately enough, but she refused to accept a home for herself and child under my roof, saying that she thanked me for my offer, but that the house which had been closed against her husband ought never to become the refuge of his widow. After that we never corresponded, and I have no doubt, Herbert, that she, naturally enough taught you to dislike me." " Not so, sir! Indeed, you wrong her I She might have been loyal to my father's memory without being resentful towards you. She said that you had a noble nature, but it was often obscured by violent passions. On her deathbed she bade me, should I ever meet you, to say that she repented her refusal of your offered kindness."

-"" And consented that it should be transferred to her orphan boy ? " added Old Hurricane, with the tears like rain-drops in his stormy eyes. "No, sir, she said not so." "But yet she would not have disapproved a service offered to her son."
"Uncle—since you permit me to call you so—l want nothing. I have a good berth in the Susan and a kind friend in her captain." "You have all your dear mother's pride, Herbert."

"And all his uncle's," put in Cap. "hush, magpie! But is the merchant service agreeable to you, Herbert?" "Not perfectly, sir ; but one must be content." " Demmy, sir, my sister's son need not be content unless he has a mind to ! And if you prefer the navy " "No, sir. I like the navy even less than the merchant service."
"Then what would suit you, lad? Come you have betrayed the fact that you are not altogether satisfied."
"On the contrary, sir, I told you distinctly that I really wanted nothing, and that I must be satisfied.'

"And I say demmy, sir, you shan't be satisfied, unless you like to! Come, if you don't like the navy, what do you say to. the army, eh ?" " It is a proud, aspiring profession, sir," said the young man, as his face lighted up with enthusiasm. "Then, demmy, if you like the army, sir, you shall enter it. Yes, sir. Demmy, the administra- tion, confound them, has not done me justice, but they'll scarcely dare to refuse to send my nephew to West Point, when I demand it."

" To West Point 1" exclaimed Herbert in delight. "Aye, youngster, to West Point. I shall see to it, when I pass through Washington on our way to Virginia. We start on the early train to-morrow morning. In the meantime, young man, you take leave of your captain, pack up your traps and join s. You muai go with me, and make Hurricane Hall your home until you go to West Point." ." Oh, what a capital old governor our uncle is I" exclaimed Cap, jumping up and clapping her hands.

"Sir, indeed you overwhelm me with this most unexpected kindness. Ido not know as yet how much of it I ought to accept. But accident will make me, whether r no, your travelling companion for a great part of the way, as I also start for Virginia to-morrow, to visit dear friends there whose house was my mother's home and mine, and who, since my bereavement, have been to me like a dear mother and brother. I have not seen them for years and before I go any where else, even to your kind roof, I must go there!" said Herbert gravely. "And who are those dear friends of yours, Her- bert, and where do they live? If I can serve them, they shall be rewarded for their kindness unto you, my boy." "o:, sir, yes, yes! you can indeed serve them! They ere a poor widow and her only son! She has seen bettor days; but now takes in sewing to support herself and boy. When ray mother was living, during the last years of her life, when she also was a poor widow with an only son, they joined their slender means, and took a house and lived together. When my mother died leaving me a boy of ten years old, this poor woman still sheltered and worked for me as for her own son, until ashamed of being a burden to her, I ran away and went to sea " .._ . _
"Noble woman I I will make her fortune I" ex- claimed Old Hurricane, jumping up and walking up and down the floor.

" Oh, do, sir! 06, do dear uncle. I don't wish you to expend either money or influence upon my fortunes • but oh I do educate Traverse! he is such a gifted ad—so intelligent! even his Sunday school teacher says that he is sure to work his way to distinction, although now he is altogether depen- dent on his Sunday school for his learning. Oh, sir, if you would only educate the son he'd make a for- tune for his mother!"

"Generous boy, to plead for your friends rather than for yourself I But lam strong enough, thank God, to help you all I You shall go to West Point. Your young friend shall go to school, and then te college," said Old Hurricane, with a burst of honest enthusiasm.
"And where shall I go, sir ?"inquired Cap,

„ "To the lunatic asylum, you imp ” exclaimed the old man; then turning to Herbert, he continued: "Yes, lad, I will do as I say; as for the poor but noble-hearted widow—" "You'll marry her yourself, as a reward, won't you, uncle?" asked the incorrigible Cap. . . . .

"Perhaps I will, you monkei, if it is Only to bring somebody home to keep you in order ! " said Old Hurricane; then turning again to Herbert, be resumed: "As to the widow, Herbert, I will place her above want."
"Over my head," cried Cap. "And now, Herbert, will trouble you to ring for coffee, and after we have had that, I think that we had better separate, and prepare for our journey to-morrow."
Herbert obeyed, and after the requried refresh- ment had been served and partaken of, the little circle broke up for the evening, and soon after re- tired to rest.

Early the next morning, after a hasty breakfast, the three took their seats in the express train for Washington, where they arrived upon the evening of the same day. They put up for the night at Brown's, and the next day Major Warfield, leaving his party at their hotel, called upon the President, the Secretary of War, and other high official digni- taries.

The same evening, wishing to avoid the stage route over the mountains, he took with his party the night boat for Richmond, where in due time they arrived, and whence they took the valley line of coaches that passed through Tip-Top, which they reached upon the morning of the fourth day of their long journey. Here they found Major War- field's carriage waiting for him, and here they were to separate—Major Warfield and Capitols to turn off to Hurricane Hall, and Herbert Greyson to keep on the route to the town of Staunton. It was as the three sat in the parlour of the little kotel, where the stage stopped to change horses, their adieus were made. "Remember, Herbert. that I am willing to go to the utmost extent of my power to benefit the good widow and her son, who were so kind to my nephew in his need. Remember that I hold it a sacred debt that I owe them. Tell them so. And mind, Herbert, I shall expect you back in a week at farthest." "I shall be punctual, sir I God bless you, my dear uncle! you have made me very happy in being the bearer of such tidings to the widow and the fatherless. And now I hear the horn blowing— Good-bye, uncle Good-bye, Capitols. lam going to carry them great joy, such great joy, uncle, as you who have everything you want, can scarcely imagine." And, shaking hands heartily with his companion, HPrbert ran through the door, and jumped aboard the coach just as the impatient driver was about to leave him behind.

As soon as the coach had rolled out of sight Major Warneld handed Capitols into hi carriage that had long been waiting, and took the seat by her side— much to the scandallsation of Wool, who muttered to his horses
"There, I told you so! I said how he'd go and bring horse a young wife, and behold he's gone and done it?"

---- -- - "Uncle 1" said Capitola, as the carriage rolled lazily along—" Uncle! do you know you never once asked Herbert the name of the widow you are going to befriend, and that he never told you I" "By George 1 that is true! how strange I yet I did not seem to miss the name. How did it ever happen. Capitola 7 did he omit it on purpose, do you think 9" ' _ _

"Why, no, uncle! he, boy-like, always spoke of them as Traverse' or 'Traverse's mother'; and you like yourself, called her nothing but the 'poor widow,' and the 'struggling mother,' and the 'noble woman,' and so on; and her son, as the 'boy the 'youth,' young Traverse,' Herbert's 'friend,' &c. for my part, had some curiosity to see whether you and Herbert would go on talking of them forever, without having to use their surnames. And behold he even went off without naming them. . "By George 1 and so he did. It was the strangest oversight. But I'll write as soon as I get home and ask him." "No, uncle, just for the fan of the thing, wait until be comes back and see how long it will be and how much he will talk of them without mentioning their names."

"ha! ha! ha I so I will, Cap! so I vril. Besides, whatever their name are, it's nothing to me. 'A rose by any other name would smell as sweet,' you know. And if she is • Mrs. Tagfoot Waddle,' I shall still thin& so good a woman exalted as a Mont- morencie I—Mind there, Wool! This road is getting rough 1" "Over it now, Marster l" said Wool, after a few heavy jolts—" Over it now, Missus I and de rest of de way is perfectly delightful." Cap looked out of the window, and saw before her a beautiful piece of scenery—first, just below them, the wild mountain stream of the Demon's Run, and beyond it the wild dell dented into the side of the mountain, like the deep print of an enormous horse's hoof, in the midst of which gleam- ing redly among its richly-tinted autumn woods. stood Hurricane Hall. (To be continued ).

div.head: WARRINGTON ToWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON ToWN COUNCIL.
ELECTION OF MAYOR.

The annual meeting of the Warrington Town Coun- cil was held at the Tows H4ll on Saturd Lv at noon, for the purpose of electing the MArcr, five Aldermen, and committees for the ensuing year. There was a good at- tendance of the public, and Members of the Council.

, The following members were present : Aldermen Harrison, Sutton, Francomb, Wright, 131 ickhurst, Bol- ton, Greenall and Hutchinson, Councillors Roberts, Heaton, Shaw-Green,Garner,Cannell, Fairclough,Plump- ton, Smethurst, Shaw, Bennett, Shilcock, Skelton,Long- ton, Baird, Woods, Lee, Furness, Monks, Duncan, Elli- son, Tinnion, Rogers, Evans, also Mr. J. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Stanley Wilson (deputy town clerk), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer),and T. Longdin (borough surveyor). The Deputy Mayor was elected to the chair pro tent.

div.head: ELECTION OF MAYOR.
div.p: ELECTION OF MAYOR.

Alderman HARRISON, in proposing the re-t lection of Councilor Fairclotwh, said that to be the leading man, and the most popular man in a community consisting of 50,000 persons was undoubtedly a great achievement, hut to be invited to take office a second time almost by the voice of popular will, was really a great honour. l'hat honour they were very anxious to confer upon Mr. Fairclough, their present Mayor. They had had of the Mayor a pleasant experience ext-encling over the whole time he had been the Mayor. (Applauae.) While he had not neglected the suaritee in modo, he had not neglected the fortitu in re (Hear, hear.) When it was neCeSmary for him to put his foot down,he had always done so firmly, steadily, and without any hesitation whatever. They had tasted of his qualitis,t, and they rather liked the brancl,hecause it gave promise of future exertions,and future industry. They had not the slightest doubt that as the Mayor had dene well in the past, he would do as well in the future. It was not necessary to say very much about him because they knew him so well, and their experience of him way so late. He (Alderman Harrison) was satisfied that if they appointed Councillor Fairclough to the honourable posi- tion ot Mayor of Warrington,they would certainly not be disgraced nor have any cause to regret it. HP had therefore very great pleasure in moving that Councillor James Fairclough be and was thereby appointed Mayor of Warrington for the ensuing year. (Applatiste.) Alderman BLACKHORST seconded the proposition. He said that he did so with the greatest of satisfactian, be- cause they knew ow well the Mayor had acted during the past year. It was absolutely necessary that they should have a gentleman at the head of affairs who had a strong will and who could carry the hip.iness through the Council with firmness. He had no doubt that as they had had a pleasant experience of the Mayor in the past year, they would have an equally pleasant year during his second term of Office. (Applause.) Alderman SUTTON supported the resolution. He said that last year he proposed the election ,tf Councillor Fairclough as Mayor, and at that time ventured to pre- dict that the Mayor would fill the office with credit te himself and to the satisfaction of the town and the whole town at large. He had no hesitation in saying that that prediction had been carried out to the fullest extent. (Applause.) The Mayor during the past year had filled the office with dignity, and his conduct had in every manner been exemplary. His impartiality- had been all that could he desired, and his generosity he could say had almost been unnre- cedented. If anyone should have any dnuht upon that, he would simply refer him to the fact that the whole of the members of the Council had unanimously re- quested the Mayor to allow himself to be re-elected far another year. He was quite sure that his conduct in the past would be continued in the future and that they would be perfectly satisfied in every respect, if they re- elected him for another year. Councillor ROBERTS said that speaking in a repre- sentative capacity on behalf of the Liberal member. of the Council, he also supported the appointment of Mr. Fairclough as Mayor for the second year. He agreed with every word that had been uttered with regard to the manner in which the Mayor had conducted the busi- ness of the Council last year. Alderman Harrison had referred to the firm will of the Mayor ac d that he had occasionally put his foot down strongly when it was necessary to do en. He thought that he had nut both hia feet down. (Laughter.) The qualities of the Mayor marked him out as one eminently fitted few the Position he had held. As far as the Liberal members of the Coun- cil were concerned, they would afford the Mayor all the assistance they could. (Applause ) Alderman Graenall also added his testimerm to the way in which the Mayor had carried out his dutiom during the past year. The MATOR upon entering the room, said that he had to return his sincere thanks for electing him Mayor. He did not however know whether they were sincere, fer he had been thinking that he should have to thank them for their kindness to him in the past year, and he was going to bid them all farewell. He however felt it a great honour to be elected Mayor for the aecond time, and it showed that the Council anpreniated the manner in which he had fulfilled the office of Mayor. (Hear, hear.) He hoped and trusted that the coming year might be as pleasant and agreeable to him as the pant had been—(applause)—and he appealed to all to assist Mm in conducting the latisinenS in that chamber in a Proper and orderly manner, and to work for the hest interests of the town. (Anplautte.) He asked them all to get with him to church the next day as it was cus- tomary to do.

div.head: FISHING BY ELECTRIC LIGHT.
div.p: FISHING BY ELECTRIC LIGHT.

On Saturday night two' anglers, one a resident of Newhaven, tried the interesting experiment of fishing in Seaford Bay by electric light. A fisherman in New- haven rowed the anglers from the Railway Pier soon after FiX o'clock, when it was completely dark. A port- able battery with a five-candle electric lamp was taken, and this lamp was lowered until a weight below it touched the bottom at 25 feet. Both battery and lamp were specially made for the trial, and the lamp was pro- tected by a galvanised crinoline and was made water tight. When the lamp reached the bottom of the sea there was a circular area, twenty yards in diameter. brightly illuminated right up to the surface. Fishing was carried on with an ordinary line on the port side, the lamp having been lowered on the starboard side of the host. A successful result followed the experiment, and a splendid dish of whiting was caught. STOKING BY MACHINERY.

At all large gas works, stoking by machinery pro- MiSPS to replace hand labour. There has just been in- troduced into the Edinburgh Corporation Gasworks at New Street a series of hydraulic stoking machines, which, to a large extent, have superseded the arduous and fatiguing manual labour associated with the hand- feeding and drawing of retorts. The installation con- sists of four eillrizirw and four drawing marhines,which travel on rails in front of the retort along the entire length of the retort-house, and which are capable of dealing with 40 retorts per hour. The machines. which are of a most serviceabls nature, are of the kind patented by Sir William Arm' and Mr. Foulis, engineer to the Glasgow Gas Corporation. The saving to be de- rived from the introduction of this machinery is esti- mated at about is. per ton of coal carbenised. The total cost of the new plant will be a little over £7,000.

TU hI
PRESS DINNER AT THE TOWN lIALL.

The members of the rress in Warrington were entertained to Dinner by the Mayor (Coon- oillor Pairclough), at the Mayor's Parlour of the Town [fall, on Wednesday even- ing. The journalis,,s present were : —Messrs Sansornts, J. Lawt )n. El. Sansome, and 'P rye ("Guardian "); 11. Isherwood and C. Gill (" Observer ") ; T. Ward, J. Blithe and PI V. Walker (" Examiner") ; C. Lyon and J. Cross (" Echo ") ; and J. J. Dean (" Express" ). There were also present in addition to the Mayor, the Tpwri Clerk, and some other officials of the Corpor- atlon, together with a few friends. An excellent, menu had been provided and after the dinner had been partaken of, the proceedings were of an unformal character. The usual toast of "The Queen " was proposed by the Mayor and duly honoured Mr. S Insome proposed the health of the Mayor, and referred to the consideration which his Worship had always shown towards the Press of Warrington. He also thanked the Mayor for his kindness in inviting them to that dinner. The toast was drunk with musicial honours. The Mayor raplied and expressed his pleasure at meet- ing the representatives of the various newspapers in the town at that dinner. He also thanked them for the faithful reports he always had from them. The toast of " The rross " was proposed by the Town Clerk, who coupled with it the names of Mr. Ward and Mr. Lawton. He said that the members of the press in Warrington were always fair in their dealings with public matters, and he spoke in eulogistic terms of the power and responsi- bility of the journalistic profession. In reply to the toast,M.r. Ward thanked Mr. Whittle for the compli- mentary language in which be had proposed the toast. The Town Clerk was, he said, a friend to the Press of the town and had always treated its repre- sentatives with the utmost courtesy. Mr. Lawton endorsed all that Mr. Ward bad said. The Town Clerk was also cordially " toasted " on the propou- tion of Mr. H. Isherwood who added his testimony to that of the previous speakers as to the uniform courtesy displayed by Mr. Whittle to the Press. The Town Clerk in reply said that he felt it to be a great honour to be the Town Clerk of his native place. He had not, he said, been without induce- ments to go el ,ewhere, but he would rather he Town Clerk of Warrington than for any other town. klr. C. Lyon proposed a toast iu honour of Mr. S'anley Wilson, the deputy town clerk, and expressed the hope that Mr. Wilson's career would be a successful one. Previous to the toast being drunk, the Town Clerk expressed his thanks to Mr. Wilson for the great assistance he had ever been to him. He also joined Mr. Lyon in his good wishes 1 tor the future. Mr. Wilson, inreply, thanked those present for the toast, and said that he wished to express his thankfulness to the Press for the great assistance it had rendered him at all times, and particularly at the time when he was the secretary of the relief committee during the coal dispute. It had always been willing to bring matters prominently before the public, and thus aid materially the distress fund.—The intervals between the toasts were spent in a social manner, and the proceedings were much enjoyed. Several members of the company gave songs, and Mr. Haynes also gave a number of his well known humorous songs, being accompanied by Mr. W. H. Payton. Previous to the party breaking Up, "Auld lang sync" was sung, and the proceedings terminated at about eleven o'clock.

div.head: NEW FURNISHING ESTABLISHMENT IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: A NEW FURNISHING ESTABLISHMENT IN WARRINGTON.
A furnishing establishment was opened last Friday, in the shen formerly occupied by Mr. Healreth, decorator, Scn„ Sankev-at. The company bears the name of flea-

. _ keth and Dutton, the former being the previous sole occupant of the premises, and the latter the head of the well-known drapery firm also in Sankey-at. Extensive alterations have been made to the shop, both in the upper storeys and the basement, the work having occu- pied about six months. There are three storeys, and also an extensive apartment below the ground floor. ample room being thus afforded for a large stock of excellent and tasteful middle-class furniture. The rooms are also well lighted and ventilated. The shop and works of Mr. Brown, near Lymm Cross have also been taken over by the establishment. Works far the manufecture of furniture have also been opened in King-street, Warrington. The shop, was visited by a large number of persons yester- day, and everyone expressed their admiration at the manner in which the various pieces of furniture had set out. A very large stock of splendid furniture had been set out, and the appearance of the rooms was further enhanced by a choice collection of chrysanthe- mums and coloured lamps which had been set about the room. Afternoon tea was provided for the visitors, of whom there were a large number during the after- noon, Mrs. J. W. Hayward being the caterer.

div.head: LORD DUNRAVEN AND THE
div.p: LORD DUNRAVEN AND THE
AMERICAN CUT.

Lord Dunraven has issued in pamphlet form Ft state ment concerning the American Cuo races, in which he deals very fully with the question of measurement, the " blanketing "of the ychts during thn first two races, the protest which he subsequently felt it neeessary to make, the foul that occurred at the outset of the second race, and other matters that have been in controversy. In conclusion, Lord Dunraven discussess the merits .f the two yachts, and records his opinion that Defender is the better on a reach and Valkyri in turning to wind- ward, while he has no doubt tha: Valkyrie is the better on a run. A Reuter's telegram from New York says— Additional evidence was given to-day of the widesnread indignation aroused by Lord Dunravea's statement re- garding the American Cup, especially on the New York Stock Exchange. On entering the Exchange Mr. Smith, chairman of the Cup Committee, received a great ovation, groans being also raised for Lord Dunraven. It is demanded on all sides that Lord Dunraven should be expelled from the New York Club, of which be is an honorary member.

WARRINGTON CRICKET AND
BOWLING CLUB.
ANNUAL DINNER.

The annual dinner of the members of the Warrington Cricket,Bowli rig, and Association Football Club was held on Saturday night at the Patten Arms Hotel. There was a large number of members present, including the Presi- dent, Mr. Thomas Morris, F.G.S. ; Mr. Robert Pierpoint- the Parliamentary representative of the borough ; Coun, cillors William Pierpoint, and D. Tinnion ; Messrs. tins- worth, A Browne, Rewson, R. T. Fairclough, William Gill, William Richardson, W. H. J. Jenkins. J. Lyon Whiffle, J. Pilling, Dr. Reginald Smith, Dunn,S.Kenyon, Ferguson, Gilbert, Grainger,C. Leigh, Voisey, J.Strange, J. Cooper. C. Plinston, J. Brundrit, Kiernan, J. Callon, Worthington, John Dewburst, H. Bolton, Robinson, W. H. Podmore, Silcock, C. J. Price, Am. The PRESIDENT submitted the toasts of "The Queen' and " The Prince and Princess of Wales," bath of which were heartily drunk with musical honours. Mr. Uriswonrn, hon. secretary, announced having re- ceived letters of apology from his Worship the Mayor (Councillor James Fairclough), Mr. J. Charlton Parr,and other prominent members. Mr. WORTHINGTON proposed "The Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," saying that he was pleased to do so as an old Volunteer who had taken the oath of allegiance 20 years ago. He coupled with the toast the name of Mr. Henry Bolton. (Applause.) Mr. HENRY Bourmr, in response, said he had had the good fortune to belong for ten years to the smartest corps of volunteers in the metropolis,and had had many opportunities of observing the state of the army. He considered it to be in a frightful state in consequence of the short service system. It was composed almost entirely of lads, who would be totally unequal to a heavy day's march. He, therefore, thanked God that they had some smart volunteers in the country—(cheers) —men who when called upon would form a strong fight- ing line. Mr. Wittiest PIERPOINT rose and humorously ob- served that he fully appreciated the warmth of their re- ception but which he knew was,of course, meant for his distinguished cousin (Mr. Robert Pierpoint, M P.) He thought their friend Mr. R. T. Fairclough should have known better than to have applied the term " Mr. Pier- point "to him whilst their member was present. He certainly had the title to " Mr. Pierpoint that night. (Laughter.) The toast he had to propose was the health of their Presideat—(Applause)—who of all the members of the club had had the greatest claim upon their con- sideration and respect. The toast was heartily pledged amid the singing of " For he's a jolly good fellow." The CHAIRMAN, in responding, said it was always pleasing te be spoken well of, even by one gentleman, but when his words were appr4ciated by forty or fifty other gentlemen it was doubly pleasing. He felt ex- ceedingly proud of being the president of their club that night. He thanked them for .naviug so kindly received the toast. .

Mr. ROBERT PIERPOINT, M.P., who was received with loud cheering, said that the toast which he had the honour of proposing was a very important one. It was "Success to the Warrington Cricket, Bowling, and Association Football Club." (Applause.) In neither of these branches of sport was he in the least proficient, only having done very little cricketing when a bey, and still less bowling,. As to football,he claimed no practical knowledge of it, never having played it. When a boy he had delighted in rowing, and this he was still fond of, though he must admit that he had no very great desire to skim along the lucid and sparkling waters of Warrington—(laughter)—nor to try his luck upon the Manchester Ship Canal. (Renewed laughter.) He had read in the werks of Shakespeare that the quality of mercy (Mersey) was not strained. (Liughter.) He was afraid if it was strained in War- rington, there would be a great deal left in the strainer. (Laughter.) He hoped that the club, which had existed for so many years in Warrington, would continue to prosper through many more years, and that all good would come from the association over which Mr. Morris so worthily rresicled. (Cheers.) Mr. R. T. FArricLonox,in responding,said their cricket ground was one of the pleasantest places in Warrington. There no politics entered. Liberals mixed and chatted with Tories, and all enjoyed themselves. (Applauie.) With respect to howls they had enjoyed themselves amazingly ; whilst in football they had done faidy well' lie hoped that in this branch they would next season do better.

The PRESIDENT toasted the "Health of the member for Warrington" amid general cheering. When Mr. Pier- point was in the Rouse of Commons during the progress of Parliamentary business he was always pleased to see anyone from Warrington if he sent in his card to him. Although he had the greatest respect for Mr. Pierpoint, yet he could not saytbat he hoped he would always be the Parliamentary representative et Warrington. (Laugh- ter.) If he said that everyone would say that he (Mr. Morris) was a fraud. (Renewed laughter.) However, he was sure everyone would heartily j-in with him in drinking the toast he had submitted.. (Applause). _ _ _ _

Mr. irgarmarrr,tn -acknowledging the President's com- pliment, expressed sincere thanks. The Chairman and himself had done some good work on committees togs- thet, and he valued Mr. Morris highly as a personal friend. (Applause.) As to his ever being ready to re- ceive with courtesy and pleasure anyone coming from Warringtm on a visit to the House of Commons, that was quite true,for he always remembered that although elected by the majority of one political party, yet he was, when elected, the representative of the whole borough. (Loud applause.) Flo quite understood the reserve with which their President spoke of the future— (laughter)—but he hoped that whatever the future brought forth for him (the speaker) it would not deprive him of the kind and courteous treatment of which he had spoken. (Loud applause.)

Mr. KIERNAN submitted the toast of "Health to the club's officials," and spoke at length of their able quali- ties. A club with such officials could not but succeed, there was no belp for it, and they,therefore,were worthy of all honour. (Applause.) The toast was responded to by Mr. Unsworth (bon. secretary), Dr. R. Smith, Mr. George Pilling, and Mr. Dunn.

Mr. JENKINS proposed "The host and hostess," and referred to the excellent manner in which the members had always been treated by Mr. and Mrs. Kiernan. Mr. KIERNAN replied, saying that he should, in the future,continue to try to cater in the beat possible man- ner for the club.

The proceedings were brought to a close by a vote of thanks to the Chairman and the singing of "Auld Lang Syne "and the National Anthem. During the progress of the toast list a number of songs were sung by several of the members. notably by Mr. W. Whittle. who is better known as "the Lancashire Chevalier" by reason of his apt impersonation of the London coster.

div.head: HAPPY INDIANS.
div.p: HAPPY INDIANS.

The average citizen of the British Empire interests himself but little with the doings of his fellow subjects in so remote a corner of Her Majesty's dominions as the Far West of Canada. Yet the fact that in this distant region there are still remnants of the aboriginal red men, who once owned the land which is now the home of the white settlers, is not altogether devoid of i^terest. It is seldom that any news of the mode of life on the Indian reserves reaches us. The Canadians appear to take good care of their Indians, and the form of govern- ment is probably the most paternal administration in the world. The Indian territory is parcelled out among the various tribes, and here they hunt and feed their horses and herds of buffaloes with an entire absence of care which might almost make us envy their lot. Once a week, on production of the tribal ticket, each man is served with a ration of flour, tobacco and other neces- saries of life. And the wants of the outer man are supplied by a gift of a blanket every year. Children are taken fram their parents, and educated and boarded at the expense of the State. The red man's life seems to he a continual holiday. Christianity does not appear to be making much progress amongst these people. The latest accounts declare that the practice of polygamy is so deeply rooted as to form an inseparable barrier to the missionary.
