HOW I SENT THAT £lO. It was a gloomy, rainy day, in the winter of 1886' The wJiter was seated in his favourite easy-chair in his lodgings in Upper Bakar-st., London. A bright fire was burning in the grate and things around me were snug and comfortable. I was and still am a ba.zhelor with money enough to live on and more too, but not incl ned to spend it on any sort of foolishness. The night was closing in, dark and wretched ; yet the knowledge of it, with a plentiful hot dinner to come made me feel only more and more content. So I sat and sprawled and smoked my pipe. Ten minutes missed. Then I threw my ;pipe ;on tho shelf, went to my desk, and wrote this letter. "My Dear Old Friend,—l send pus £lO as a loan. If you can ever ay it—why,all right. If not, don't worry over it. Yours, Sm." Enclosing the money I backed the envelope to a name and address in Edinburgh, and then went out in the torm and posted it myself. Non for the wonder ! I had sent t hat money to a man whom I had neither seen nor heard of for twenty years a man who was prosper- ous when I parted from him, and of whose whereabouts Iliad no more idea than you ha re. Now for a greater wonder! In forty-eight hours I received a letter from him, dated at that very spot,full of athetic gratita le swing I had saved him and his family from thc pangs of hunger and cold. Hypnotism ? Mesmerism ? Second sight ? Account for it as yor may ; it is God's own truth. Blind fools t tat we are ! Who knows the ways of Providence ? In the winter of 1890-91, Mr. Henry Fish, of West Malvern, was so ill that it was not expected he would last more than a few days longer. For over a month ha had not got no sleep whatever, except when supported in an upright position on his crutch. He could not even lift his hand to his mouth, and had to be nursed night and day. One doctor said he had heart disease, and that hip heart was big as a bullock's. An- other doctor told him that it made him worse to take any nourishment, and the less he ate the longer he would live. He sank lower and lower, until people marvelled that death delayed to come. Mr. Fish's illness began in the previous October, with symptoms which many will recognise, because they are so common. He had a bad taste in the mouth, a poor appetite, and pain in the chest and sides after eating. In his written statement he says: "I had a gnawing, sinking sensation in the stomach, pain and weight at the right side, and my eyes and skin were yellow as a guinea. Later on I had rheumatic gout in my feet, and erysipelas set in and spread all over my legs and feet. My legs became puffed and swollen to a dreadful site, I and were wrinkled as if a cord was tied tight around them. Then the pain struck to my heart, which thumped and palpitated all the time. My stomach was swelled to double its natural size, and although faint from want of food. I could only take slops, the pain after eating being more than I ceuld bear. I soon lost power to walk and had to hobble about on crutches Then I grew worse, and was delirious for days. Subse- quently I was unable to lie in bed, as I felt suffocated whenever my head touched a pillow." After this, followed the state of things first described. There seemed no prospect of recovery. The poison oft indigestion and dyspepsia (Mr. Fish's real ailment) had produced rheumatism, gout, and dropsy—the latter the immediate result of the stagnation of the liver and kid- neys. This might at any moment swamp the heart or nags and end in death, as sudden as by a rifle ball ,through the brain. Now for another strange thing. While in this condi- tion—with the shadows of death's dark night already falling around him—Mr. Fish one day received a com- munication recommending him to use a certain remedy he had not yet tried. There was nothing about this communication to show who wrote it or mailed it. But he gave heed and procured the medicine at once, and began taking it. What effect ib had we will leave him to tell.

He says: "Even in a few days I felt better. I had little appetite and digested light food. Then day by day the pains left me, the dropsy abated as the kidneys I acted, ani I began, as you may say, to back Keay from the side of the grave. I was so low it took a long time to get up my strength, but it returned at last, and I have ailed nothing since. When my friends asked what cured me, I answered,' Mother Seigel* Curative Syrup, the remedy urged upon me in the communication so un- expectedly received. It has saved my life, and I wan everybody to hear of it." Mr. Fish has been in the employ of a builder at Mal- vern for thirty years, and is a painter by trade. And to the facts of his remarkable case he made a solemn de- claration according to law, at Great Malvern, Worcester County, on the 12th of January, 1893, before Mr. Edward Nevinann, a Commissioner to administer Oath in the Supreme Court of Judicature in England.
Wonderful indeed are the mysterious powers which govern human affairs. - .. _
J. M. P.
London, January 17th, 1893.

div.head: "FAMOUS SCENES -IN THE BRITISH
div.p: "FAMOUS SCENES -IN THE BRITISH
PARLIAMENT."

LECTURE AT THE BOLD-STREET SCHOOLROOM. Mr. DENNISON W. ALLPORT, of London, delivered a lecture on Mondoy night, in the Bold-st. Schoolroom, upon "Famous Scenes in the British Parliament." The lecture was in connection with the Wesleyan Guild and there was a fairly large gathering of members and their friends, tho chair being filled by the Rev. G. D. Mason. The LEcTungft gave a most eloquent address, and by his fervour he quite carried his hearers away, and he was frequently interrupted by outbursts of applause. He commenced by referring to the order of precedence which the three great powers of the State • had occupied during the past four centuries. , Under the Plantagenets it had been Lords, King, and Commons; under the Tudors it was King. Lords and Commons ; hut in the hale of the great rebellion it was Commons, Lords and King. The times had verily changed since Henry VIII. practically ruled absolutely by torcing the passage of , Bills through the Houses under the threat of execution, as instanced in the case of Lord Montague. The Dower which the father possessed passed to the daughter,though in a slightly modified form ,f or the nation had been daily becoming more and more impatient of restraint during the reign of Henry VIII. Elitabeth kept a tolerably tight hold upon the "meddlesome Commans,"as she was wont to call them,and on one or twat occasions had ventured to I withhold her assent to Bills, having no other object in doing so than that of maintaining the full power of her prerogative. James I. well understood the growing power I of the Commons,and rarely called them together except when he required money, and whenever he did call them together he quarrelled with them. Under the Stuarts there were many struggles between the Crown and the people in the cause ef liberty, and one ot the most ill- ustrious statesmen in favour of the popular cause wa Sir John Eliot, who might he called the originator of one of the most exciting and extraordinary scenes eve r witnessed within the walls of Westminster. It was in March, 1629, during the reign of Charles 1., that the Commons first refused to obey the King's command. Sir John Eliot rose and attempted to address the Efouse,but the Speaker (Sir John Finch) jumped up and said it was , now time to adjourn. Sir John Eliot remained standing, and as the Speaker was about to vacate his seat he pro- duced a remonstrance addressed to the King against levying tonnage and poundage. He desired the Speaker to .read it, but he would not, saying, that he had the command of the King to adjourn the House. Not being able to get the clerk to read it. Sir John Eliot read the remonstrance himself, but the Speaker refused to put it to the vote, again saying that the Bing had commanded him to adjJurn. He then rose, and was about to leave the chair when two members, Hollis (son of the Esrl of Clare) and Valentine, who were on either side of him, forced him down into his seat. The Speaker trembled and hesitated, and Sir John Eliot then began to speak. The doors of the House were locked, so that no one from without could interrupt the proceedings. When Eliot had finished the Speaker was again requested to put the resolutions to the House. Again Sir John Fin:th tried to leave the chair, but was again prevented, being told that he should be made to sit there until it pleased the House to allow him to rise. He refused a second time to put the resolution, to the House, where- upon Hollis did so. Everything was now in an uproar, and the more timid members tried to leave, They were, however prevented. The Sergeant-at-Arms, who had been previously communicated with by the Ring, lifted the mace from the table, hut it was taken from him and returned to its place. Each resolution, as it was submitted,was confirmed by about 400 members, and as soon as this had been done the doors were opened and the members rushed out, passing •the guard of soldiers who had been sent by the King to quell the tumult. A week afterwards Sir John Eliot was a prisoner in the Tower. He was faithful till the last, and the doors that closed upon him never opened again while he lived. For the cause of liberty be had given his strength freedom, and life, and those who entered upon that splendid heritage should keep his memory ever green in their hearts. The lecturer afterwards gave a large num- ber of equally interesting passages in connection with the history of the British Parliament, and at the conclu- sion of the lecture the Rev. G. D. Mason, on behalf of the audience, tendered to Mr. Allport an expreseion of their appreciation.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Board , Guardians was held at the Workhouse on Wednesdae' morning. Mt. William Houghtoh presided, and there were also present the Revs. Father Moore, T. R. Matthews, J. H. Riddette, Messrs. S. Davies,G. Thomp- son, A. J. Jollev, J. Billinge, T. B. Malkin, W. Cross, A. Long, W. Hickman, J. Clarke, J. Houghton. G. Piling, j A. Jolley, T. Mather, J. Dignum, J. W. Knowles, J Ball, Dr. Patterson, J. Warburton, J. C. Sutton (clerk), C. H. Ward (master), H. M. Mines (superintendent). MOUSE COMMITTEE -INCREASE OF TEE CATEOLIC INSTRUCTOR'S SALARY.

The House Committee recommended that the salary of the Catholic Instructor (Father Ryan) be increased from £lO to £2O per annum. They also recommended that the usual Christmas dinner with beer be alio ed to the inmates.—Mr. CLARKE moved the adoption of the minutes.—Mr. A. J. JOLLEY seconded, and the motion was passed unanimously. THE COST OF THE WORKHOUSE AND PM:GATE SCHOOLS. In response to a request from Mr. THOMPSON, Mr. WARD said that the total cost of the workhouse was £4,614 2s. 7d., or an average of 4s. lid. per head per week. Mr. MINES said that the average cost at Padgate school was 6s. 61-d.per bead per week. This,he said, was much cheaper than at alarge number of Unions in various parts of the country.—Mr. THOMPSON said that he thought that the question he had asked was more with regard to the rations. He took it that the rations for nine officers amounted to £l7 15s. per head per week, while he found that at Padgate for twelve officers it amounted to £23 10a —Mr. MINES : There are seven, een.—Mr. THOMPSON : There are only twelve. He did not include the washerwoman. Be thought that they ought to take up some other place. Be thought that an increase of 10i per head over the Workhouse was too tauch and he objected strongly to it.—The CLERK said that therations for the officers at both schools were supposed to have the same dietary.—Mr. THOMPSON thought that the mat- ter ought to be gone into thoroughly, and he moved that the House and Schools Committee be armonited to inquire into it. With regard to the washerwomen. they paid Ea. per week to there, and it appeared that rations were also included. He thought that was excessive,and ' that some arrangement should be made whereby the washing should be done at the House or that same of the women be drifted to Padgate.—Mr. KtrowLas se- conded the motion, and he also thought that some different arrangement should be made with regard to the washing. AN UNADVERTISED 'TENDER. The Rev. J. H. RIDDETTE asked whether a tender of certain repairs in the schools at Padgate had been ad- vertised for. It appeared that only Mr. R. Heaton had been asked to offer any tender, it being, explained that the work required to be done at once and there was no time to advertise.—Mr. RIDDETTE tllol3illit that it was most unfair to other tradesmen. The subject alerwards dropped, it being shown that the committee were u nanimous in the matter. , THE PROPOSED NEW INVIE'v ART.

~„. The Infirmary Committee reported that tiny had ac- companied the Clerk to some land adjacent to the Workhouse of about five acres which would cost £4OO per acre. They recommended that the land be pur- chased.—The CLERK then gave a brief history of thr Workhouse. He said that the present buildings were built in 1851 upon seven acres of land which cost £1,050, and after several increases in the buildings, Padgate schools were erected in 1880-1-2. Owing to the great increase of the population, it was found necessary to further increase the buildings hence the present scheme of a new infirmary.—The CHAIRMAN moved, and Mr. PILLING seconded, the adoption of the recommendation. —Mr. HICKMAN said that he objected to the site, as there was a smallpox hospital on one side, a works on the other, and a railway on the other.—The CLERK said that there would have to be a special meeting of the Guardians before the matter could be settled, and after further discussion it was decided to adopt the recom- mendation, and also to endeavour to acquire possession of the late smallpox hospital in Dallam-Line.

div.head: APPLICATION. FOR INCREASE OF SALARY REFUSED.
div.p: APPLICATION. FOR INCREASE OF SALARY REFUSED.

The application for an increase of salary by Mr. T. G. Garnett, the relieving officer for No. 1 district, was then conaidered.—Mr. KNowLas- moved, and Mr. HICKMAN seconded, that the application be beard in open board, and Mr. RIDDRTTE moved, and Mr. LANG seconded an amendment, that the application be heard in committee.—The amendment was lost.—Mr. Davin paid a high tribute to Mr. Garnett as a relieving officer, and said that he was a very painstaking official and very in dto the poor whom he had to deal with. His work khad increased of late, but be could not see hie way to move for an increase from £l6O to £lB5, but instead would move that it be to £175, and he believed that Mr. Garnett was thoroughly deserving of it.—Mr. G. PIL- LING SOCOndPa the motion.—Mr. A. .1. JOLLEY while en- dorsing everything that was said about Mr. Garnett by Mr. Davies could not see his way to support the motion, and announced his intention of voting against it.—Mr. Davies after a little more discussion said that seeing that there was no chance of his motion being carried he would withdraw it. It was afterwards pointed out that in many places, relieving officers only received up to £l2O per annum.

div.head: PROPOSED MAXI-MUM SALARIES FOR OFFICIALS.
div.p: PROPOSED MAXI-MUM SALARIES FOR OFFICIALS.

Mr. LANG thought that maximum salaries ought tl be decided upon so that the offidials could know what they would receive. He thought that it put them in a false position when this was not the case. Maximum salaries were adopted at may places. They could not blame Mr. Garnett for his application that morning, and he hoped that his (Mr. Lang's) suggestion with regard to the salaries would be adopted.

div.head: WARRINGTON JUVENILE BURIAL
div.p: WARRINGTON JUVENILE BURIAL
SOCIETY BALL.

A tea party and ball was given by the Juvenile Burial Society in connection with the Grand United Order of Oddtellows, Warrington District, at the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-st., on Monday evening. Au excellent re. past was provided, several ladies kindly giving their services at the tables, amongst whom were Mesdames Clough, Roylance, Dutton, Tavlin, Savory, Hill, Clare, Daniels, Cross, Crozier, Taylor, and Miss Appleton. At the conclusion of the tea a short meeting was held, when the chair was occupied by Mr. Robert Savory. There ' were also on the platform—Messrs. Samuel Joynson (treasurer), William Speakman (district master), John Pownall (secretary), James Appleton, William Hill, and others. The principal event of the evening was the pre- sentation of a new banner to the Warrington District. The banner, which is a very beautiful o ,e, and bears the emblem of the society, with the words " We succour the widow and orphans," is made of patent woven silk, and was specially manufactured for the society by Mr. George Toothill, of City-road, London. At the request of the Chairman, Mr. Samuel Joynson, in making the presentation, observed that he might have been better prepared had he been made acquainted with the respon- sible duty which he had to perform. The banner was a very beautiful one, and he hoped all would be well sati-- fed with it. The committee had done their best to pro- cure a flee one, and they ought to thank them for their kindness.—Mr. William Speakman, in receiving the emblem, said he feV the high honour which had been done to the Warrington district by the Board of Direc- tors. On behalf of the Warrington district he tendered a hearty vote of thanks to them, and he hoped that that meeting would not be the last of its Pind. (Hear, hear.) The annual report and balance sheet were then reed, from which it appeared that there are 910 members con- nected with the seciety, which is doing a good work. The directors had much pleasure in issuing to the parents of members and t.,e public in general their annual statement of accounts, which showed a saving of £B7 13s. 4d. for the past year. Since the formation of the society it had paid 480 death claims and grants in various sums from 15a. to £lO, amounting to £1,489 lie. 61. The directors still continued to use their best endeavours to further, the interest of the society and members. (Applause.) A vote of thanks having been accorded to the Chairman, on the motion of Mr. John Powell, seconded hv Mr. James Appleton, this part of the proceedings terminated. Dancing was then commenced, Mr. Percy Randall' band being in atten- dance, and was continued until a late hour, when all dispersed declaring they had spent a very pleasant even- ing. The M.C's. were Messrs. J. Crannigan, R. Savory, and J. Appleton.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

Tin HILL CLIFFE AND STOCKTON HEATH UNITED BAND OF BOPS held its fortnightly meeting at th• Ehenez-r Chapel, on Monday night, when the Chapel was crowded. The Rev. J. S. Hughes occupied the chair. The Chairman gave an address on the week's encouraging features for temperance workers. The fol- lowing programme was given :—Recitation, " The rea- son why," M..ster Tom iirereton ; recitation, " The May Lilly," Miss Jesse E lison ; anthem, " Hear the Saviour's voice," choir ; recitation " Keeping his word," Miss Proud ; recitation," The Drink Pitria," Master G. div.head: MAYOR AND CORPORATION AT
div.p: THE MAYOR AND CORPORATION AT
CHURCH.

On Sunday morning the customary procession to church by the newly-elected Mayor, members of the Corporation, officials and others, took place. The weather was very showery, and cabs had been provided to take the nrocessionists to oh rob, but fortunately they were not required owing to a temporary stoppage of the rain. 'rho Mayor had on his right the member of the borough (Mr. Rohert Pierpoint) and on his left his chap- lain (The Rev. E. C. E Carleton) Then followed Alder- men Franeomb. Hutchinson and Wright, and Councillors Bard, Green, Elepherd, Shaw, Bennett, Evans, Smet- hurst. Furness, Tinnion, Rogers, Shißuick, Lee ; the Town Clerk (Mr. J L. Whittle), the Assistant Tows Clerk (Mr. Stanley Wdson), the Borough Treasurer (Mr. John Fairhurst), Assistant Borough Treasurer and Borougli eollector (Mr. W. 11. Woodcock), Borodgh Surveyor (Mr Longdin), Assistant Borough Surveyor (Mr. J. Sutcliffe). the Deputy Magistrstee Clerk (Mr. George F F. White), the Water En in.-er and the Man- ager of the Longford and intercepting der d's (Mr. Dean). the Curator, &c., of the Museum (Mr. Madeloy), Mr. Hunt (head constable), Dr. Starkey Smith (police surgeon),the Secretary of the Gas Works (Mr. F. Taylor), the Cashier (Mr. W. S Howard), the Cemetery Registrar- (Mr. R. Young) ; with Messrs Thomas Morris, J. W. Hayward. J.°., Alfred Jolley (Board of Guardians), Mr. Witliam Hickman (Board if Guardians), Lawless, H. Tuft and Critchley. The police and member,' of the Fire Brigade were also present,the fornaer under the direction of the Head Constable, and the latter under the direc- tion of Superintendent Turner. The procession was met at the church gates by Councillor Woods and Mr. R. T. Fairclough, who conducted the memb.!ra of the Corpora- tion to their coats. The prayers were read by the Rev. Canon Willis, and the lessons by the Rev. A. A. Mark- ham, while Mr. W. A. Woods presided at the organ. The preacher was the Rev. E. C. E. Carlton, who took for his text the words " 0 Daniel, a man greatly beloved.' The preacher said that Daniel's career was indeed a wonderful career, considering that he was a stranger and a captive. His strcesa was all'he more extraordin- ary as he was both courtier and favourite, the minister of five succeeding monarchs for 90 years—An instance of human prosperity to which history offered hardly a parallel. He was greatly beloved, and his heart was for the good of others. His heart was in the service that he gave his Sovereign, in the service he gave the State, and the service he gave his Ged. All might have their times of trial, when evil-dispomed and envious per- sons might plot for their destruction, as they did for Daniel's, as they had read in the chapter that morning ; but if they did not allow themselves to be turned aside from the line that conscience marked out for them, sooner or later their vindication would come, and God Himself would make their righteousness as clear an the light and their just dealings as the noon-day.. At the close of the service the precession wag re- formed, being joined by Ccuncillor Woods, Messrs. R. T. Fairclough, S. Davies. Arthur Browne, S. Wright, Dunn, and others. Arrived at the Town all light re- freshments were provided.

Such was the subject of a celebrated sermon preached in Manahester, but the more practical problem 01 the day is bow to rohke life worth living on earth. One of the important tri- butaries of the river of happiness is the possession of a com- fortable home. A home made bright and cheeriul not only by the kind and loving disp tsitions of those living there, but made attractive by the good taste displayed in the furnishing. Furnishing is a very important factor in the matter of con- tinued sell-satisfaction. So much jerry new London furniture is being now retailed by drapers that one needs to pause be- fore rushing impetuously into the first draper's because of a cheap red ticket. High-class makers, such as Lamb.Gillows, and Garnett,st ill exist, to whom the wealthy can still go with a long purse but to most people this would be a too expensive experiment. Again the average man nowadays has a strong liking for a bargain ; anything obtainable at about half or quarter the cost has a strong fascination f r him. Is it possi- ble to obtain such an advantage in furnishing? Yes, and more than possible, it is an absolute fact. We cannot do better than recommend a visit to MR. WOESLEY'S FUR- NISHING PANTHEON, GAYTHOUN, MANCHESTER.

THE Successful Establishment of any of the large ware- -1 houses of Manchester is always of interest to the citizens. One of the most brilliant examples of the valoe of perseverance, enterprise, and tart is the now busy hive of industry so well known a, The Pantheon, which occupies such a prominent position in fias thorn, near the C ntral Station, Manche.ter The bui .:iug is a massive pile of modern design, 150 feet long, six storeys high, with show- room accommodation covering an area of over one million square b-et. The plate-glass windows are each 12 feet square, each square if broken costing nearLy £3O to replace. len of the,e immense show windows form a portion ot the frontage. This will give a faint idea of The Pantheon" in outward appearance, but ah —here pen fails alt, gel her in attempting to do justice to anything like an adequate description of the interior. "The Pantheon" was sped i lly built to give the largest and most convenient floor space for showrooms, and cost £28,000, the floors specially constructed tocarry enormous weight. To-day it stands as one of the smartest furnishing houses in England, containing by far the largest and most comprehensive stock of any two houses in this large city. From basement to roof, from fluor toceiling, "The Pantheon" is tilled to overflowing with thousands of well bought, care- fully selected bargains, to attempt description of which would Le as futile as Liverpool attempting to crush

div.p: PRESS OPINIONS ABOUT
J. GERSHON,
THE UNIVERSAL FURNISHING ARCADE, 44, OLDHAM-STREET, IMANCFIESTER, (Next to the Alelphl Batik).
READ WHAT THEY SAY:-

- One of those modern monstre establishments, whose re- sources are so boundless, and whose stocks are so comprehen- sive, that it can, with equal care and despatch, furnish throughout a cottage or a mansion, is to be found in the famous house of J. GERSHON, furnishing contractor of 44, Oldharn-street, Mancheater. This colos.aal businesa was commenced in 1870. and being conducted with remarkable ability, energy, and foresight, and on sound commercial principles, It rapidly grew in public (avatar and patronage until at the preserr, time it is the largest and most represen- tative house of its kind in Manchester. Mr. Gershon at- tends to every customer personally, and does not leave cus- tomers in the hands of salesmen. Operations are carried on in a magnificent block of four-storey buildings, occupying a prominent and attractive position, and hiving a splendid frontage, They comprise shops, offices, and capacious show- rooms on the ground floor, and further suites or extensive ehowrooms on the first, second, and third lbors, together with showrooms at the rear of vast capacity, and filled to re- pletion with an immense collection of valuable goats. Mr. Gershon is a thorough exponent of the general house , furnishing, and stocks held are unrivalled in Manchester eitherin magnitude, variety, or worth ; if wide experience, and tar-seeing policy are absolutely requisite in proper selecting and getting together such a stupendous conglomer- ation of mi cellanems goods, it is equally true that a great aomunt of ability of leo common order is necessary to arrange and group them with such admirable effect, and to maintain at the same t ime such regard for the comfort and convenience of visitors Where every thing that can possibly be considerei to belong to this branch of business is folly represented, It is an endless task to attempt anything like an enumeration in detail, it will be sufficient to indicate the leading lines with whieh the house is occupied. Superb an I comprehen- sive stocks are held in Drawing. Dining, and Br akfast Room Sillies, made of all the best woods. artistically elegant in design, and magnificently and gorgeously upholstered in all materials of various colours, shades, and tints. Bedroom Suites made of the most dainty materials, and of the choicest patterns. And substantial, solid-looking Library, Stm4y, and Hall Furniture, together with inex- haustible supplies of splendid couches, ottomans, and so as, duchesse stands, aid eloo ,rds, book-cases,eheffoniers, cabinets, Davenports, easy, occasional, and other chairs dining tables, dressing, work, card 100, a d occasional tables. whatnots, overmantels, chests of drawers, as well as a large assortment , of bedsteads of every description, p ttern, size and price ; bedding, matt”esses, curtains, fenders, fireirons and carpets, rugs, and mats of every pattern and design, from all the most celebrated makers. Briefly, the stock embraces every article of whatever kind that can possibly be required in furnishing any or every kind of residence, from the cottage to the mansion of the noble; and not only is each in- dividul article to be found in these marvellous stores, but each article is represented by a large collection, often unique in its kind, anti including a wide selection in style, quality, and prices This enterprising firm have also manufacturing premises of considenble extent, and thoroughly equipped with plant and machinery of the newest and best kind and a large number of skilled workmen are constantly employed in the ma ufacture of cabinet work of all descriptions Repairs, too, are executed on the premises, a little army of assiatants is employed in the control of this stupendous establishment, and competent men are sent all over the kingdom to fit up private residences, hotels, offices, public buildings, and mansions, in conjunction wi h their business. The connection of ties representative house is tar-reaching and most valuable, its goods hive acquired the highest rep.- tation in Lancashire and the neighbouring counties, and the name of •• Gershon "Is an ample guarantee for everything th it is super or to his line of business. The proprietor is a man of extensive experience and d great and varied know- ledge in the various branches of the business in which he ,s engaged. Hi* able and energetic supervision is given to Ihe whole of the concern, and the utmost vigilance is used that nothmg shall emanate from his establishment which 'Mali tend ,o detract from the high and well-merited reputation the firm has achieved. Mr. Gershon is held in great eAeern lii private life for his ability, public spirit, and commercial integrity. We strongly advise those about fernishing to call at Mr. GERSHON'S Universal Yurnishing Arcade, 44, OLDHAM - STREET. MANCMRSTRI‘i . (Next door to the Adelphi Bank).

SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 16th, 1895.

-- Tan Marquis of SAnisavav had an The Guildhall Speech, extremely attentive audience when he delivered his speech qt the Len" don Guildhall on Saturday. The interest in the speech was not, it is needless to say, due to SOY expectation that the Prime Minister would old" line a glowing programme. of domestic reform. Domestic reform is not Lord SALISBURY'S orol4 point, nor is it a subject of absorbing interest te City of London magnates. The question that Lord SALISBURY was expected to deal with, and which as a matter of fact he did deal with, was one of foreign affairs. There had been ominous rumours during the whole of the week of possible serious differences of opinion between some a the great European Powers, Great Britain included, in regard to Turkish affairs, and aS COOSBQUenCe the money markets of London and the Continent had been agitated and depressed. Lord SAL BURY'S speech was on the whole reassuring,though no attempt was made in it to deny the gravity of the situation. The most important piece of in- formation that the speech cor.tained was the as- surance that the six Powers—Great Britain,

div.head: M.DOUGALL'S PATENT SELF-RAISING FLOUR ONCE TRIED ALWAYS USED. •
div.p: M.DOUGALL'S PATENT SELF-RAISING FLOUR ONCE TRIED ALWAYS USED. •

Russia, France, German v,Austria, and Italy—who are endeavouring by more or less urgent pressure to put a stop to Turkish misgovernment, are act- ing in perfect accord with each other. In other 11 Words, the much-famed European " concert" is ant at the present time broken by any discord. That is really a vital fact. If this unity of Purpose and action amongst the great Powers can be maintained for a sufficient length of time and with sufficient intensity the long-pending Eastern Question is,for the time being at all events, deprived of its greatest danger. There can be no question that what the 411 Powers unitedly and firmly demand the Turk- iSli will be compelled to concede. Turkey has long been the "sick man "of Europe, and it is in a weaker and more hopeless condition to-day than it has ever been before since the oarliest conquests of the Ottoman hordes. In all the provinces of the Empire there are unmis- takable signs of an approaching disintegration. The Stivrarr has not, therefore, under his own control a power of resistance which could with- stand the pressure of even one of the European Powers, to say nothing of the whole six. And as matter of fact he makes no pretence to having ,411137 such power. His one hope is now and has ueen all along that of playing off one power against another—Russia against England for instance. %knows that either England or Ruqsia if not in agreement with each other and with the other powers woula long hesitate before using armed force on their own account,for then, as Lord SALISBURY pointed out, "there Would he the danger that the fire th 3re lit should spread to other nations, and should involve all that is most powerful and civilised in Europe in 'dangerous and calamitous contest." But, if the European concert is, as Lord SALISBURY evidently thinks it is, in perfect working order,the SULTAN iS deprived of his last resort. Ho will have to carry out the promised reforms for the protection of the kinenian and other Christian subjects or the end Of the Turkish empire is much nearer at hand Than most people expect. With rekard to the ether and newer Eastern question, which will, in L°rd ROSERERY.S opinion, soon be of greater im- Portance than the old one, Lord SALISBURY had llothing to say that was not satisf ictory. He ,briefly described as "false" the news that a secret n'eaty had been concluded between Russia and Ihina by which the commercial interests of Eng- ' 'and would be injured. No such treaty exists, 4nd we have Lord SALISBURY'S assurance that 4.` Whatever may happen in that region, be it in the way of war or in the way of commerce, we are Nual to any competition which may be proposed, ,Itnd we may look on with absolute equanimity at !he actions of any persons, if such quo bk, who uluk that they can exclude us from any part of that fertile and commercial region,or who imagine that if we are admitted they can beat us in the hmlarkets of the world." On the whole, the Guild- t_l4,ll speech of this year has answered a very use- Purpose. It has settled many wild rnmours of :11Pending war, and it reveals to the country that dcare hasbeen really no break of continuity in the Ntion's foreign policy.

A COLOURED WOMAN AT THE POLICE COURT.

A woman of colour named Ellen Johnson was sum- moned at Runcorn Police Court on Saturday morning be- fore Messrs. Itnison and Taylor with being drnnk and disorderly in Church-street the previous night. Constable Kendrick stated that the disturbance created by the prisoner caused a large crowd to colleJt.—The woman in a voluble statement contended that this country waS as free to her as anyone else. She had been deserted by her husband, who married her in India. She had given information to the police that he was in town, but with no result. She was not drunk, but weak, having had no food during the day. If she went to gaol she would in- stitute proceedings for false imprisonment.—A fine of 53. or EeW!TT imprisotimlnt was imposel. THE FORTHCOMING SCHOOL BOAR ELECTION.

Mr. Ashton, the returning officer, has now fixed the dates in connection with the election of members on the School Board. 'rhe notices were issued on Tuesday, and nominations are to be handed in to him by 4 p.m. on the 19. h inst. Withdrawals will be allowed up to 4 o'clock on the 23rd, and the polling, if found neces• vary will take place on the 30th inst. No new candid. dates have yet been nominated, but the School Board have taken steps to fill the vacancy caussd by the death of Mr. Thomas Handley, J P. —On Saturday afternoon a special meeting was held at the Town Hall, under the presidency of Mr. Pritchard. There were also present— the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. Taylor' J.P.. C C., Mr. Imi.l son, J.P., and Mr. Moss (clerk). Mr. Taylor proposed that Mr. F. J. Norman be elected a member (Atha Board in place of the late Mr. Handley. He believed that Mr.' Norman had a thorough acquaintance with educational matters, and had had some experience as a manager of the Wesleyan Schools,which bad lately been transferred to the B;ard.—Mr. Imison seconded the proposition, endorsing all that Mr. l'aylor had said as to Mr. Nor- man's qualifications.—The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi and the Chairman supported the mo ion which was carried un- animously. Mr. Walter Collier has been spoken of dur- ing the week as a probable candidate at the forthcoming election.

div.head: RUNCORN- AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN- AND WIDNES.

PROMOTION OF A FORMER RUNCORN POLICE SERGEANT. Many will be pleased to learn that Sergeant Thomas Morris, who for some years was on the Runcorn Police Force, has been promoted to the rank of inspector, and will succeed Inspector Dodd, of Hyde. ST. JOHN'S BAND OF ROPE. A lantern exhibition and musical entertainment was given on Tuesday evening in the schoolroom. Mesirs. Rubinson and Newburn were in charge of the lantern, whilst the musical items were given by Miss Davies, Mr. R. Morris, and Mr. Ankers. There was a good attend- ance, and a pleasant evening was spent. 10-mortaow's FOOTBALL MATCH. Tyldesley are to be the opponents of the Runcorn team on the Irwell-lane enclosure tomorrow (Saturday). The following will line up for Runcorn :—Full-back,J. Jolley; three-quarter backs, T. Warder. G. Robinson, FL Myers and W. Gayter ; half backs, S. Abrams and J. Faulkner; forwards, W. Faulkner, J. Langley, R. Reece, J. Moores, S. Walker, F. Gayter, U. Williams and W. Lightfoot. THE ELECTION OF A GUARDIAN AT RUNCORN. As was anticipated, little interest was manifested in the election af a representative on the Board of Guar- dians for Heath Ward, and a meagre poll was the result. The election was conducted in Greenway-road Board Schools on Saturday, and the presiding officer was Mr. G. Ashton, and the poll clerk, Mr. F. Johnson. The poll closed at eight o'clock, and the result of the counting was as follows :—Rev. J. Simpson. 70 ; Mr. Reynolds, 42. There are 421 electors in the ward. The first named gentleman was present at the meeting of the Board held at Dutton Workhouse on Tu-sday. THE SHIPMENTS OF SALT FROM RUNCORN AND WESTON. During the month of October the following shipments have been made from this locality .—White salt from Runcorn and Sup Canal to United States (south), 800 tons ; West Indies and Central America 307 ; Russia 800; England 353; Ireland 455 ; Scotland 190 ; from Weston Point England 482, Ireland 426,Scotland 292. Rock salt from Runcorn and Ship Canal,to Holland 835 tons; Eng- land 25; Scotian', 175 ; from Weston Point,Holland 230; Ireland 12,making a net total of 4,341 tons fr )m Riincoru and 1,642 tons from Weston, as compared with 2,887 for Runcorn,and 2,545 tons from Weston respectively,ia the corresponding month in 1894. BETHESDA LITERARY AND SOCIAL CLASS. At the weekly meeting in connection with this class held on Tuesday evening, the Rev. J. Simpson delivered an admirable lecture on Tennyson's "King Arthur." After giving a brief description of the idylls of the king, Showing how Arthur influenced the knights of the Round Table he passed in review the elements which contributed to the greatness of the character of Arthur, speaking of his great faith in (he unseen, and his manhood—strong in truth and equity, a soul pure and guiltless, and a mind magnanimous. An interesting discussion after- wards took place. BILLIARD MATCH AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. A billiard match between the members of the Chester and Runcorn Liberal clubs was played at Runcorn on Wednesday evening. The club has been recently re- novated and decorated, and now presents a most attrac- •ive appearance. The Runcorn men proved victorious in their engagement by 144 points. DEATH OF MR. ROYLE.

Many will regret to hear of the death of Mr. Robert R lyle, of 9, Halton-road, Runcorn, who passed away en Thursday morning after along and painful illness. He had attained the age of 74 years, and leaves behind him a widow and four children He was exceedingly well- known in the town, and was one of the pioneers of the Runcorn Co-operative Society. At its inauguration he was appointed on the directorate,and had been connected with the society for a period of 33 years. He was also on the executive of the Cheshire and North Wales confer- ence of the Co-operative Union, a position he occupied until recently, when he resigned in consequence of ill- health. He was a well known advocate of Co-operation and had often spoken in its support from the platform. In religion he was a Nonconformist, and was connected with the Methodist Free Church. He was the first super- intendent of the Methodist Free Church Sunday school in Runcorn, and a local preacher. The interment will take place an Monday afternoon. At the meeting of the •,.mmittee of the Runc-rti Co-operative Society on Thursday night a vote of sympathy with the bereaved way passed.

div.head: BRUNSVirICIL MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.
div.p: BRUNSVirICIL MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS.

The programme at the meeting of this class on Wed- nesday evening was" Heckling." Mr. Walter Millington submitted to the ordeal of being heckled—a practice much carried on in Scotland during the elections. In this case the questions to be answered were written on paper and placed in a hat. The Chairman (Mr. Simister) took possession of this and then called upon Mr. Milling- ton to answer them. The questions covered a very wide range, a few of which were as follows :—" Ought Sunday school managers to provide means of eecreation for the young people during the week-day ?" "Do Governments influence trade 2" " What should be the policy of the Nonconformists at the forthcoming School Board elections at Runcorn ?" "Is the Methodism of to-day what John Wesley meant it to be 2" "Is specu- lation right ?" "Should pew rents be charged ?" etc. Mr. Millington displayed considerable ability in answer- ing the questions,and the proceedings were so interesting that it was decided to Wend the meeting for another half-hour. At the close, Mr. Millington was tendered a vote of thanks on the motion of Mr. J. D. Jones. FUNERAL OF A RUNCORN SHIPWRIGHT.

The funeral of Mr. Edward Flough,of Cavendish-street, Runcorn, took place in the Cemetery on Sunday. The deceased was well known in the town, and was a'ship- wright by tradeibut owing to illness he had been unable to follow his employment for a number of years. He had been a Rechabite for P bout 50 years, and at one time was secretary of the Zion lent, Liverpool, of which he was a member. Mr. A. Jones, of Liverpool, represented this Tent at the funeral and other Rechabites present in- cluded :—Mr. J. E. Warburton (district secretary),Bros. Loa, Leadstone, Booth, and Quayle. The bearers were Messrs. W. Dunbavand, J. Brownhill, J. Grrsty, J. Cousins, M. Jones. W. Joynson, J. Lightfoot, and James Bowyer. There also walked in the procession a number of shipwrights and others, including :—Messrs. H. Dale (secretary Shipwrights' Society), J. Taylor (trea.urer), G. H. Kirkham, M. Sweetman, T. Bowyer, J. D. Jones, Birkett,R. Eden, R. Cross, Johnson Ingham, H.Brough- ton' T. Cooke, W. Hulas, E., J., and E. Peck. The Rev. H. B. Firth was the officiating clergyman.

div.head: MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.
div.p: MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.

An excellent entertainment was given at this mission on Tuesday evening. In the absence through illness of Mr. Shaw (missionary), Mr. Byfield occupied the chair. Songs were given by Mr. T. Woods, Mr. G. Cupid, Mr. Ankers, Mr. Philip Shaw, and the Misses Temple gave a duet. Mr. Ellison 's humorous songs were greatly ap- preciated, and a f •ature of the evening's entertainment was the performances on the mandoline by the Misses Kenyon, of Widnes. Miss E. Mack, and Mr. Roper recited, and Miss Shaw contributed a pianoforte sole. There was a good attendance and a most enjoyable evening was spent. A vote of thanks to those who had taken part was passed, on the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr. Cooke.—At the teachers' meeting in connection with the Institute on Sunday, it was unani- mously resolved that a letter of condolence should be I sent to Mr. and Mr. Ef -xworth in the sad and sudden loss they had sustained by the death of their son (William) who was drowned during a gale off the Welsh coast a short time agn.The deceased was a member of the select class connected with the Institute. RUNCORN POLICg COURT. —CHARGES OF THEFT. —Be- I fore Mr. James Handley and Mr. E. Imison, at Runcorn Police Court, on Friday morning, two charges of theft were heard. Jane Cooke, 60 years of age, was again charged with stealing 28lbs. of coal the property of the Manchester Ship Canal Co., on the 30th Oct.—Mr. Knowles appeared on behalf of the defendant and stated that since the woman had been remanded,Mr. Meadow- croft, the agent for the Ship Canal Co., had nut himself in communication with the authorities in Manchester, and they had decided to withdraw the charge with the consent of the magistrates. They wished the public to be informed that although the 'coal seemed to be lying about loosely, it remained the property of the Ship Canal Co., and people were not allowed to take it. The magis- trates agreed with Mr. Meadowcroft concurring with what Mr. Knowles had said, to discharge the defendant. —Charles Logan, a farm labourer, was charged with having at Halton stolen a cockerel and two pullets, the property of Jcseph Walker, his master,—Mr. Walker. of Hallwood farm, Halton, stated that the prisoner had worked for him during the last six months. He gave him orders on Wednesday night to take a horseto Chester for sale, and he was informed that the prisoner left early the following morning to do so. He identified the fowls produced as his property and valued them at 6e.—Peter Hughes. of the Railway Inn, Dunham Hill, stated that about eight o'clock on Thursday morning the prisoner called at his house and had some conversation with him. He asked witness if he wanted to buy some fowls,and in reply witness asked him where they were. Prisoner said he had them in the provender bag,and in comnanv with witness he went to the road and pulled the fowls pro- duced out of the hag, stating that they belonged to the waggoner at the farm he canto from. Witness bought them from him for 34. 6d.—Sergrant Hunt stationed at Dunham Hill Police Station, said from information re- ceived he went to the pesoner MI questioned him about the fowls. In consequence of the contradictions he made witness took 'him into custody, and brought him to Frndsham where he handed him over to Sergeant Ben- field.—P.S. Benfield gave evidence as to charging the nrisoner with stealing the fowls from Mr. Walker's, and he replied, "I took them." Be now pleaded guilty, and was fined 104. and £1 15s. costs or inidefault 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: BUILDING SOCIETY MEETING..
div.p: BUILDING SOCIETY MEETING..

The annual meeting of the United Cheshire and Lan- cashire Permanent Benefit Building Society and Savings' Fund was held in Trinity Girls' schoolroom, Runcorn,on Thursday evening. The chair was occupied by Mr. T. Simister,and amongst those present were Dr.McDougall, Messrs. John Johnson, William Fisher, Joseph Li tier, George Moss, Jos. Pritchard,John Wilson, J. L. Briscoe (Widnes). Richard Webster (Widnes), Albert Jordan, William: Handley, A. Lake, H. B. Toone, J. K. Digges, Broadhurst, A. Lightburn, and Mr. .J. W. Lightburn (secretary). The directors presented their 32nd annual report which showed that the nett profits of the past year amounted to £l,OlB 15s. 7d. which with the sum of £95 19s. carried forward from 1894 to meet exceptional repairs, made a total of £1,114 14s. 7d. out of which it was proposed to pay a dividend : of five per cent, which would absorb £l,Oll ss. 3d„ ' leaving a balance of £lO3 9s. 4d. to be carried to the reserve fund. The total reserve fund now amounts to £10,571 us. 101. The report was adopted on the motion of Mr. Briscoe, seconded by Dr. McDougall. The elec- tion of officers was then proceeded with. Mr. Simister was reappiinted president on the motion of Mr. Broad- hurst, seconded by Mr. Toone ; and the following were also re-elected :—Treasurer, Mr. S. Taylor, J.P., stewards, Mr. H. B. Toone and Mr. J. K. Digges ; auditors, Mr. Albert Jordan and Mr. W. Handley ; and Messrs. John Johnson, Joseph Pritchard and Richaid Webster were re-appointed on the committee. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

SUCCESS OF MR. J. BRUNDRIT, J.P. At the Broadheath coursing meeting on Saturday last, Mr. J. Brundrit's Bessie Rose divided the Ship Canal Stake!. At the Altcar Club meeting, Mr. Brundrit'r Bessie Tylor and Bessie Cartwright have each survived the third round in the Croxteth Stakes and are both in the semi-final. The stakes are valuable, and include a piece of plate, value £25, for the winner. THE PROPOSED CHEMICAL WORKS AT WESTON. Rumours have been current in Runcorn and district during the week that the Castner Kellner Alkalia Com- pany had definitely decided to come to Weston. The option of purchase of the land expired on Wednesday, but we understand that the purchase has not been made, and further, that the Company has obtained an exten- sion of the time specified for making the purchase. There are still difficulties about the price to be paid for wayleaves, and until these are satisfactorily settled no decision will be made. It may be stated that the Com- pany have another site in view at Middlesboro'. At the general meeting of the Aluminium Company on Monday, the Chairman (Right Hon. Gerald W. Balfour, M.P.) ridiculed the statements made in the newspapers that the Castner-Kellner process would be dangerous to those employed. DEATH ANDFUNERAL OF A RUNCORN TRADESMAN.

The funeral of the late Mr. John Crowley, chandler and hardware dealer, 29, Church-st., Runcorn, and for- merley of Liverpool, took place on Wednesday, at Run- corn Cemetery. The first mourning coach contained Mr. Tom Crowley, Mr. Joseph Crowley, Mr. Fred Crow- ley, Mr. John Crowley, and Mr. Charles Williams, sons and son-in-law. In the second, rode Mr. George Williams, Mr. Arthur Williams, Mr. Robert Wright (Liverpool),Mr.lielly(Everton),and Mr. Joseph Cuthbert- son. The bearers were Messrs. H. Wright, W. Wright,W. Brimelow and A. E. Jon-s. The Rev. W. George was the officiating minister. Choice floral tributes of affection were placed oa the cuffs. These included a beautiful cross by Mrs. and Miss Crowley,wreathe by Mr. Thomas Crowley, Mr. Joseph Crowley, Mr. George Williams. Mr. Arthnr Williams (grandsons), Mr. and Mrs. D. U. J•nes, Miss Robinson, Mrs. awl Miss Lloyd. The deceased had been connected with Runcorn for about 25 yearn.
GRUESOME DISCOIFERY AT RUNCORN.

The headless body of a woman at present unknown was recovered from the Canal at Top Locks, Runcorn, on Monday morning. An inquest was held on the body in the Board room at the Cemetery on Wednesday miming by Mr. J. E. Woreley. The first witness called was Alfred Darwell, 12, Sp.takman-street, boatman, who stated that he found the body at the Top Locks of the Bridgewater Canal, on Monday morning. There was only a pair of socks upon it. The head had been decap- itated and the body was much mutilated. —Thomas Hallwood, 24, Surrey-street, dock labourer,^ave evidence as to assisting to remove the body from the water. On the same afternoon he found a piece of blue serge material in the propellar of the steam tug Broadheatli, which was then in dock and carne from Manchester on Sunday. Those in charge had reported that the tug struck something when near Savage's bridge. Nothing else was found.—Sergeant Lee gave Lvidence as to examining the body. It was that of a female. ' apparently about 30 years of age. She was strongly built. She had no rings upon her lingers, and there was no distinctive mark upon the body to identify her. They were common socks on her feet. Her hands seemed to suggest that she was a labouring woman. The head was completely severed from the trunk, and had not been found. Teere were several large cuts on the body which apneared to have been caused by the propeller of a tug. There were no stabs or marks or rnything to sug- gest violence. A notice had been sent out giving a des- cription of the body but without result. There was no one about Runcorn reported as lost. She bad probtblv been in the water a week or a fortaight.—The Coroner said the enquiries so far had failed to find any clue to the mystery, but perhaps the newspaper reports might elucidate something. In the absence of the head there were little -neans of identification. He suggested that a verdict of found dead be recorded. The jury concurred.

div.head: SAD DEATH THROUGH DRINK NEAR RUNCORN.
div.p: SAD DEATH THROUGH DRINK NEAR RUNCORN.

SUFFOCATED IN A DYKE. ' Mr. J. E. Worsley, coroner, held an inquest at the As- ton Arms Hotel, Aston, on Tuesday afternoon, on the body of a general labourer,named Michael Ford,a native of Northwich, and nicknamed "Salt," who met with his death under most deplorable circumstances on Sunday night. Thomas Massey was the first witness called ,and stated that he bad worked with the deceased on and off,for the last 16 years. Deceased was named Michael Ford, and belonged to North wich. He had worked at Park Side Farm, Aston. Witness was in his company on Sunday night, when they were drinking together at the Bridge Inn and the Aston Arms, near Frodsham Bridge. De- ceased borrowed sixpence 'rum him to buy whisky. Wit- ness left him at the Aston Arms, and did not see him alive again. Police-Sergeant Benfield deposed that about 7.30 a.m. on Monday he received information that a man was lying dead on the roadside near Co Sutton Bridge. He proceeded there and found the deceased lying dead in a , dyke face downwards, near to the roadside. There Was a bottle containing whiskey lying close to biro. He ex- amined him but found no marks of violence. There was froth coming out of the deceased's mouth. He had II him removed to the Aston Arms, and then communi- cated with the Northwich police to see if they could find any friends of the deceased. He had not yet received any reply to his communication. In reply to a question P. 6. Benfield (a member of the St. John Ambulance Association), stated that he did not think the man died from a fit but from the effects of drink. The man had fallen iuto the dyke and had been unable to get out again. He bad known the deceased previously and had seen him going along the canal in a state of intoxication. .

Edith Roberts, barmaid at the Aston Arms, gave evid- ence as to supplying the deceased with a gill of whiskey about 9.30 on Sunday night. She indentified the bottle produced as being the same one as she supplied:Wm with. He was sober when he left the house. _ .
-- -- Joseph Lightfoot spoke to supplying the deceased with a glass of whiskey at the Aston Arms. He was then sober. - -

The Coroner characterised the case as a very sad one. There seemed to he no doubt that the man fell into the dyke and was suffocated. The jury returned a verdict that the deceased was suffocated whilst in a state of Intoxication.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURI)AV, NOVEMBER 16. 1895.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURI)AV, NOVEMBER 16. 1895.
RUNCORN BOA ItD OF GUARDIANS.

A meeting of this Board was held in the Board room at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. Knowles occupied the chair, and in addition to the members of the Rural Council being present there were the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Rev. Canon Wood, Rev. J. S Simpson, Mr. S. Yarwood, Mr. A. R. Norman, Mr. J. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk), and Mr. Cunnah (workhouse master).

div.head: EXTENSION OF THE WORKHOUSE.
div.p: THE EXTENSION OF THE WORKHOUSE.

The Local Government Board submitted copies of an order authorising the Guardians of the Runcorn Union to expen I an additional sum not exceeding £26 iu the erection of a casual ward for females at the work- house of the Union.

div.head: TAINT or PATIPERIShf.
div.p: A TAINT or PATIPERIShf.

The Chesterfield Umon having passed the following resolution, submitted it to the Board, desiring them to co-operate in making an endeavour to get amended the section referred to in the resolution. They considered that the school cards were quite unnecessary now school fees had been abolished and the school attendance officers appointed to see that all chil- dren of school age attend school regularly. But until the section was amended relieving officers had this unnecessary duty to perform for children whose parents were in receipt of out-door relief, such children being at times marked out and annoyed by other pupils in conse- quence. Toe resolution submitted was " That other Boards of Guardians and District Councils be invited to join the Chesterfield Board in presenting a petition to Parliamer.t to modify section 40 f the Elementary Edu- cation Act, 1876,50 as to do away with the necessity of children wh aie parents are in receipt of out-doo, relief. having to procure school attendance cards to be marked by the sehoolmasters and schoolmistresses."—The Rev. Dr. Gast ddi inquired whether there were such cards in Ru,.corn Union.—The Clerk said they were obliged to have. The argument was that the cards in use carried with them a taint of pauperism to the children.—Mr. Williams was of the opinion that the cards were useless, and they branded the children as paupers. He proposed that they adopt a resolution similar to that passed by the Chesterfield Union.—Mr. Heywood seconded.—Dr. Gastaldi moved as an amendment that the letter be laid on the table. It was useless to deal with it until the fees question had been settled.—Canon Wood seconded the amendment. From an educational standpoint, it was not advisable to attempt to make any small changes of this kind. It was very likely that the whole educa- tion question would be entered into during the neat session and anything that was done in this way might not have any influence at all. The fees question might be reconsidered altogether.—The Chairman said the amendment was really a negative. Nine voted in favour of the motion, and only one, Dr. Gastaldi, voted against.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF THE SCHOOLNISTW' SS.
div.p: RESIGNATION OF THE SCHOOLNISTW' SS.
Miss Moran tendered her resignation as schoolmistress at the workhouse.—Mr. Aaron proposed that it be ac- cepted, and that a successor be advertised for. This was agreed to.

ASSISTANCE FOR THE MATRON. In accordance with notice given Admiral Parry moved that an assistant be appointed to look after the cooking and laundry work and that she be a general assistant to the matron. He stated that the cylestion had been threshed out in that room for some time past. The com- mittee had considered the matter end recommended that the appointment be made. Mrs. Cunnah had already been laid up for ten days, and there was no one able to keep up her work. She had been greatly in need of assistance for some time.—Mr. A. R. Norman seconded, and said he would be very sorry to increase expenditure, but he thought this appointment would he in the hest interests of the ratepayers.—The motion was carried by 14 votes to 10.—The salary was fixed at £lB per year.

div.head: FINANCE.
div.p: FINANCE.

Mr. Heywood submitted the financial statement,show- ing that the payments included for out-relief—as for Runcorn, £3O for Froisham, mad £lB for Budworth. The accounts for pavmmar amounted to £164, leaving a balance in hand of £368 94 51. NOTICE OF MOTION.
Mr. Wright gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the standard for labour certificates at Halton School be raised from the 4th to the sth standard. This concluded the bwiness.

div.head: WESLEYAN FO EIGN MISSIONS. RUNCORN.
div.p: WESLEYAN FO EIGN MISSIONS. RUNCORN.
ANNIVERSARY SERVICES.

The foreign missionary anniversary in connentinn with St. Paul's Wesleyan Church and Sunday School was held on Sunday and Monday. The Rev.o wen Wat- kins, of Warrington,and formerly a missionary in South Central Africa, preached on Sunday to large congreea- tions. A meeting was held in the Sunday School in the afternoon in Brunswick Sunday School. Mr. J.D. Jones occupied the chair, and there was a large attendance of scholars. Addresses nn missionary work were delivered by the Rev. C.de Patron Gliddon and Mr. John Simpson. Mr. John Birkatt read the report, which showed that the children had done better than in any previous year in collecting for Wesleyan Foreign Missions. At the close of the meeting it was found that the sum raised by the children throu!thnut the year totalled £lOO. The annual missionary meeting was held in St.PauPs Chapel on Monday evening, and was well attended. Mr. Edward Taylor occupied the chair. and there were also on the platform the Revs. T. Brackenhury, W. George, C. de Futron Gliddon, Owen Watkins, and J. Simpson, Simister, F. J. Norman, 11. Rawlinsnn, and R. H. Posnett. The Rey. C. de Peron Gliddon submitted general report of the Wesleyan Foreign Mis- sion Society showing that the total income was £125,806, and this included £19,000 from the young people, which he considered was a very noble offering from the children and young people in their church. There w-s .Iso £BOOO for the foreign field. The expenditure had been £127.457. The num- ber of chapels and preaching places in the foreign mission field was 2 101 with 348 missionaries and assist4nt mis- sionaries, 2,541 naid agents, and 5,201 unpaid agents. There were 80 721 scholars. 40.979 members, and atten- dants on public worship 163 426 The nutnher of con- verts from heathenism during the year was 2,000. The Rev. W. George in presenting the local annual report expressed his pleasure at being ab!e to present such a satisfactory report. The young people of their church had done well before, but this year they had beaten the record. (Applause.) The ladies had collected in boxes RR follows :—miaq Winifred M. Robinson, 154. 81. • Mrs. Soulhy, £6 Bs.•, Mrs. W. George, £4 I3s. ; Mrs. 'Lloyd Davies, £7 93 ed. ; Misses Rimkin and Taylor, £2 14s. 61. ; and Miss Norman, £ll 9s. At the Sunday school the bops had given £l4 2s. 6L, and the girls. £6 6.. 54d. The amount col- lected by hops with books, £l3 194. 9id., and by the girls, £5O 9s. 4d. (Applause.) The increase in the amount collected by the former was £3 18s. id., and The latter, £lO 9s. 70. The total sum obtained by the scfinlars last year with £B5 18s. 2.1 : but this year it bad reached £loo—(applause)--an increase of £l4 is. 101. The total amount raised in connection with St. Paul's was £144 Os. id., compared with 131 14.. 4d. last year. The collections at the public meeting last year were £39 Bs. 101., but he did not know what it was to tin that night. In the Runcorn circuit the amount contributed to the society was £22945. 2d. The Chairman in the course of a short address made a reference to the long connection of his family with the Runcorn circuit missionary branch. He spoke of .his lardent hones when young, when hearing of the success of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions, that the world would spoll be converted, but he had now different ideas. But be thought they were making satisfactory progress He hoped they would continue their efforts to convert .the world to Christianity. The Rev. John Grimshaw, late missionary in British Guiana, said it gave him great pleasure to find a really live missionary Simday school, and he was pleased that they did not divide their contributions as was the case In some planes, giving one-third each to the Foreign Missionary Society, the Home Missionary Society, and keeping R third for themselves. The work the young people had done was as necessary as the work he or Mr. Watkins had been privileged to do. After describ- ing the country where lie had been a missionary and which contained a pr,pulation of 300,000, ho referred to the method of work he had adopted, and Spoke of the satisfactory progress that was being made. He wanted them not only to give their money, but to give their daily sympathy and praye.s that God would bless the missionary services wherever they were, so that the natives might take the management of their own affairs in their own hands, and enahle the English missionaries to en to other fields. (Annlause.) _ _ _

_ The Rev. Owen Watkins at the outset of his ad- dress urged them to increase their yearly subscriptions, and then proceeded tn spoqk of his work in South Cen- tral Africa,and staled that nowhere had God so honoured their labours. In South Africa they had 60,000 mem- hers, 200,000 persons in their sanctuaries, and 150,000 children in their day and Sunday schools. The greatest merchants were to be found there, and the majority of them were Wosleyans. Their workers were doing great things for God and Christ. Referring to the South African goldfields he said millions of English money were being gambled on them, and let them mark his words, the day of reckoning was coming, and it would not be long before it came when the Eng- lish people who had been gambling in gold stocks would pay an awful penalty amid an awful smash. In ormolu- sion he spoke of the evangelistic work they carried on in the night schools in South Africa, and referred to other methoris they adopted in winning the heathen to Christ. The collection afterwards tak,m up realised £35.
