div.head: WARRINGTON D EBATING SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON D EBATING SOCIETY.
DISCUSSION ON "THE RECENT TORY
TRIUMPH."
SPEECHES BY MR. R. PIERPOINT, MR. P. B. SCOTT, MR. JOHN CROSFIELD, MR.• A. CROSFIELD, COUNCILLOR ROBERTS, MR. F. MONKS, COUNCILLOR BENNETT, AND TEE REV. E. C. E. CARLETON.

On Tuesday the Warrington Debating Society commenced is season, 1895-6, under auspices the most favourable yet recorded. The Masonic Hall, Bold-st., Was crowded to the utmost, due chiefly to the fact that "The Recent Tory Triumph" was going to be discussed pro and con by the very men who, as far as Warrington was concerned, were beet calculated to explain the subject exhaustively and well. With such an excellent start, the Debat- ing Society should, this season at any rate, main- tain its hold upon the interest of the 'public with greater vigour than ever before. The fact that no definite programme has been arranged, and that instead it has been decided to have the debate each fortnight on some current tepic, will certainly con- duce to that result. Mr. R. PIERPOINT, M.P. took the chair, and the speakers mentioned above accompanied him on either side. Messrs. E. J Hall and F. R. Roberti(hon. secs.) were also present. The CHAIRMAN said it was his first duty as well as pleasure to thank them as members of the Debating Society of Warrington for the honour they had conferred upon him in electing him as their Presideat, and to ex- press his pleasure in presiding that evening. (Applause.) He had enquired of Mr. Hall as to his duties that even- ing, being as some of them were aware a member of tho House of Commons, and he was under the impres- sion that his position was in a humble degree somewhat similar to that of the Speaker of the House. He was given to understand,however,that the aristocra- tic tendencies of this assembly were so marked that they preferred to look upon him as Lord Chancellor presiding over the debates of House of tlie Commons. Mr. Pierpoint said it gave him also great pleasure o meet his friend Mr. Scott that evening. (Applause.) He was sure they would allow him to say, RS having the great hon )ur to represent the town in Parliament, that he was proud indeed of the fact that he could reckon amongst his personal friends,both of his opponents. (Applause.) He had had put into his hands the following notice " that so much interest has been taken in this debate that it is impossible for all who wish to speak to do so this night, but the debate will be renewed under the title of " The Cause of the Liberal Defeat" a fortnight to- night, when the debate will be opened by Mr. Arthur H. Crnsfield,"whom the speaker was glad to see present. (Applause.) Mr. P. B. SCOTT said that if they would permit, before opening the debate, he would like to say a word or two on a ma ter which was not altogether pertinent to the cause of that night's assembly. It was simply that he would like to add his tribute of praise to the gentlemen who constituted the committee of the society when in their wisdom they decided that the member for the borouele for the time being, should be the president of their society. (Applause.) That night he thought they met under very happy auspices in having Mr. Pierpoint to preside over their deliberations, and he felt sure that at no part since its formation had the society had one more wishful 'o act impartially in the chair, and be mere honourable and courteous than their chairman that night. (Applause.) Mr. Scott's duty was to discuss a subject which, he was perfectly sure they would sYmnathise with him, was very unpalat- able. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He should have liked, had he been one of those who were reepon4ble for the choosing of the title of the subject, that they had called it by some other name, as for instance "The Resent Tory Ascendancy." (Appl,nsie.) A few months ago, no doubt, it was a triumph but during the short Period since Parliament assernl,lecl he must frankly state that he could not review it in that light. (Laughter.) He said "not triumph " and in saying so he believed he was acting advisedly. Any remarks he would have to make that night he did not think in any large degree would apply to the Borough of Warrington. Had they been discussing the reasons ' for the late victory here he should have had some very flattering remarks to make. They were not discussing Warrington but the so-called Tory triumph throughout the country, which he ventured to think had been won or. gained by more means than one. (Hear, hear.) He could not help thinking that the Tories gained on the principle that " All's fair in love and war," a maxim which he had never believed in and he trusted never would. (Hear hear, and applause.) They promised, and he had only ton good reason to believe that they delivered those promises without intending to fulfil them, because, taking their case in Manchester where they ha I lost eight seats out of n ne on one ground only, and, judging from that ground and what they had seen since Parliament assembled, they had not fulfilled their promises to the electorate of Lancashire. They had the petty schemes of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain—the Old Age Pensions—an,i if they were to gather anything from the Duke of Devonshire's utterances,he believed that these pensions, so far as the Tory party were concerned, were as far off as ever. He had not come there that night for the pur- pose of vilifying the Tories. He had never disguised the fact since he heard the subject of the debate that night that he did not believe there was very much good to be derived from the discussion. The speaker doubted very much whether they as Liberals had anything to gain by discussing the facts of their recent loss. He thought rather it would be their duty to look to see what they could do to reverse things, Particularly the loss they had sustained. (Applause.) But for the purposes of friendly desiate he took it that at any rate they must speak plainly,and to really do so, a man had perhaps to a much greater measure than he intended,to lay at the hands of the Tory Party a deal of blame. The Liberals themselves ware not free from blame. In 1892 when the Liberals came into office they came in with a so-called Newcastle Programme embody- ing Home Rule for Ireland, Disendswment and Disestal - lishment of the Welsh Church, Local Veto, and many other items. All knew perfectly well that the Liberals passed in the Ho ice of Commons by a large majority— considering the majority which they had when they entered office—the Home Rule Bill for Ireland. They knew what it met with at the hands of the House of Lords, and he said that night that for them to have at- tempted, on the dissolution of the late Parliament, to Appeal to the country with the Newcastle programme, was a farce from beginning to end. That was one cause and one only for many Bills not becoming law during the late Parliament. If that was so then why did they not try to remove the cause of the disastrr They came with the same old programme, and the same old items, and the elector- ate were sick of it. (Applause.) Home Rule for Ireland was very well it way, but it would never be granted until they had removed the obstacle which he had mentioned. (Applause.) He repeated that they had ton many irons the fire. And what was the consequence ? Instead of their iron being red hot, they found their fire out—(laughter)—and the result was the same as it would be if there was a an- nouncement of a concert at which a pianist was engaged to play, and when he arrived, he found no piano to play on. If the concert was a failure the result would be richly deserved. It was the same with the Liberal party. They laid themselves open to the charge that they promised but they did not perform, and the result was that the Tories were re- turned to power. They had a huge majority, a majority which made it incumbent upon them to turn it to the best use. He had said that he was not certain that that dis discussion was going to do them much good, but if in discussing the extent of the disaster, and trying to arrive at the cause of that disaster, they might possibly by ascertaining the Cause, steer clear of that in the future. (Hear, hear.) His contention was that they had only one thing to do in the future, and that was to place before Liberals and educate them to the one fact, and that was, it was not a series of measures they wanted to pass, but that there was one obstacle they wanted to get rid of. Then the others would follow. (Applause.) If that was done, they need have no fear of the future. There was another ground on which be thought Liberals were not faithful to their own state- ments, and that was, they denounced the House of Lords, yet at the same time he was sorry to :ell them that they created peers. (Hear, hear.) He hoped that every Liberal in that room would not forget to take note faf that fact, and they ought to take care that until all power so far A 9 it was a legislative assembly was taken away from the House of Lords, no Liberal Government ever made another. They wanted none of them. The House of Lords to-day to a very large extent was made up of brewers and of rich county magnates. (Hear, hear.) Those men were never going to do anything for true Liberalism. They did very well for the Tories, who were welcome to them so far as he was concerned. He thought that undoubtedly the electorate of England had lost trust in the Liberal party, because Home Rule for Ireland had been before the country so long, and also Welsh Disestablishment and several other items which did not, to any large extent, benefit the English electorate, and, he said that seeing that those hills had notonly been before the House of Commons, but had passed the House of Commons,and there was no possible chance of them becoming law until the House of Lords was removed, and seeing that the Liberals themselves had not educated the masses to remove that—he said that they were tired and thought they would give the Tories another chance. Let them not forget this, that the Tories came before the public promising this, that, and the other. If is man promised them something and they had 'no reason to doubt his good faith, then he said that they could do nothing less than believe in him. That was very much the case with the workingman electorate throughout the country. Thav expected that the Liberals would come with ene good wholesome dish,instead of which, they had brought

half. a dozen, which it was impossible at that time to digest. And although many Liberals, and Liberals in high office, even the late premier, Lord Rosebery, said that it was the gullibility of the British people, be (Mr. Scott) did not think they were gulled. (Councillor Roberts: I do.) He did not agree with that idea. The electorate thought that the Liberals' had been given a fair chance, and they did not make the best of that chance, and he did not blame tisem for turning round to see what somebody else would do for them, and to a large extent the last election was lost on that ground. (Hear, hear.) Be maintained that he had not said one word too much, or too strorg act:that the party to which he belonged. It was time that they awoke to the fact that they had themselves to blame for their defeat. He was perfectly certain that what he had said that night did not apply to the borough of Warrington, because he did not believe that they lost the contest on the grounds he had mentioned. There were also ether reasons which accounted in a large measure for their defeat through- out the country. They bad sustained the loss of the .ight Hon. W. E. Gladstone, a man whom he ventured to say was held by either parry in the highest commendation ; by his large experience, and his unique personality, his age, and being the greatest of living statesmen—he (Mr. Scott) said that when he retired, the Liberal party lost in him something which was very great indeed. (Hear, hear.) He had brought ia the Home Role Bill, and he bad fought for it in the last year of his political life, and he also sounded the death knell qf the House of L)rds. He had retired at the very crisis of their existence, and when they could most do with him. It was a blow to the Liberal party 4thich it would probably take years to pull back. Then again, throughout the country, the Liberal party was badly off so far as having a medium for propounding the views of Liberalism. He spoke of the Press. No matter where they turned, Tory money and Tory ascendancy had bought it up. It was no use discussing the fact. It was so palpably plain to every one. Let them take Warrington. Thr-y had a neutral mediumoto far as it was neutral,and they had a Liberal paper. But they had a Tory paper, which he was glad to say had tr.eat-ed him very fairly personally. But he would like to notice what he saw in it a fortnight last Saturday. Mr. Scott then referred to a paragraph with reference to the swimming gala, and said that he did not accept the position of Chairman for the purpose of furthering Ws candidature in Warrington, and he also disclaimed any idea of doing so on similar occasions. Mr. Scott lalso mentioned clubs as being one cause of the ascenTancy of the Tories owing tc their wealth. In con&usion Mr. Scott contended that if they let the Tories alone they would go to sleep. Tories could go to sleep in municipal mitters—(laughter)—and they would do it in Parliament, and he hoped that himself or someone more worthy of their support would, perhaps, soon.' than a good many of them expected, be able to

chair which Mr. Pierpoint occupied that night, and IlleL tins subject of the debate would. be " The recent Liberal majority." (Laughter and applause.) The Rev. g.C.E. CARLETON said he thought they would allow him to express his very great appreciation of Mr. Scott's kindness in coming that :night. While assuring him of the Society's welcome the speaker thought that he might also assure him of always in that room meet- ing with that courtesy to which he was entitled, of course tempered with that candour of speech which he hoped they all felt due to themselves on that occasion. He had come to speak on Mr. Scott's address,which how- ever had rendered his task an easy one because the in- dictment whi..h he had brought against the Tory party was nothing like as formidable as he anticipated. His view of the Tory triumph was that it was a simple matter and entirely owing to the Liberal defeat. (Laugh- ter) There were many things that contributed to the Conservative triumph, and as regards party tactics the Liberol party had shewn themselves lamentably incap- able. In naval warfare he believed it was good tactics to avoid exposing much broadside to the enemy. The Radicals in the conflict most generously exposed all the broadside they could and gave themselves away in a most lavish manner. There was hardly a clause in the Newcastle programme that each could not spot his own particular grievance in. It was a curious thing with regard to Home Rule that Mr. Gladstone appealed to the country to give him a sefficient majority to enable him to defy the policy of Mr. Parnell and his friends, and when they did not, the same statesman went everywhere and asked the country to accept the policy of Mr. Parnell and his party. The ' only construction that could be put upon such conduct was that Mr. Gladstone was desirous above all things of getting in offi e either with or without Home Rule. Those legislators who refused to submit their measures to the people and were trying to pass their measures in spite of the people, tried to raise a cry against the House of Lords, which was simply insisting upon the people being consulted. Could anything be more ridiculous ? The destruction of the House of Lords was only one step towards the destruction of the House of Commons. (Laughter) Mr. F. MONKS LP., expressed his pleasure at hearing both political parties discuss the same question with friendliness and referred to what would have been likely occur at the time of the first return of Sir Gilbert Greenall. As to the cause of the Liberal defeat in the country generally he viewed it from a different stand. point. The decision of the nation had been very empha- tic and there was no possibility of any mistake as to what the nation meant. • In the old Liberal days the Liberal party had a programme that was not the pro- gramme of a mere faddist, but one that appealed to thern people and was calculated to improve their moral and social condition. He thought the Liberal party had failed because they had not continued the programme which they had held for the past 30 years. They had wrought a wonderful change in the condition of the working classes within the past thirty years, and if they had continued to legislate for the good of the nation at large, instead of pandering first to one small party, and then another,they would have occupied a much stronger position than at present. They bad paid more con- sideration to questions such as one man one vote, which was what he called sham legislation, instead of

endeavouring to improve the existing evils connected with the largest portion of the electorate,viz.,the agricul- turists. The pre,ent Radical party, he said, was not the Liberal party. He was as much a Liberal now as ever he was in his life, but he was not a Radical in the sense in which the Radical party had been since Home Rule. Commenting on the great depression in agriculture, Mr. Monks said Mr. Richard Cobden was perfectly right when he said that the blessings that would arise from the free-tradY in land were greatly in excess of the blessings arising from the free trade in commerce. Those were questions that both parti^s could take up. One of the things that the Radical party was mistaken in was that they seemed to be tryinx to fasten upon the Unionist party the crimes and mistakes of the old Tory party which passed away in 1832. Mr. Monks referred to the question of Imperial Federation as one which the majority of the electors was favourable to, and said that the Liberal party would do well if they paid some attention to this and other like matters. (Applause.) Councillor Roasnrs J.P..said that he did not know ba- fore coming into the room that be would have to speak. and the result was that he had to rely pretty much upon the remarks of the previous speakers. He still considered Mr. Monks as a friend and he hoped that some day, when he was clothed and in his right mind--(laugbter)— he would be a friend of his politically. Referring to Mr. Monks' statemeFits with regard to the reform of the land laws, Mr. Roberts asked whether they ever expected any reform worth having from the party of landlords. His friend, Mr. Scott, did not believe in the gullibility of the British workingmen, but he thought that that WAR one of the greatest features in the Liberal defeat. If the working classes were but educated in the past history of

- the Tory party he ventured to say that that party would not again be placed in office for the next century and a half. (Loud laughter and applause.) The workingman had not, however, troubled himself about the matter; ho had been too ready to swallow all the promises of the Tory party, at the recent election, and had thus brought about the downfall of that party who had ever cham- pioned his cause. Mr. Roberts then proceeded to describe the measures which the Tory party had opposed untd they dared oreonse them no longer, particularly measures for the relief of Nonconformists, of which body he said that he WAS, proud to make public confession that he was one. He attributed the Liberal defeat to the" three F's," falsehood,fraud and fear. With regard to the first, the cotton operatives of Lancashirehad been misled with a promise that the duties on cotton would be taken off ; and the agriculturists had also been given a promise which had been recently knocked on the head by the Duke of Devonshire. They hid promised everything, and never inter ded to fulfil their promises. As to fraud,did they think that a combination of the spirituous and spiritual forces was anything else tint a gigantic fraud ? Oil and water could not mix, and he thought that such a contradictory alliance as that between the clergyman and the beerseller was destined to an early destruction. (Applause.) With regard to fear he said in justification tor using that term that a number of week-kneed Liberals had been frigh- tened nut of the party of progress by the wild vapour- inc.s of members of the Independent Labour party. Re was not surprised that those who lived in the slums of London, who had no possibility or any chance in life, said wild things or even did wild things, but the Liberal capitalists had made a great mistake in leaving the Liberal party; they should have remained with the party of progress, and have used their energies in tempering the demands of the men, and keeping them within reanneable bounds. In conclusion, he did not grudge Mr. Pierpoint the next five or six years he might have to sit as the Tory representative of this borough in the present Rouse of Commons, but depend upon it, he would do his very best follimit his possession of that office to the time of the present Parliament. (Laughter and applause.) Councillor BENNETT expressed surprise at Councillor Roberts attributing the defeat of the Liberal party to the gullibility of the British workingmen, who had hitherto been regarded by that party as the very per- sonification of wisdom. Ile (the speaker) thought that the more reliable reason was that the British working- men had become enlightened. They had plainly seen that the'policy of the Liberal party was nothing but one of humbug, that they have been given a stone by the Liberals when they had asked for bread, and that they would have to look to the much-abused Tory party for any beneficial legislation. s Mr. Joan CROSFIELD, J.P. said he felt like a patriarch lin tiutt assembly and that the young men had taken his

1 place ; but at the same time he had the old opinions Istill. (Hear, hear and applause.) Ia the first place he would like to confirm the remarks made by his friend Mr. Monks about the pleasure it was to him to see in that room gentlemen belonging to the two different political parties, met together in good humour and good will to listen to opposite opinions to their own. He could recollect the last election in Warrington in which the hustings were in the Old Market Place, and where if ( one went he ran a very good chance of getting a paving. Stone or nalf a brick knocking his teeth out. (Laughter.) ; Happily those days were gone by but in the few minutes . he had Me wished to refer to the great Tory victory and the great Liberal defeat of the last election. He was thankful that at the time he was out of the country. (Laughter.) When be crossed the Atlantic Ocean and reached Q..ieenstown the newspapers came on board ; there were also on board one or two Tories whom he - had tackled severely once or twice, and they came up to him with the newspapers announcing 132 of a indjority for their side. Mr. Crosfield said to 1 them that he was very glad of it and hoped 'it would be 150; the bigger it was and the sooner they (the Tories) would go to pieces. (Laughter and ap- plause.) a:Hs own opinion of the reason of the Liberal defeat and Tory victory was that it was the Local Veto Bill. (Hear, hear.) A letter he had received from a friend of his, Mr. T. C. Horsfall, of Manchester, referred to that very queation. Mr. florsfall said the working- men of England must have some place for recreation. As it was they went to public-houses for recreation. If they were by an Act o:Parliament to close two-thirds of the public-houses the workingmen would be compelled to find something in the way of clubs to replace the public-houses. There was no cry, said the speaker, in his opinion, that came stronger from workingmen than the old cry Of" robbing a poor man of his beer." In a club there was no one whose interest it ,Vas to make a man drink more beer than was good tor him. He be- lieved that the establishment of chute of that sort would be a great benefit throughout the kingdom. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Crosfield then mentioned that he was as strong a Liberal as ever he was—(hear, hear)--and be- lieved in Liberal politics. He had said to Tory friends many a time that they ought to go down on their knees three times a day and thank God for what the Liberals had done for them. The finest measures of the day and blessings Eagland possessed had come trorn the Liberal party. Tne Tories opposed the repeal of the paper duty, and repeal of the newspaper stamp duty, and if it had not been for the Liberal party, they could not bave got a paper for less than 61. in itead M.P. as now. (Hear, hear.) They might thank the Liberal party and ~ that Grand Old Man, Mr. Gladstone—(applause)—for all the reforms that be gave them ; we English people were a queer people and forgot the benefits of the past and i ity looked at to-day. If they could remember as he could, all the blessings which had come to the country through the Liberal party they would thank God that there had been a Liberal party in England. (Applause.) Gladstone, if he had done nothing else took the duty off the soap—(loud lattgliter),—and they could understand that that was enough for him. (Laughter.) He had lived long enough to see that the Tories had had to be educated and had gone along with the tide of Liberal measures and progress. Lord Beaconsfield himsclf had said he had had to educate the party. (Hear, hear.) ' The Speaker concluded by stating that he was very glad indeed that the Liberal party were defeated at the last election. It would do them a world of good and remove ' a lot of the faddists of the party—(loud anolause),—and bring back those with common-sense. (Applause.) Mr. PIERPUINT, replying to toe various arguments advanced, expressed the opinion that the Liberals had , been defeated by reason of their not being a hornogene- OW party. It consisted of many sorts of people. There : were the latter-lay Liberals, the extreme Radicals, Irish ' Home Rulers, Welsh Disestablishers, and so forth. The ouly way to keep such a parry together was by promis- ing a measure to each and every section. The Govern- ment had so crowded out the agenda paper of the House of 'Commons as te make it utterly impossible to carry them by the slow and safe method adopted by -Parlia- mentary precedent. Mr. Pierpoint went on to deal with other reasons, notably the creation ef Peers by the Liberal party while at the same time they were agitat- ing for the abolition of that Chamber. In conclusion,he . explained that Mr. Scott would be present in a fortnight heuce,for the purpose of replying to the arguments ad- vanced.
The debate then adiqurned.

He went, and to k the toy with him. Without saying anything about helping the lad he used mast abesivelenguage, and et.gnsting expressions, ind would Hot listen to the constable's statement. div.head: OUR. LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR. LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL eRURCH. SERMON TO YOUNG MEN.

On Sunday the Rev. John Yonge, pastor of the above place of worship, preached a splendid sermon to young, men from the text " And Caleb stilled the people before Moses and said. Let us go op at once and possess it for we are well able to welcome it.' But the nen that went with him said We he not able to go up against this peonle for they are stronger than '" Numbers xiii. 30-31. In his sermon the preacher sad that there were multitudes of men to-day who were constantly resenting' the stern necessity that compelled them to work or strive for a living ; and who looked with envious eves upon the more favoured few, who, born with a silver spoon in their mouths and cradled in the lap of luxury, grow up with every need provided for. If they did hot know it, the men who had to work and rrive for a liv- ing were far happier than they who were horn to an in- heritance of indolence. There was no need for any man to be scared at the prospect of toil,or to be in a funk be- fore the prospect of difficulty or to be in despair because opposition lay in his path. Men who were unwilling t 3 work—even to work hard—were amongst the worst members of society ; they were in the direct road to mischief and they were the very curse of any country. Men who quailed before diffi- culty were not worthy to be called men. Difficul- ties were meant to he overcome and they could he overcome by a manly courage, especially by a manly faith in Gad. Sometimes they heard i said that there never was a day in which it was so difficult to get on, to make headway, or to gain success. In some respects that night tie true, hot the rev. gentleman thought that probably there never was a day is which there were I better opportunities for, men to rise. There needed to be a resolute determination and willingness to work hard and well, and to postpone many of the recreations and indulgences of life to maturer years. Mr. Yonee's counsel to young men that night who had life before them,was to be deaf to the pessimistic talk which would make it out that " life is not worth living," and that it was impossible in these days for ordinary men to get on. Life was ever being surveyed and reported on by a num- her of cowardly and misleading spies, who distorted its facts, magnified its difficulties and clrawbacks,and dwelt largely noon its impossibilities. .These witnesses were not to he trusted, and their report not to he acted upon. It was the advice of cowards who were always false in word and in deed.

div.head: NORTHERN RUGBY UNION. RUGBY. WARRINGTON V. LEEDS.
div.p: THE NORTHERN RUGBY UNION. RUGBY. WARRINGTON V. LEEDS.

The Leeds team have never been to Warrington be- fore Saturday, and therefore their advent on that day was very interesting, arm drew a large crowd of specta- tors to the Wilderspeol enclosure. The visitors came with a very good reputation as they have been noted cup fighters,and a few years ago they worked their way to the final of the Yorks cup, each game being won by large mejorities. In the final, when they met Hunslet, their near neighbours, they were however beatesi de- , cisively, by three goals and three tries to nil. They have not performed so well in the Northern League, although in the Yorks section they had worked their way to the secon I position. They have been without their crack players Summerieill and Walker previous to the present month,and probably this has had something to do with it, but now that these players find that they ean maintain their amateur status while playin4 for a Northern Union club, thP Leeds team is very much strengthened, and the above-mentioned players had a great deal to do with the victory of ',Perla over Warring- ton on Saturday. The spectators had a very long wait on Saturday, for altheugh the kick-off was announced to be at three o'ciock,the game did not commence until about ten minutes to four owing to the late arrival of Leeds,who had come br a special train. The consequence was that by the time the game was finished the shades of ia•enin% were fast falling, and the game could not b.. seen very distinctly. Mr Ingham. of Oldham, acted as ; whistle blower, and the fellowing were the teams which were under his supervision r : Warrington : Hee-em, full back Barber, Cross, Bur- . ton and Broady, threequarters ; Foden and Houghton, half Packs ; Burrows, Saunders, Nevins. Thornton, Andtewm, Fairteirst, Wilceek and Hill, forwards. Leeds : Walker, full ha-k ;H. Flainstock, G. W.Hain- stork. Close, and Walton, threequarters ; Summerseill and Midgler. half backs ; Fletcher, Pickles, Riley, Armstrong. Perfit, Greg, Bietle. and Hirst, forwards. H II kicked off towards the pavilion goal, and there being no return, the first scrimmage took place in favour of Warrington, but this advantage Was not maintained, fo Summersgill early showed a tas,e of his abilities by securing the hall and eluding all the Warrington players ' until he c 'me tn Ileesom. His pass to H. Haisstock was keoeked on. otherwise the latter player had a clean field. The ball was seem brought nut in the loose by the War- rime on forward., who dribbled well to half way, where, however, a round of passing between Sinnmereeill, Mideley, Close and the two Hainstocks, almost ended in disaster for Warrimlton, hut fortunately Barber stepped in and prevented anything tangible. Several scrimmages took place in dangerous proximity to the Warrington line, and the Warrineton hacks had all their work cut out to keep hack the invaders. The attack was at length htnueht to a termination by a dribble headed by Hill, Yeithinet and Nevins, and the opposite end of the field Was reached,and Illiestock was penalised for an off-side tackle of Bather not far from the line. Burton attempted a Place kick, but the hall went wide, and was secured by the irrepressible Flainstecks. and a fine bout of passing again made thin.a hot for warrington. After a spell of give aed take play, in which Cross, Barber, Burton and Rieedy were yet, neeeniennue. Leeds again returned to tl e attack, and fe,rn a scrimmage near the line, • utn- meregill se -"tad, and running round the scrimmage, he eluded the home helves, and eeered at the corner. The trr was at a ton difficult angle to be increased to a goal. Immediately after the restart, Barber made a magnificent run. eluding all his opponents with the exception of Walter. No other Warrington player was ready to receive his peas. -•nd thus a grand chance of equalising Was inst. Play confirmed very even, and Burton per- formed a similar feat to Barber. hut with an equally un'ertimate result. The rest of the half was rather in favour of Warringtnn, hut although they played with a will, they Teemed the ability to score, and half-time arrived with Leeds leading by a try to Ml. Thornton met the kick off, and made a sensational rue in retu n, and the run was not brought to a ter- mination entil Walker was reaehed. He managed to seeette the hall, and ha' one of his ponderous kirks, in tench, almost regained all lost ground. Leeds got the better af Warrington from the line nut, and chiefly by nvans of Close. Semmeregill, and Midgley they attacked strongly, but only a minor rewarded their efforts. Some most peiseational play ensued after the drop nut, for Bill, Cress, Burton. and Broady, rushed the ball to the line, and Leeds had a very narrow squeak indeed. and War- rington had nt comae Pquiall. hard line.; as it was, Wal- ker managed Co stay the rush just in the nick of time,end a scrimmage took plane on the line. Semmenseill smartly gathered the hall, and passed to G. W. Hainstock, and this player fairly electrified the spectators by a run from hie own goal line to within a yard or two from the other, passing throne!) the whole of the Warrington team Birher set off in hot pnranit, and tackled him just as a score seemed tertain This effort was completely nulli- fied by a snlendirl dribble which went the length of the field, and taken part in by almost the whole of the War- ringtnn team. After this exeiting play, the ball was !rent for the next ten minutes in Leeds territory, and gave the eeerte men an ennertenity of showing their de- feneiye qualities A fine round of passing between Forlen, Br Arly, Burton, Cross, and Barber, was freitless, and soon after, Feden Was called hack after getting te the line. Cross again, was scarcely quick enough in getting the hall aWRV, o.herwiee a score would almost certainly have enaned. De what they would, Warring- ton were to net over the line. although it was simply marvellous however they WPTP kept out at times. Walker in narticular aid wonders in the defensive line Summersgill raised the ire eif the spectators at this period of the name he his dilqtrn.c. mnvemnnts, as he Was evi- dently bent unrin wasting time. ind the rest of the LlsedS team Were evidently of a simil mind, especially as the darkness was cemine me, They were certainly bent upon keening their Utarl of three nnints at whatever cost. The last two of the three minutes clav waa mere even, and one rush was well oe ginned by n..VSM. Neither aide could hewever score anything more. and Leeds were thu. the winners by the narrow majority of three points to nil.

div.p: WIDNES v. WAKEFIELD TRINITY.

Played at Widnes on the Lowethouse ground on Saturday before 2,500 spentet -rs. Widnes were without Barber through friotion with the committee. Thresh kicked off for the visitors, hut Widnes were the first to attack, and Peters got well down. The leather was re- turned, and Nevitt reoeiving sprinted up the field,where Whines had hard lines Good combination by the visitors' forwards carried nlag to the Widnes 25, where Rianan smartly cilared Griffiths. A scrimmage near the home linen looked ominous,. hut hostilities were ranidlv transferred to the ether end.where Todd kicire dead. This dose was rrpmated a minute later,after which ael 'arance was offer tend Wakefield secured a minor. Tirennan saved a dangerous run, and Drummond floored his man near the line. Widnes were severely pressed for the next few minutes. Then Torii, at the other end,got in some good work, and it was with the greatest diffi- culty that Widnes were prevented °enuring something tangible. Brennan caught the oval, hut his responsive kirk was weak in the extrrine,a nd Millstone merle a good run, which was nullifier near the home lines Fventually Howell got through and scored a try, hut Todd failed to improve. At half-time the visitors were loArling by one try (three points) to nil. In the se-nd half Wakefield had the hest of matters At first thew' pressed strongly, and obtained a goal, but A rtPTVC.TrifI the locals got under weigh, and for a ti me put a different complexion no the face of affairs. Peters was to the fore with a brilliant run, and was floored on the line, hut ultimately Whines secured a t,y, which ii,eenan improved upon. Final result :—Wakefield Trinity, one anal one try (eight point.); Widnes, one goal (five points).

div.head: RUNCORN v. WIGAN.
div.p: RUNCORN v. WIGAN.

There would be nearly 4.000 spectstru A present when these team fared each reher on Saturda-- at Wiean. Wigan had re-arranged their team whilst Runcorn had two changes. Johnson and Farmer being out of the for- wards. After Webster had7not the hall goine,Pseveral sharp but very brief scrimmages took place in mid-field, I Robinann nipped an effort by the home f arwards. and liater,wido passing by Flowers lost his aide ROMP ground. Abrams was prominent in a dribble down touch. Winstanley being safe he returned the ball well into touch at half-way. Gradually Wigan's frant rank bore down to the Runcorn line, where Myers yrii.h Robinson collared very safely. though Jaen and Walkden were on the alert Warder bron.ht relief, and getting a pass from J. Faulkner, gained ennsiderable headway. From the line out the ball travelled across the ground, Railton following up a kirk by. Jam). Gsyter,however, WAS Slfe. The game continued to be very fast, the play being of a very even character. The interval arrived with no score. Faulkner restarted, and Walkden and Jeller ex- charmed kirks. When the teams got fairly settled down the same hard fast game was seen that had character- ized the first half of the play. Some smart exhibition was frequently shown by the Runcorn harks, Myers and Gayter gaining ground. Thin advantage was not held long, as Wigan tic the aid of Winstanler, got up n ar the Runcorn line. Bereahout play was very keen. The Runcorn captain, however, by a strong effort got the ball away, and Warder still further improving the situa- tion, the danger wan averted. J. Faulkner later raised the hopes of the Runcorn con'ingent by a fine dribble I right down to Winstanley, who was, fortunately for Wigan, equal to the pressure. Then another favourable chance to score was lost. Some smart passing by Robinson, Myers, and Gayter was witnessed, but Jagn and Wilding being well up the chance was lost. Play continued very keen and exciting to a degree, and as the time was nearly up both sides were trying their utmost to score a winning point. The game, however, ended without a score.

WARRINGTON " A " v Lazs.—The " A" team of War- rington on Saturday paid a visit to Lees, near Oldham, to play off their fixture there. They were without O'Brian (full back) and Savage (forward). The weather and field were equally bad. The teams were composed as follows :—Warrington : Royle, full back ; Moores, Lawless, Carey, and Foster, three-quarters; Price and Clarke,half-backs; Hampton, Higham,Hughes, Royce, Thorniley, Swift, Monks' Platt and Coop (Lees substitutes) forwards. Lees: W. Lkes.full back ;Scholes, I Underwood,S. Wormall,Hill, three quarters ; Wynneand Phipps half backs; Taylor, Hoyle, Steel, Clayton,Barker, Andrew, Bromley and 'tattersall, forwards. The game commenced with Lees playing with the advantage of the slope. WarrinfAon however immediately got the upper hand and a smart rush put Highatn in possession and a score was the result after two minut2a' play. Lawless failed at the kick. From this point the game was beyond proper description, the homesters playing in such a haphazard manner as to defy passing or open play on into touch part of Warrington. Foster however be kicking touch put Warrington c n the offeusi.re and Carey made a brilliant run threequarter the length of the field, but was knocked into touch. A free kick was granted Lees, and Wynne gavo temporary relief by it. Immediately afterwards Warrington had the same privilege and gained considerably, but Lees became dangerous several times and were near scoring. Half time arrived with Warrington leading by a try to nil. In the second half Warrington took the initiative, and got well down the field. Scholes relieved and Tavler took a free kick which was granted his side, and almost put Lees sheid. Moore retaliated by making his mark, but his kick was returned. Lees then got the upper hand and play waged fiercely on the Warrington 25 flag. Lawless got away but his pass was misr•ed and Tattersall kicked Into touch. Another rush brought Lees into a danger- ous position and would they hays scored but for the fool- ish hesitation of one ot their forwards,who,when within a clear jump of the line hesitated and was immediately grassed by Clarke. Shortly after, " time " was called, and Warrington retired victors of a hotly-contested game by 1 try (3 points) to nil. RUNCORN V. WIGla "L" TRAM3.—Tae first of the season's engagements between these well-known" A" teams took place on the Irwell-lane enclosure. Runcorn on Saturday afternoon. The following was the Runcorn team :—Butterworth, back; T. Richardson, J. Lightfoot B. West; W. Gregory, three-quarter backs ; W. Paudle- bury and E. Woodward. half backs; H. Williams, W. Lightfoot, G. Shaw, A. Clarke, H. Urmson, F. Richard- son. F. Jones and F. Jeacock, forwards. Referee, Mr. . .

Frank Turner, Warrington. W. Lightfoot started, and after the usual preliminaries J. Lightfoot sent the ball into touch at the centre. A lot of pressure was put on the home lines, the burly Wigan forwards keeping the ball tight in the packs. W. Lightfoot eased the pressure by a splendid dribble. This was followed by some fine passing by the home backs,and Gregory was almost through. However, a moment later, F. Richareson got over from a line-out, but J. Lightfoot failed to " majoriza.'"Phe home forwards gave the visitors an anxious time, their short sharp passing fairly bewilderiag them. Lowe and Dixon were the means of giving relief, and things looked ominous for Runcorn when they were penalized in front of the posts,but Fair- dough's kick sailed outside. The homesters now had a turn, and some splendid passing was witnessed. The pressure was kept up,the pace now telling on the visitors. Woodward and W. Pendlehury kept the home three- quarters fairly at work. Immediately after Gregory and Woodward had the hardest of luck, whilst from a mark, J. Lightfoot's shot went under the bar. The in- terval arrived with the scorsi—Runcorn,two tries; Wigan nil. McNimara restarted, and some exciting passages took place, Mitchinson giving Roberts plenty of work, but he failed to effect an opening. At length Woodward gave to W. Pendlebury, and another fine exhibition was given by the home backs, which West finished by scoring in a favourable position, but still the goal kick failed. Following the kick out Clarke secured and made an excellent drop at goal, it being a very near shave. Wigan now paid a flying visit, hut Butterworth soon sent them to the rightabout, he having displayed good form throughout the game. A brilliant game ended in , another win for Runcorn by four tries to nil.

div.head: WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE WOMEN'S LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
SALE OF WORE.

On Monday afternoon a-t-id 'eV-Wing a small sale of work got up by the members of the above Association was held in the Council Room, of the Liberal Club. The object of the sale, which consisted of good of a chiefly useful naeure,mostly made by the ladies themselves,was, if possible, to raise the sum of £25. When the proceed- ings commenced at 4 o'clock there were present : Mesdames Z. Armitage, W. Pierpoint, H. Roberts, J. W direr, Cook. Barker (all of whom assisted at the tills), Scott. R. Garnett, Yonee,W. Roberts, Wyllie. H. M. Ashton, J. R. Young, Mounfield, Crampton, Rodger, Price Edels,en, Misses Barker, Cornell, etc. ; Mr. P. B. Scott,Councillor Roberts, Councillor Tinnion, Messrs. Z. Armitage, J. H. Fleming, C.J. ilolmes, Cooke, Highley, Haskoll (Manchest‘r), and Crumbleholme (Bolton). Among the articles tastefully displayed on the stalls were notably the handsome prizes presented by Mr. A. H. Crosfield for the Christmas billiard handicap. In opening the proceedings, Mr. ARMITAGE (who pre- sided),said it was hardly necessary for him to introduce Mr. Scott to them,as he was tolerably well-known at the Liberal club. (Flear,heer.) He had come amongst them that afternoon for a very definite purpose, and that was to assist the ladies of the Liberal Aesociation to realise • small sum of money for the education of their friends in the constituency. (Lpplause.) Mr. SCOTT, who was warmly received, said it gave him great pleasure to come amongst them that afternoon for the purpose of formally declaring the sale of work open. They had met for the purpose of realizing a sum of money to assist the work whieh the ladies of the Association had been carrying on for a considerable time. It was work of a very proper kind, the work of educe- cation, which as Lord Rosebery said the other day at '.icarborough, was needed more than anything else by the Liberal party. They must educate ! educate ! educate ! (Hear, hear' and applause.) They had never lost sight of the fact that the ladies were the backbone of their parts, and that they could do more to help them if they would than aaybody else. He was perfectly certain , that the efforts they put forth at the late general elec- tion accounted to a large extent for the good result ob- tained, while with regard to the recent municipal elections he belieeed they would not have come out of ' them as a p irty in such a magnificent manner, and have returned so many Liberals to the Town Council, if it had not been for the help of the ladies. (Hear, hear and ED- plawe.) He very much regretted that in Bewsey Ward, in which their club was situated, they had !net their representation. He hoped, however, that they would soon be able to recover it. In the Town Hall Ward they had lost by only four votes, and he could assure Mr. Clay that they regretted his loss exceedingly. (Hear, hear.)Flis (Mr Clay's) better-half had been more lucky,as she was a member of the Board of Guardians. He wished her husband had been able to obtain a seat in the Town Coon, il, but that would be secured for him before very long. (Applause.) The money that was about to be raised was to enable the Mies to propound their views to other ladies in the district. He hoped the ladies of Warrington would rally mind Mrs. Armitage, their president, and others who were aseocisted with her, and attend the sale in large numbers. Three years ago they held a baz tar which real;zed a very large sum of money, and the ladies were good enough on that occasion not to keep it all to them- selves, and 12 months ago another sale of work was held, the proceeds of which were given to assist in the expenses of the municipal elections. And that was of great assistance in getting gentlemen to stand for muni- cipal affairs who otherwise would have had to refuse on the ground that they were not able to boar the whole cost themselves. He hoped that the sale would be a successfu one, and that a large sum would be realized. He would make it his duty to go round and see what he could purchase to be of use, and what was not of use be would ask Mrs. Armitage to give to the benefit of some institution for the betterment of the poor of War- rington. (Applause.) Mr. Scett concluded by declaring the sale open. Councillor Tremtme, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr Scott for his presence and services, said their candi- date was the sort of gentleman they had been looking for for a considerable time in Warrington. However large a number they might have had to select from they could not have found one more suitable to tight their battle at a Parliamentary election, and to dischatge the multifarious duties belonging to such a position. (Hear, hear.) His kind and courteous manner had won for him the respect and esteem ef all with whom he had come into contact. (Applause). Be had always been fund ready and willing to assist in everything that was for the good not only of the Liberal party but of the inhabit- ants generally, end the least they co:•Id do, when he in- convenienced himself by coming from Manchester to assist them, was to accord him a hearty vote of thanks. (Applause ) Couocillor ROBLIRTS seconded, and observed that they might safely take that opportunity of congratulating Coencillor Tinnion, as the junior member of the Liberal party in the Town Council, and themselves upon having secured his valuable services. (Hear, hear.) Speaking as the oldest member of the Liberal party in the Council he weke tried him with all the ardour of his Celtic nature, and he was certain that they would not be disappointed in him, but that he would enable them in that illustrious cham- ber to render services to that illustrious borough. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He endorsed all that Councillor Tinnnn had said, and it was the general opinion of the party and of the town that they bad secured in Mr. Scott a valuable ally for all the forces that made for the good of the town. (Applause.) Mrs. ARMITAGE apologized for the absence of Mrs. John Crostleld (who had sent them a cheque for two guineas), Mrs. Clay (who was somewhat seriously indis- posed) and Miss Dutton (who had also sent them a con- tribution). The resolution was then put to the meeting and un- animously agreed to. and Mr. Scott having briefly re- turned thanks, the sale of work was commenced at once and the business of buying and selling contiuned briskly during the day. Sengs, acc., were rendered in a very able manner by the Misses Fleming, Gomel', and Birchall, and Messrs. Frank Haskoll, Fred Fieldhouse, and others. The am- ount realized at the sale was over £35, including a cheque for five guineas from Mr. Scott, who was also the purchaser of several articles of value.

The returns for the week ended Friday, November 8, show a eati‘factory increase in the traffic to and from the various docks and wharves on the Ship Canal as compared with the preceding seven days. The arrivals and departures of sea-going vessels numbered 150, as against 103 in the previous week, and the aggregate net registered tonnage usinc, the port was 38,408, 5272 tons more than in the preceding week. Foreign trafficshowed an augmentation nf five ships and 4,532 tons, and the coasting trade of 42 ships and 740 registered tons. On Monday evening Mr. Wilkinson the popular lantern exhibitor gave an interesting and instruc- tive lime light entertainment in the above place of worship, this being the first of a series of monthly Band of Hope meetings to beheld during the winter season. Mr. Wilkinson very kindly secured material for a new subject entitled "The Gambler." The slides were well got up, and the instrument being manipulated with the exhibitor's usual ability and precison the pictures were thrown upon the canvas, with great clearness, to the astonish-. ment and perfect satisfaction of all present. Mr Thornton at the exhibitor's request did not read but related and commented upon each and every picture, just giving the most interesting and salient points of the narrative. This being over,a number of other slides were introduced of a comic and lively character, eliciting repeated cheers, and roars of laughter from the audience. Hymns were also thrown upon the canvas from which the audience sang with life and vigour. The meeting was interspersed with music. Two solos were excellently rendered by Mr. Glover, and two duets were given with pest credit on bass instruments by Messrs. R. Bennett and Jones, and two violin solos were given with usual satisfaction by Master A. Bennett. After an hour and forty minutes' en- joyment, votes of thanks and the Doxology brought the meeting to a close.

LYMM V. BROADEMATH.—At LyMM before a good gate, the visitors bringing a large following. Broad- heath won the toss and elected to play down bill with the sun at their backs. From the kick off the game ruled very fast, both sets of backs being frequently tested. After 15 minutes' play a long shot from one of the visitors' half backs was only partially clea ed by Leigh, and O'Flara rushing up scored the first goal for the visitors After this reverse the home forwards played up splendidly, and %Nilson equalised with a good shot. Lymm continued to have slightly the best of the play, the forwards playing a good game,and Sidley gave them the lead before half time. In the second half the game became rather rough, and one of the players was ordered off the field. Although playing a man shrrt the home- eters had no difficulty in preventing further acoring,and the game ended Lymm two goals ; Broadheath one.

The express, which had about thirty pas- sengers for the north, had reached St. Neota station, when, owing to a fracture of the rail, some of the vehicles In the back portion of the train were derailed, and dashed with terrific force against some coal-laden trucks in a siding. The leading carriage was wrecked, and the remainder damaged. The front portion of the train travelled a quarter of a mile before it was dis- covered that an accident had occurred, On the wrecked portion being examined it was ascertained that bliss O'Hara, a young lady residing in Crouch End, London, had been killed, and that five other persons had beets injured, more or less seriously. The injured persons were immediately attended to, and the front portion afte r , wards proceeded northwards with the uninjured pas sengers. Sir H. Oakley, general 'Kantor, attributes the accident entirely to a faulty rail.

THE WARRINGTON LEAGUE OF THE CROSS.

On lilnnday evening at the League Hall, Bewsey- street, a successful gathering of the members and friends ot the L ague of the Cross, took place, to celebrate the 24th anniversary of the founding ot the League. Dancing commenced at eight p.m., and was kept up until shortly after eleven p.m. During the intervals songs were given by Messrs. Thomp-on, Freeth, Brown and Dalton, each singer receiving an encore. The League band played for the dances in excellent style, and all enjoyed them- selves to their heart's content. 't'he meeting, proper, was held durinz one of the intervals of dancing. Mr. Mullins first addressed the meeting giving short history of the League since the commence- ment, and trusted they would all be spared to cele- brate, next year, the silver jubilee of the League of the Cross,in the largest hall in Warrington.—Mr. J. C. Dalton said the opponents of the total abstin- ence movement, had no better argument against them than insult and abuse. They called them fanatics, and wild dreamers. But if there was any- thing of fanatici-m or of useless drerming about this movement, he for one would not waste his time over it. Could they call such men as Sir William Gull, Sir Andrew Clarke. Dr. Norman Kerr, Dr. Richardson, Dr. Horsley, Dr. Parkes and Dr. Ridge, wild dreamers, or fanatics? (Applause.) The speaker quoted several authorities, and asked how in the face of such a testimony could anyone have the face to dub the workers in the total abstinence movement, fanatics and dreamers ? He concluded his address by exhorting all to help the work of the League, and so they would raise their people to a higher level in the sight of God and man. Mr Dalton then sang " You'll Remember Me," and in response to a hearty encore gal "My pretty Jane.' for which he was applauded.—The dancing then proceeded, and after a most enjoyable and instruc• tive night the meeting came to a close about a quarter past eleven. Much praise is due to Mr. Mullins, and the members of the band, for the able manner in which they played the mu-ic for thi- dancing.

MISSIONARY SERVICES IN THE PARISH CHURCH The annual missionary services in support of foreign missions were held in the Parish Church,on Sunday, when the pulpit was occupied, both at morning and afternoon services, by the Rev. J Douglas Lord, of Liverpool, late missionary of Ali- mednagar, in India. On Sunday evening the same gentleman preached before a good cont,,regation in the Mission Room,Prestonßrook, when an interest- ing sermon was delivered. In spite of the unfavour able weather the attendance was very satisfactory. and the collections at the Parish Church, Mission Room. and Moore Church Institute amounted to .£lO 17s. lid. At the usual missionary meeting, on Monday evening, in the Sessions-room, Mr. Lord addressed a well-attended meeting, and spoke of the various features of missionary work in India, illustrating his remarks by maps, pictures, &c., which made the subject interesting, The Rev. H. Smith presided, and before introducing Mr. Lord re- gretted the absence of the Vicar through ill-health. At the chse of Mr. Lord's address a collection was made, which amounted to £1 Os. 4d. The total amount in the missionary boxes distributed through the parish, the chairman announced, was .£9 10s. 2id., making on the whole the sum of £2l 16s. 7d. this year, a slight increase on last year, which may be considered satisfactory. In response to an appeal by Mr. Lord four new boxes were ap- plied for at the end of the meeting. The Rev. J. Gilbertson also spoke, and before the termination of the meeting proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the lecturer. This was seconded by Mr. Darlington and passed, and the meeting terminated. div.head: PRESBNTATION TO COUNCILLOR .DR. CANNELL,
div.p: PRESBNTATION TO COUNCILLOR .DR. CANNELL,

On Saturday evening, Dr. Cannell was made the recipient of another present, this time from em- ployes of the Corporation, congratulating him upon his and ebony walking stick with a silver handle, which contained the following inscription : the " Presented to Dr. Cannell by the Warrington Cor- poration Employes." The text of the address, which had been written by Messrs. Brookes and Sons, illu- minators, Warrington, was as follows :—" To Coun- cillor Dr. James Connell. Dear Sir,—We, the em- ployes of the Warrington Corporation, beg to con- gratulate you on the occasion of your beinir re-elected to the Council unopposed, and take this opportunity of asking your acceptance of an ebny stick with inscribed silver handle, as o small token of the high esteem in which you are held by us." The addressed was signed by 36 of the employe, including William Ashton (secretary) and William Todd (treasurer). The presentation was made at the doctor's house in Academy-street, The presen- tation was made by Mr. Ashton, and he and others spoke ef the great esteem in which the doctor is held. Councillor Connell responded in feeling terms. AMBULANCE LECTURE AT DARIO:WRY. On Monday evening the second ambulance lecture was given by Dr. Bower in the Beard School, about 28 students attending. Ihe doctor commenced by recapitulating the instruction given at the previous class, which treated generally of the anatomy of the human body. Hemorrhage formed the euhject of the present lecture, and the doctor, aided by dia- grams, proceeded to point out the main arteries in the human system, showing at the same time how and when the circulation might be arrested when necessery. Arterial, venous, and capillary bleeding were then minutely described, and simple modes of distinguishing one from the other given. The different ways of arresting hemorrhage, whether by pressure, position. cold, &c., were then explained and useful hints given The latter portion of the lecture was taken up with the uses and modes of application of the triangular bandage, each student in turn manipulating it upon his neighbour.

CAUCUS MEETING OF THE TOWN COUNCIL.
SELECTION OF MAYOR, ALDERMEN, AND
COMMITTEES.

A caucus meeting of the Warrington Town Coun- cil was held in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall on Thursday evening, the Mayor (Councillor James Fairclough) presiding. There was a full at- tendance of members. • THE MAYORALTY.

Councillor Fairclough was unanimously invited to accept the mayoralty for another year, and be agreed to accept the position.As the Mayor is one of the Councillors for Sr. Austin's ward who will retire text November the members of the Council gener- ally agreed to use their influence to secure his un- opposed return. There was a similar agreement with regard to Councillor Tinnion, the Liberal mem- ber who was elected last week. Mr. Tinnion will be under the necessity of retiring next year in the event of tho extension of the borough, which will considerably enlarge St. Austin's ward.

div.head: WARRINGTON MIN DROWNED IN THE CANAL AT LATCHFOItD.
div.p: A WARRINGTON MIN DROWNED IN THE CANAL AT LATCHFOItD.
ANOTHER RESULT OF INFLUENZA.

Last Friday afternoon, at the " Dug and Dart " Inn Grappenhall, Mr. Yee, coroner, held an inquest on the body of John Boyd, Aiken-st., Warrington, who was drowned in the Ship Canal on Thursday noon. John Frown, 571, Kuutsford-road,was riding along the road on the canal side on the day in question in order to cross by the ferry, when he saw the deceased on the op- posite side of the canal take off his jacket and cap and lay them on the bank. Witness remarked to a friend that deceased was perhaps going to have a wash, when he rushed straight into toe water and disappeared. Witness at once went to the ferry man and reported what he had seen. There was no one on the bank at the time.

Mr. Marshall, lock-master, said that at noon on Thura- day a youth named John Brown in the employ of the Ship Canal Company, brought word to the Locks that a man had taken some of his clothes off and put them on the bank, walked down the slope, and plunged into the canal. Witness immediately went to tne place in a boat and commenced to grapple, and afterwards resorting to a boat hook, in a short time succeeded in bringing the body to the surface, and conveying it to the Locks. Pre- vious to recovering the body witness informed the police and on their arrival the body was conveyed to the "Dog and Dart "Inn. On searching the coat, which was found on the bank, a watch was found in the pocket, and en- graved in the case was the name and address of deceased. From this witness was enabled to inform the deceased's relatives of the occurrence. . _ _
P.C. Brew said that at 2 p.m.he went to the Latchford Lock and brought the body to the Inn. On searching the clothes he found 2s. 101 in money and a pipe, keys,and knife.

Mrs. Boyd said her husband was a wiredrawer,and 57 years of age. He had been, ill for some time in conse- quence of having influenza. He had been off work for about 13 weeks, and for some time he had been strange in his manner. She had contemplated placing him in an asylum. Deceased never attempted or said he would commit suicide. This last week he had been much better, and Dr.Braide said he thought he was all right. Witness last saw deceased about ten on Thursday morning taking the dog for a walk. He said he would not he long, but at about two o'clock she heard ef the occurrence. She identified the body as that of her husband. He had no money troubles. The Coroner said they were all very sorry for Mrs. Boyd. The case was apparently only another result of that dread disease, influenza which had rendered de- ceased nervous and brought him under the influence of a kind of melancholia.
The jury returned a verdict of "Suicide whilst tem- porarily insane."

CAN FINITE MAN KNOW INFINI IE TRUTH. Sir,—Your 'Frisco correspondent " Colin Clout" who began to doubt with Page Hopps and went too far with Bradlaugh, asks " Can we know the truth " ? To this, one answer only is possible—No ! The truth is all the truth, which can never be known to us with our finite faculties. All that we may hope to attain is some small fragment of the truth. But our confessed inability to know the truth by no means prevents us from detecting and denouncing discoverable errors. And, on the entirely reasonable supposition that there is a God of Truth, it is our duty to eliminate from His service, all such errors when detected. And yet, with what persist- ence the churches still insist upon the inculcation of the dead dogmas of ancestral ignorance, too often alas! to the total neglect of the living virtues. Hence we see the cloistered monk mumbling from his man-made manual and saturating himself with his barren ritual while so much of his Master's work awaited his helping hand out- side. And one of the evil consequences of this immurem- ent,'rnental and bodily isolation is—that its victims, the preachers and practisers of a hide-bound ecclesiasticism —past or present—think more of what nip be inimical to the church or the sect rather than of what may be harmful to those little much-neglected virtues the presence or absence of which is the fertile source of human misery or of human happiness. And this kind of crystalised Christianity is very prevalent among us to-day. Hence I think my friend Colin may " call" as he says" upon the world known as Christian to be at least honest, and confess at once that the Bible is not the inspired word of God." • Now I think we are justified in calling upon the Christians to be honest—but, as I may "call spirits from the vasty deep," without the remotest chance of their ever coming—so you may call yourself h. .arse ere you get the average Christian to break his shell and think for himself—at "once." The time accumulated crust of custom is not thus easily to be broken; your "floe old crusted "Christian has made up what he is pleased to regard as his "mind " long ages since. There he planted his foot, and there he now stands, a meter'. • .ioly mark, by which to measure the advance of others. F 4 him the theological world does stand still, and Bit-Al- ai astronomy and geology rest upon Mr. Gladstone's Impregnable Rock as firmly as ever. No! my dear " Cohn" it is useless for you or me to insist upon sudden reformation in such a one, to come out and do a bit of . thinking for himself. But, although there are ears thus deafened by the" drum ecclesiastic," it is still our duty —yours and mine dear Colin—to he sowing the good seeds of truth, justice and mercy, that some of them mayhaP fall upon good ground and fructify to the bless- lug of mankind. And new, sir, I hope "Cohn" will forgive me if I point out what to me seem discrepancies in his last and penultimate paragraphs. In one he tells us " infidelity " Is not spreading among us. In the other, that the masses are anti-Christian. Now if for the word " infi- delity " atheism be substituted all would be right. In- fidelity is now very respectable. I have it on the highest authority that His Grace of Canterbury is an infidel—to a turbanded Turk. Both are infidels—each to each other. "For modes of faith let graceless bigots tight, Ile can't be wrong whose life is in the right."

THE PROPOSED W ARRINGTON CATTLE MARKET. Sir,—The suggestion of J. H.. ef Whitecross Ward is very good on the face of it, but I think we of the said ward really have our fair share of trouble by being visited occasionally by different infectious complaints, especially in Howard-St., without baying pig patients down with the foot and mouth disease. I supest that there should he a vote taken of the whole town to decide on the best and most proper site for the fair. I would further sugge.t that some returns ought rightly to be allowed to he made out of the Old Barracks,and that it would be greatly to the benefit of the town if the an- nual horse fair was held there.—Yours truly, F. D.
Erafield-St.

Sir,—The stiavestion offered in last week's issue, re- garding existing facts, in relation to the best and least offensive site for the new cattle and horse fair, is not entertainable, though admirably selected and nicely located. In the first place,the plot of ground mentioned is too small in area, and being lined on two sides by rail- ways would prove dangerous to market evolutions. Again the ground would require expenditure in leveling and high boarding. Its great defect is its small area,

there being no possible path in it suitable for movements usual in every cattle market or horse fair. It is in nearer proximity to the railways than any other site but most of the horses come by road within near radius of the town's centre. The compensation which this site offers as regards railways would be lost in that it offers no pos- sibility of enlargement unless the piece of ground opposite to it were taken, which would not be as a main road divides them, and dwelling houses of the working class (who are quite as sensitive as the Wilson-Pattsn-street people) adjoin. Above all, the Corporation hold in their hands,hesitat- ing only at the behests of people living fully a hundred yards away from it. the best possible and least off-n- -sive site the old militia barracks, the rooms of which I believe are already in Corporate use. There are within its walls lengthy sheds admirably suited to stabling cattle or horses, and also office and other accommodation very acceptable to dealers. This site would entail no expense of note, and is outside the town almost, with a long unpaved rcad at its end suitable, being houseless, for trials of speed and action. The large tract of land at Orford is Iry-ant—so the elec- tors of that ward understand—for a public pleasure ground or garden even,a much more pleasing and needed purpose in a densley crewded area than he added con- jestion of a great trade fair. However, the venture is professedly temporary. Generally the Council waits for public opinion to declare itself and then begins opera- tions. Average men opinionate for the Barracks as the only idea really workable, having, as it has, a large vacant plot of ground close by for possible extension. This vacant ground has often been used by travelling circuses which proved no nuisance to the neighbourhood and so occasional fairs would not under the sanitary re- sources of the Corporation. The large hotel adjoining, also offers commodious stabling. To-day unnecessary expenditure of public money is forbidden by a higher authority than the clique-fearing council—the ratepay- ing electors. It is fairly maintainable that no nuisance would really arose from the high-walled Barracks as a horse and cattle market. The seasons in which the fairs are held are all against it, while the houses are all, with the exception of six, sufficiently removed from the pur- lieus of the site as not to inflict anything beyond imagin- ary ills on their tenants. The L.N.W. low-level runs alongside it. The site is near to the Bank Quay cattle and goods station, and nearer the Cheshire roads than any other sites are, unless the Corporation went in for large field-accommodation at Wilderspiol. Apart from this, the Barracks should be put to its admirably fitted use—that of Warrington's half-yearly cattle and horse fairs.—Yours, Arc:, Warrington.
