PARISH COUNCIL Meeerrece—A meeting of the Parish Council was held in the Girl's school, flaltin, on Tues- day evening. The Rev. G. D. Wray occupied the chair and there were also present Messrs. J. Ackerley, J. Looker, W. McCulloch, R. Hughes.J. Astbury,S. Barrow, J. S. Jeacock, J. Stokes, and A. Woodier (clerk). The business of the meeting was chiefly with reeard to the path leading from Halton to Halton Brook, and the Hanging Rock-road.—The Clerk stated that he had com- municated with the Runcorn Rural Council with refer- ence to the latter road but had not received any reply. —After same discussion it was decided that a commit- tee be appointed to inspect the roads mentioned, and re' port as to what they thought necessary to a further meeting. The following were appointed on the commit- tee : Messrs. J. Astbury. J. Looker, J. Astbury, and W. McCulloch.—The Clerk reported that four interments had taken place in the Cemetery since the last meeting. He was authorised to purchase a dozen trees to be planted in the Cernetery.—This concluded Ithe,busitiess. DEATH AND BURIAL OF MISS SAUNDRRS. —On the sth islet., Miss Louisa Saunders, aged 30, succumbed to the ravages of consumption. She belonged to the Wesleyan Church, was a member of Society, sang in the choir,and taught in the Sunday school. As long as health per- mitted, she discharged her duties in a faithful and con- scientious manner, gaining the esteem and approbation of those amongst whom she laboured. The interment took place on Saturday afternoon, in the Halton Ceme- tery. The teachers and scholars of the Sunday school, walked before tee coffin, which was borne by the following members of the choir : Messrs. W. Rowe, W. Moors, W. Astbury, E. Mulkey, J B. Houghton, R. Sutton, C. P. Bradbury and T. W. Barrow. After the coffin, walked : Mrs. Saunders (mother), Messrs. Samuel, John and Albert Saunders (brothers), Mrs. Marsden and Miss Amy Saunders (sisters). Mr. J. Mason (brother-in- law), Mrs. Clarke (aunt), Misses E. Saunders and E. Mason (nieces), Mr. S. Mason (nephew), Mr. S. Clarke (cousin), Mr. and Mrs. Lockett. Miss Kneen, Miss Foster, Mrs. J. B. Houghton, Miss Rowe, Messrs. Kneen, J. Looker and S. Tomlinson. The first part of the burial service was conducted in the Wesleyan Church, the officiating minister being the Rev. C. P. Gliddon. The hymns "Rock of Ages" and "Shall we gather at the river," were sung ; and as the coffin was conveyed out of the church, Mr. Sutton played the Dead March. Wreaths, etc, from the following persons, were placed on the grave: Mrs. Marsden, Mr. and Mrs. Mason and family, Mrs. Clarke, Lady Brooke, Miss Rowe. Miss Boys, Mr. and Mrs. Houghton, Mr. and Mrs. W. Nixon, Mr. and Mrs. Aspull (Liverpool), Misses E and A. Howard, and the young ladies of the Sunday school. REV. T. BRACKENBITRY AND PREJUDICE IN PUBLIC AFFAIRS.—In a sermon preached in the Halton Wesleyan Church on Sunday night.the Rev. T. Brackenbury spoke very strongly against prejudice in national, social, and political life. He said the English people have their full share of national prejudice. Our intercourse with the people of other countries,is characterised by haughtiness of manner, and we speak of them with a contempt which arises from an overweening self esteem. Hence, African life is held to be very cheap ; the Flindoos, with all their millions, are regarded as people to be managed by such superior persons as ourselves ; some South Sea tribes are doomed by us to pitiless extermination ; no Irish need apply for some situations ; and one English- man is said to be equal to an indefinite number of Frenchmen. Christianity has done a very great deal to extinguish and chasten this pride ; but we have still much to learn. Prejudice should he guarded against in social and political life. Every Christian community should be marked by candour, sincerity, and mutual charity, goodwill, and forbearance. The end of all public. discussion should he to arrive at righteousness and truth ; and all public. bodies should seek, above all things the advantage and welfare of the neighbourhood and nation. But we are very far from this state of things at the present time. Some speeches made in Par- liament and on political platforms, are directly intended to create or strengthen prejudice. A spirit of partis- anship very often stands in the way of a manifest public good. The constant strife between capital and labour shows the strong prejudiee between clan and class. How easy it is to assume that workingmen are always unreasonable and selfish, or that employers are always avaricious and oppressive. Look at the present discus- sion on the subject of national education. What an enormous amount of prejudice there is in the clerical mind. It is assumed that a denominational schdol under the direction of a clergyman, must be a factory that produces superfine humanity,a training ground in which children are developed late patriots and saintr. On the other hand it is assumed that a board school manaeed by representatives of the ratepayers must be godless, mischievous,almorrt a den of thieves, because it does not give the full teaching of a semi-popish catechism, hut only teaches us what is in the Bible. This prejudice causes a very good deal of social estrangement. People living in the same neighbourtrand, regard one another as strangers and aliens, because of some little difference in their social status, or because they belong to different Christian c ngregations, or different potitin.l parties. et cannot be a Christian thing for two sections of the com- munity to stand face to face, and each think that no good can come from the other. If Jesus Christ were to live in EnglancLas he once did in Palestine, he would re- buke this prejudicial pride ; he would once more say, If ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others ? Do not even the publicans the same ?"

MARRIAGE Or A WARRINGTONIAN IN AMERICA. "The Chicago Globe" of October 26th, contains the following : "The wedding of Mr. D. D. Dixon to Miss Esther Llewellyn, youngest daughter of Mr. R. Llewellyn, Catherine-street. Warrington, took place at the home of Mr. C. H. Dixon, Chicago, on Satur- day evening, October 19th, the Rev. A. Waller, of Whiting, officiating. The ceremony was nerformed at 8 o'clock, in the presence of about 70 guests." After the happy couple were joined together, over sixty sat down to a hot supper, after which the bride and groom left amid showers of rice and old shoes to spend their honeymoon at Roseland, Illinois. The groom is one of our most exemplary young men and the bride, who came more recently from England, is also highly respected by all of her acquaintances. We join in wishing them a happy, useful and prosperous life. The presents were numerous and useful."

Lord Wolseley admits that in the Coornassie affair he was in grave personal danger. He and his advanced force were surrounded and hsmmed in. and it became nearly a hand-to-hand fight. He noticed one man in civilian attire who was literally surrounded, but who calmly went on potting Ashantees with hi g rifle. This turned out to be Mr. H. M. Stanley, the correspondent of the " New York Herald." " You were lucky to escape." said Wolseley. " Did you not see you were surrounded ?" " Well," replied Stanley, " I guess I was too much occupied by the niggers in front to pay much attention to those behind." And Viscount Wolseley adds :—" I took a liking to him on the spot, and we be- came great friends. Nor has anything occurred since to alter my opinion of him that his courage is of the best quality."

EARLESTOWN A.ND NEWTON. EARLESTOWN ESLEY GUILD. At the weekly meeting of this Guild held in the Lecture Hall of the Earlestown Wesleyan Chapel, under the presidency of the Rev. J. Bartley,a paper on"A brief review of Nathaniel Itawthorne's Scarlet Letter," was read by the Rev. F. G. Howland. A short discussion afterwards took pl9ce and a vote of thanks to the essayist terminated the meeting. 1.0.G.T. EBENEZER LODGE. This lodge held its usual weekly meeting in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Tuesday evening. The session was called to order at eight p.m. by Bro. W. Hatton, (3.1'. Eight members having been initiated the programme was rendered. Bros. W. Brown, Broster, and others, gave songs, and Bro. J. Taylor gave a very interesting Lancashire reading after which the lodge closed at 9-45. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. At the Earlestown Police Station on Monday morning, before Mr. C. B. F. Borrou and Mr. J. W. Emmett, Patrick Drudy of Newton CoMM3B, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in , Market•st., Earlestown, on Saturday night, and was fined 2s. 61. and costs.—John Grady for a similar offence in Crow Lane, Newton, was tined ss. and costs. —James Davies of Lyme-st., Haydock, for being drunk and disorderly in Market-se, Earles- town' was tined ss. and costs.—Re was also charged with kicking and striking P.U.'s Green and Bulien when being arrested, and for this offence was fined ss. and Costs. SERIOUS ILLNESS OF Mn. BRIERLEY. It is with regret that we have to announce that Mr. Brierley, clerk and surveyor to the Newton District Council has been seized with a sudden and serious Hines. He was engaged at the office on Monday when be was apparently in his usual health. About four o'clock he had occasion to go into one of the side rooms for some papers, when he experienced a sensation in the head which de- prived him of the use of his right side and he fell , against the shelves. He managed however to Cr Lwl out into his office, and a few minutes later Mr. John Ball, school attendance officer, found him there incapable. He called assistance, and he and Mr. Parry the hal; keeper removed him to a cab and he was conveyed home. Dr. Watkins was sum- moned and found Mr. Brierley to be suffering from partial paralysis. At the time of writing, however, he was slowly improving. EARLESTOWN ORCHESTRAL SOCIETY. In order to assist the funds of the Medical Aid Society, a concert promoted and managed by the Earlestown Orchestral Society, was given in tt•e Town Hall on Thursday evening. The artistes with one exception were entirely local, and they ac- quitted themselves in an excellent manner. The oand.which has latterly made considerable progress gave four selections including "L'Amour au Village" "Donau Wellen." "Bohemian Girl," and " White- hall," each of which were submitted efficiently. The other items on the programme were, song, " Thy foe,' Mr. Higham, song, " Should he upbraid," Miss May Clare, song "Alone on the Raft," encored. Song with violin obligate, " Star of the Desert," Mr. J Higham, song, "Angus McDonald," Miss May Clare. The humorous portions were given by Mr. A. G. Davies of Huyton, whose contributions were of course encored. Mrs. Latimer efficiently per- formed the onerous duties of accompanist. EARLESTOWN AND DISTRICT MEDICAL AID In order to assist the funds of this worthy society a collection was last week end made amongst the workmen employed at the Viaduct Works, and the sum of £8 us. 3d. was subscribed. Last year when a similar collection was made, the amount of the contribution was .£lO Is. 3d. Although there are almost double the number of men employed at the Viaduct Works their contributions this year only exceeded those of the Vulcan Foundry last year by something like five shillings, the total ot the col- lection at the latter place last year being SS 16s. 10d. We are requested to state that the appli- ances of the Medical Aid Society, and the services of the nurse are requisitioned by the employes of the Viaduct Works to a very tauch larger extent than any of the other works in the district, and their contributions are not by any means commen- surate with the advantages they derive from the society.

div.head: RUNCORN TONIC Sol-FA CEIOI.P. CONCERT.
div.p: RUNCORN TONIC Sol-FA CEIOI.P. CONCERT.

On Wednesday evening the Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa prize choir opened its eleventh season with a grand con- . cert and there was a most encouraging attendance. The programme was of a miscellaneous character and in- cluded songs tor each of the three principal vocalists en- gaged, and also a trio by them, as well as some part songs, an anthem, and a glee by the choir. Miss Lillie Wormald, Mr. Tom Thomas, RA M., and Mr. Stanley Cookson were the principal artistes—the latter having previously appeared before a Runcorn audience. " Les noces de -Jeanette "—the song of the nightingale—was Miss Worinald's first effort. It is a song abounding in difficult passages and her interpretation of it was such as to attest her possession of a cultivated and sweet, although not powerful, soprano voice. The trills in imitation of the feathered sweet songster were heard to advantage. Miss Wormald gave an equally intelligent interpretation of the two songs " Astliore;" and Taubert's "In a distant land." In his first contri- bar ion, Mr. Thomas treated us in his rich tenor voice to a fine rendering of the song " Alice !• where art thou ?" and he was also successful in his singing of " The Heavenly Song," and " The Last Watch." The latter song was given with that sparkling vivacity which showed that he had fully caught the spirit of the words, and in response to the vociferous applause of the audi- ence he complied with a recall, and sang " Mary Lee " with such pint and finish as to still further delight the audience. Mr. Stanley Cookson at once earned the goodwill of the auditory by his singing of " The Arabian Lover." Mr. Cookson is the possessor of a robust bass voice and sings well. " The Bandolero " was a song well suited to his style, and he made the most of the piquant points of the story of the gallant outlaw—Ban- dolero. In this song he was encored, and complying, he gave an excellent interpretation of the amusing song, "Laugh while you may." A further contribution " Only to Love," was the concluding item of the programme, and he sang it with musicianly taste and skill. An in- teresting feature of the evening's concert was a trio by the three leading vocalists, entitled " The Tt ree Dreams" (Macrarren), purporting to deal with the superstition that if a girl dreams thrice of her lover, the third time the dream will be realised. But it is of the work of the chorus that special mention should be made. It was in this department that the chief interest lay, andgit must be admitted that the choir con- sisting of about seventy vocalists, acquitted itself admirably. The well-known and popular part song "Excelsior," was their first contribution which was given in a manner which left nothing to be desired. "The Shepherd's Lament" was another very agreeable item performed by them, and was a test piece in the competition at the Crystal Palace, London, in 1894, and at which the members of the Runcorn choir distinguished themselves. Their interpretation of it on Wednesday night was alike creditable to them and the conductor— the robustness of attack and the subtle gradations of tone being all that could be wished for. Another selected piece was the anthem "Come unto Me" (Grounod), but it would be invidious to make special mention of all , their contributions which also included the part songs "The Fisherman's Goodnight," and "The Message" (Manchester competition test piece), and also the glee "When winds breathe soft." All were given with that excellence of precision and taste for which the choir has long been noted, the ensemble being a musical treat. Mr. J. Holford. L.T.S.O the energetic conductor of the choir is to be congratulated upon the high state of effi- ciency the choir has obtained—a goal which has not been reached without considerable perseverance on the part of all concerned. air. William Cooke satisfactorily fulfilled the duties of accompanist.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of this Council was held in the Boardroom at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. Mclatyre, J.P., occupied the chair, and there were also present—Admiral Parry, Messrs. H. E. Heywood, J. Brandreth, J. M. Williams, T. Baxter,C.C., G. Priestuer, J. L. J nee, S. Woodward, E. Aaron, J. B. Chadwick, J. Knowles, W. Bradford, T. Wright, T. Lewis, J.W. Bagu- lep, J. Stokes, J. Weir, J. Lowe, J. Spruce, C.Mounfield, E. Bretherton, and Mr. Ashton (clerk), Mr. G. Ashton (deputy clerk),Mr. Farrington (nuisance inspector),and Messrs. Diggle and Swinton (surveyors).

_ - LIGHT RAILWAYS AND eurucnurturn. Mr. Whiteside, secretary to the Fylde and Garstang Light Railway Committee, wrote bespeaking the co- operation of the Couucil in promoting the object of a re- solution similar to one passed at Great Eccleston, on th 3 2nd October, in which it was desired to represent to the Government that the construction of light railways in rural districts would be of great local advantage,and a substantial bPnefit to agriculture, Sand respectfully ur,,ed that legislation with that object might be under- taken during tht next session of Parliament. The Chairman stated that by supporting the proposition they would be able to do away with agricultural depression. (Laughter.)—Mr.Baxter said if they were made it would be at the expense of the ratepayers.—Mr. Heywood pro- posed that they support the proposition.—Mr.Woodward sPconded, and it was carried.

THE QUESTION OF INCREASED HOSPITAL ACCOMMODATION. The report of the committee appointed to consider the question of an infectious diseases hospital stated that the committee decided that the Clerk should communi- cate with the Northwich District Council asking if they had any views of providing a district hos- pital, and would they join them. If so on what terms as to contribution of cost ? Also that he enquire of the other district councils who had combined to erect such hospitals and en what terms? Also to write to the Runcorn Urban District if the' would join the Rural District,and if so upon what terms? —The report of the committee was cmnfirmed on the motion of Mr. Williams, seconded by Mr. Heywood.

THE NIGHTSOIL QUESTION AT WESTON. The report of the committee appointed to meet the Parish Council of Weston on the subject of nightsoil was read by the Clerk. It stated that after a long discussion it was resolved that two places for the disposal of night soil be provided, one for the Weaver ward, and one for the Weston ward, and that the com- mittee of the Parish Council ascertain where such places could be obtained and on what terms.—This re- port was cocfirmed on the motion of Mr. Wright, seconded by Mr. Chadwick.

ITELSBY WATER fitIYPLY. Writing with reference to this matter, Messrs. Potts, Potts, and Gardner, solicitors, Chester, stated that they felt sure that a meeting between the committee and the promoters of the companc would remove a good deal of misconception on the subjsct.—The Clerk read the re- ports of meetings of the committee to consider the goes- Hon of water supply tor Flelsby,held on the 2nd and 9th inst. The first meeting was presided over by Mr. J. Maclntyre, and after a long discussion it was resolved on the motion of Mr. Heywood. seconded by Mr. Wood- ward that it be a rec..mmendation to the Council that the resolution of the 3rd of September, 1895, with refer- ence to the terms upon which the Helsby and District Water Company be granted permission to open the highways be rescinded, and that a resolution in the ' following terms be adopted : " That facilities be, granted to the Helsby and District Water Company for construction of works of water supply to the contributory place of Helsby, pro- vided such works be constructed, and the charges for the water 'supplied he regulated under rules and re- gulations to be embodied in a provisional order or other- wise, as the Local Government Board may determine." —The minutes of the meeting had on the 9th inst. set forth that Mr. Heywood presided, and after meeting a committee for the promoters of the company, it was re- solved on the motion of Mr. Wood, seconded by Mr. Wil'iams, that it be a recommendation frem the coin- piny of a suggested scale of charges with an undertaking to pay £5 towards the costs of an enquiry, the Clerk re- quest the Local Government Board to hold an enquiry hs settle such scale of charges.—Mr. Aaron asked if the Water Company had guaranteed that Helshy should have a regular supply of pure good water.—The Clerk : , Pratically they de.—The Chairman : There will be a publi.; enquiry and they will have to meet the require- ments of the Local Government Board.—Mr. Aaron said they had a great deal of trouble at Weston, and there ought tsbe a clause in the agreement that the company should be compelled to supply the inhabitants with water.—Mr. Woodward thought Mr. Aaron's suggestion would be required to be carried out by the Local Government Board,and tbe company would have to meet their requirementsas tO a sufficient supply of good water at a satisfactory price. He moved the adoption of the recommendations of the committee, and Mr. Heywood I seconded. The motion was carried.

MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT. Dr. Adams reported a case of typhoid fever at Moore, and he attributed it to the drinking water. He sug- gested that a further analysis of the water be taken. Several fresh cases of scarlet fever had occurred in Stockton Heath.—The report was adopted. This ccncluded the business.

div.head: "PECULIAR PEOPLE"
div.p: THE "PECULIAR PEOPLE"

At the Essex Assizes on Wednesday a labourer named Cable, who was indicted for having " neglected " his children in a manner likely to cause them " unneces- tary suffering and injury," was found not guilty. The accused is a member of the sect styled the " Peculiar People," one of their peculiarities being to refrain from calling in medial assistance to relieve their children, no matter from what deadly or painful disease they may be suffering. In Cable's case it was proved that four chil- dren died from diphtheria and that no medical assistance was rendered to them. Nevertheless Mr. Justice Hawkins held that Cable was "a man of great humanity."

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARS.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARS.

I The weekly ses-sion-oi-tlie---11-o-Pe .of Earlestown Lodge of Good Tetnplars was held at the Co-opera- tive Hall on Monday evening. Bro. James Hatton, C.T., presided. Two candidates were initiated and several others proposed. The report of No. 1 Con- vention held at Warrington on Saturday was given by Bro. Newman and adopted. It was arranged to have a Christmas Carol party, Bro. G. Clarke to be conductor. Bro. James Hopkins offered -to give a very useful book as a prize to the member introduc- ing the largest number of candidates during the quarter. The offer was accepted, thanks being I accorded Bro. Hopkins for his gift. At the con- elusion of the business the lodge was declared open and there was a large inflax of friends, the room being crowded. Bro. G. Clarke who was responsible presided, and gave a short address. An excellent programme of songs, readings and instrumental selections was ably submitted by Bro. Willis, G. Clarke G. W. Dennis, Muscroft, W. H. Crowther' Sisters ella'. and Newman. Thanks were accorded V Bros. Clarke and Willis on the motion of Bro. Hatton, seconded by Bro. Drew. At the close of the meeting, several friends intimated their wil- lingness to join the order. CLAIM FOR WAGES BY A COLBORNE FARMER. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday before his honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, James Mavwell, of Dean Dam Farm,Golberne, sued Garton Bros., seed experimentalizers, of Newton, for £4 165., one month's wages in lieu of notice.—Mr. Browne,who represented the plaintiff.explained that his client was engaged by the defendants in Novem- ber, 1894, at the weekly wage of .£1 4s. and house rent, a month's notice being agreed to be given on either side. In September last, when the harvest was over, the defendants, without any cause, in- stantiv dismissed plaintiff, who now claimed dam- ages —Plaintiff corroborate i his solicitor's opening statement. Mr. R. Stuart who represented the de- fendants contended that a fortnight's notice was the time originally agreed unon, and that in May, in consequence of the plaintiff's unsatisfactory con- duct, the defendants gave him notice, and rein- stated him subject to seven days' notice only.— Robert Garton bore out this assertion.—His Honour remarked that there seemed to have been some sort of agreement between the parties for seven days' notice. He would therefore give judgment for the plaintiff for .£1 45., the amount of a week's wage, and costs.

div.p: YOUNG PEOPLE'S -§-OCIETY OF OHMS-
TIAN ENDEAVOUR.
MEETING AT NEWTON.

On Thursday evening a public meeting of the above society, embracing the three local societies connected with the Baptist, Congregational and Primitive Methn- fsiat churches, wag held in the Congregational Church, Newton. The Rev. James Allatt presided, and he Wag supported by the Rev. W. H. Towers (nreaident. of the maecheater and District Union of the Y.P.S.C.E.). Rev. C. Humble, Liverpool, and Rev. D. W. Roberts (late of Warrington). After the formal opening with hymn and prayer. the Chairman briefly introduced the object of the meeting, and exnlained the workings of the Society, The Rev. W.' R. Towers trusted that seed which might he sown that night, would make the Christian Endea- yonr have a warm place in the hearts of those who did not actually belong to the movement. They were hut a I stripling 14 years of age, hut they had grown acrcsa ' Continents and Oceans, on that they had planted them- selves in almost every Christian country on the face of the earth, and they numbered in ranas to-day, some 500 peonle whose skins were red, some 20.000 people whose skins were yellow, 109 000 People who belonged to the negrn race, and 2,343,000 white people, they would see that the mos ement had had a phenomenal growth. When it was first commenced there was no idea that the Christian Endeavour could ever in the whole course of time reach the proportions it had reaeh,d. It was the outcome of one Pastor's earnest thought for the spiritural wellbeing of the young people in his church, and when Dr. Clarke 14 years ago, drew up the pledge oPthe Chris- tian Endeavour, and gathered his young people together in his parlonr,there was no idea they were beginning a movement which would go to China, Janus, India, Madagasear,that scene of nnhl nd heroic effort. When the war broke out they had 93 societies, and in Turkey, notwithstanding its misrule, there were between 30 and 40 Christian Endeavour branches. These societies in foreign lends were largely the outcome of American Missionaries, because in America they found that the Christian Endeavour movement was from beginning to ending a religious movement ; they saw what was good for young converts at home, could not he but helpful to young converts on heathen soil. He then gave an out- I line of Christian Endeavour pledge and said it seemed to be a Vera' unwieldy one, as people read it, perhaps for the first time,but they would afterwards find that it contained isdcthhrosAmn life.elements(fAorrptihaeubse‘llding up of a strong vigorous The Rev. D. W. Roberts also addressed the meeting on " The Christian Endeavourer, a Witness Bearer." The Rev. C. Rumble, of Livernool, gave an address which was followed by a Consecration service conducted by the Rev. W. H. Towers. A collection in aid of the expenses was nude.

div.head: ODDFELLOWSHIP AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: ODDFELLOWSHIP AT EARLESTOWN.
ANNIVERSARY AND PRESENTATION.

The anniversary dinner of the Loyal Viaduct Lodge of Oddfellows, MU., was held at the Wellington Inn, Earlestown, on Saturday evening. About 60 members and visitors sat down to a substantial repast, which was thoroughly enjoyed. An interesting feature of the after proceedings was the presentation of a marble timepiece to P.P.G.M. Gilmour, for meritorious services. After the removal of the cloth the chair was occupied by P.G.M. W. Sutton, N.G.W. Bray being in the vice-chair. The Chairman said he was really only a young mem- ber of the lodge, but he had taken a great interest in it the last cew years. It fell to his lot a few weeks ago to attend a delegate meeting held at Blackburn to discuss one of the burning questions that had come before Friendly Societies, that of old age pensions and State aid. The Mayor of Blackburn in eited delegates from every district in Lancashire to see what decision they might come to. During the discussion, it turned out that the majority were for State aid. Those who were against it had, in his opinion, no sound argument, as to why they should not have State aid. As an instance he would take their own lodge. If a man became 60 years of age, and they could pay him five shillings per week, during his lifetime, the State could step in and say "we wilj give you five shillings per week also." Many who attended the meeting said that by accepting State aid they should be making paupers of themselves. Was there, he asked, a member of that lodge who, when he became 60 years of age would refuse the five shillings offered by the State in addition to what the lodge would allow ? As one of the delegates at Blackburn said, all the Friendly Societies must send delegates to their A.M.C., workingmen delegates, and not delegates who were independent of their Friendly Societies ; they could soon show by throwing this burning question out that they were independent of it, and did not require the State aid. It behoved all districts of the M.U., to send delegates to the A.M.C.' who would push forward the question of State aid. (Applause.) P.P.G.M. P. Connor in giving the toast of "Manches- ter Unity and Board of Directors," said that in propos- in. the health of the M.D., they proposed the health of 739,449 men,who were paying funds in for one common purpose, and those people had got over £8,000,000 of capital divided into various forms. In 1874 the number ot members was 496,529, so that they bad made great progress in 21 years. The capital of sick and funeral funds in districts was on the 31st December, 1873, £3,412,498. During the past 21 years the Order had e spended the large sum of £12,725,946 16s. 3d. ; the cap tal of sick and funeral funds in lodges anil districts had increased by over £4,000,000. (Applause.) After seversl songs had been given, the presentation to P.P.G.M. W.Gilmour was proceeded with. P.P.G.M. John Walker, a late trustee of the lodge,said they had placed him in rather an awkward position. Wi.en he came into the room, and in glancing over the programme he congratulatedlhimself that he could shake a loose leg,as he did not see his name on the programme but still he would discharge the task set him,to the best of his ability. They all knew they were presenting that clock to a very energetic and good worker for that lodge, and one who had been such for a good number of years. He was very pleased to be the medium by which it was presented to him. It was presented by the lodge for meritorious services. He had had some very onerous duties to perform lately,for which he would not receive any remunerati.m,and the committee thought it well to recompense him in some other way, and he had very great pleasure in presenting Mr.Gilmour with that handsome clock, and he thought he was very worthy of it. (Cheers.) The members here rose and drank the health of Bro. Gilmour, singing" For he's a jolly good fellow." The dock bore a silver plate with the inscription " Presented to P. P. G. M. Gilmour, by the members of the Loral Viaduct Lodge 1.0.0. F. M.U.F.S. November 2nd. 1895. For meritorious services."

Ilro Gilmour in acknowledging the gift was much moved. He said that in the lives of most men there was a great difficulty in expressing their feelings on occasions of that sort, and he could tell them, he felt in that position that evening. They were well aware if it was a District meeting they were to send him to, and it was some question they wanted him to defend, they could depend upon him if there was to be any fun. He should have been extremely delighted had P. P. G. M. Tunstall been in sufficient health to pertorm the duty he intended to do. He felt certain it was a great sacrifice on his part, and he felt sorry for the cause which pre- vented his being present. With reference to the remarks of?. P. G. Ms Walker, he could say that so far as being a brother and officer of the Lodge, he had done nothing but as a brother of the Lodge. He had had his own way of doing things and had done them in his own way. For a quarter of a century, he had acted in one capacity and another as an official of their society, and he had Prided himself upon belonging to the Loyal Viaduct, Ledge. There was not another Society, if they were to turn out, which would compare with their lodge. He felt prouder that night perhaps than even the Lord Mayor of London. He was delighted when their committee decided to recommend what the Lodge should do, when he refused to receive any renu- meration for services which he had performed, and it was left in the hands of the cenamittee, and what they saw before them, was the result. He remembered Robert Craven, one of their old trustees Charles Owen, Matthew Jolley, and coming down even later, he remem- bered Richard Mawdsley,so that they must admit he had seen some changes in the Viaduct Lodge. It would be a satisfaction in generations to come; for his descendants to say, "this is grandfather's clock and it was given by the members of the Viaduct Lodge." The inscription on the clock, no doubt, would be handed down to posterity and he again thanked every member of the committee, every officer and member of the lodge. He appreciated their kindness more than he could tell them, and he would guard that clock as sacred property, and no matter where he went, he should preserve the present they had given him. (Cheers.) The Chairman announced that the Secretary, Mr. W. Ball,was unable to be present owing to illness, a circum- stance which he much deplored, as he would have been of very great ansiatance to the meeting. Bro. P.P.G.M. J. Dolan gave the toast of " Ashton-in- M 4kerfielri and District." P P G.M., P. Connor in giving the toast of "The Loyal Viaduct Lodge," said he was satisfied he was pro- posing the health of men who were honest and healthy. Every man who had joined that lodge since it was opened, had got every penny he was promised, so that they would see there was no fraud about it. He was glad to gay there was no man who could point a finger at the Viaduct Lodge. They were the youngest lodge in the districNhad been the most imposed npon,had paid £l,lOO more than it cost to bury their dead,and they had many things to contend with. A lodge of any society that had nothing to exist mann but itself was soon scattered,
thought the work was dangerous. He would make it his duty to visit other paper mills, and if he found any improvement could be made, he would give notice that it should be done.

Mr. Barton expressed regret at the occurrence, and mentioned that deceased bad been there 25 years, and three other men who worked with him in turns had been there 27, 24 and 12 years respectively at the work. The Coroner summod up, and the jury returned a ver- dict of " Accidental death," recommending that any suggestion made by H.M. Inspector of Factories should be carried out by the firm.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST FOREIGN MISSIONS.
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST FOREIGN MISSIONS.
MEETING AT EAKLESTOWN.

The annual meeting in support of the Primitive Metho- dist Foreign Missionary Society was held in the Primi- tive Methodist Chapel on Monday evening. Mr. Thomas Ormand presided, and he was supported by the Revs J. Birkett, returned missionary from Fernando Po, and E. R. Davies.

The Rev. E, 11. Davies, after the formal opening, presented the annual report of the Society,which showed satisfactory progress in various directions. The Chairman thought it would be impertinent on his part if he were to attempt to make a speech, when they had two such able exponents of missionary work as theix own minister and Mr. Birkett. They had met to hear what Mr.' Birkett had to say about missionary work,and if be he only charmed them as he had done himself and many others the previous day, it would be a very de. Ilightful evening indeed. (Hear, hear.) The Rev.J. Birkett was pleased to have that opportu- nity of addressing them upon a topic which he was sure they were all interested in. It was in January,lB9o,that he left this country for the Island of Fernando Po. He had heard and read of heathen lands and of savagt tribes, but the pictures drawn in their minds were not always true to nature. They formed their ideas before they saw places, and when they did come in contact with the reality they had to confess that while their imagination was artistic, like many other artists, im- agination did not exactly adhere to detail. And when Lie got to Fernando Po he found the people and the island were far different to what he had conceived. Fernando Po was a mountainous and forest island. Some of is elevations were a considerable altitude ; Clarence Peak was something like 1,000 feet above the level of the sea, and was covered with luxurious vegetation. The a bori- ginal people of the island numbered about 30,000. Tney were called Boobies. Physically these people were not badly developed ; they were fairly tall,and to all appear- ances, looking at them superficially,they appeared t•3be robust. Their maindisfiguremonts were scars cut across the face. They were very unclean, dirty, filthy in their personal habits, and their uncleanliness exp3sed them to many skin affections, and their exposure to th, weather, especially during the rainy season, exposed them to rheumatism and kindred ailments. Their climate was the worst in the world, and the malaria produced the West African fever. Mentally they wer, not very poor, in comparison with some other of the West Coast tribes. They know nothing except what the missionaries have taught them about reading, writing ana arithmetic. What was a singular thing was the children almost seemed to give promise ol superior intelligence, and they appeared to be quite as sharp as children of this country, but when they reached a certain point they ceased to develope intellectually. He then exhibited some specimens of the handiwork of the natives. Morally they were very low, but they were not murderers. They were not a savage, ferocious, dangerous people, cases of murder were exceedingly rare, they were not a very dishonest people, they had no thieving propensities, but there was no judicial penalty which prohibited stealing. There were, however, three forms of vice which terrorised these people, lying, Indolence and licentiousness. They were masters in duplicity. Their laziness was proverbial ; most of the West African tribes were generally indolent but none were so lazy as the Boobies. He then went on to deal with the customs of the people,their marriage and bvial ceremonies. The advent of the missionaries had, he said, improved the social and moral condition of the people to some extent. They had day and Sunday schools and many of the people Could now read the English bible. He attended to the establishment of the Cocoa farm on which the natives now worked. Twenty- five years ago he said there was not a Christian Booby living in the bush, but Bow there was a great change. Votes of thanks were afterwards accorded the Chair- man and speakers and the meeting terminated. The annual services in aid of the missions were held on Sunday when appropriate sermons were preached by the Rev. J. Birkett.
WESTON.

CRIMIWT CLUB Dxxxxn.—There was a large attendance at the annual dinner in connection with the Weston Cricket Club, held on Fri Jay evening at the Prospect Inn' Weston. After a sumptuous repast, served in Mr. and Mrs. Vose's beat style, the president of the club, Mr. T. T. Sill occupied the chair at the subsequent proceed- ings. He was supported by Messrs. J. J. Speakman, J. G. Tatters, J. W. Vale, James Tudor. D. Kirkham, S. Dodd. Joseph Ball, J. Mather, W. Tweddell, J. Mitchen- son, J. Fraser, J. Mort, G. Robinson, and D. Somerville (hon. secretary). After the usual loyal toasts had been honoured, the Chairman proposed "Success to the Weston Cricket Club." This was responded to by Mr. Tudor. It may be here stated that the balance sheet showed that the year commenced with £3 3s. 4d. in hand, and that the receipts, including this amount, came to £26 4s. After meeting all expenses the balance in favour of tee club was £l3 18s. The report for the past season showed that the first team had played 13 matches, of which five were won, three drawn, and five lost. They had scored 691 runs, at a cost of 108 wick,ts, compared with their opponents' 648 runs, and 109 wickets. The A. team had played eight matches, won two, lost five, and tied one. The runs numbered 348 for 74 wickets, against 59 runs and 77 wickets by the opposing teams.—Mr. Somerville gave "The health of the President," anti the toast was enthusiastically drunk, the company singing, "He's a jolly good fellow."—The President sincerely thanked the company for the flatter- ing manner in which they had responded to the toast Die enthusiasm displayed was not deserved. It had always been his pleasure since he Came into that district to take an interest in the cricket club, and to do what he could for its success. Se long as he remained in the village it would be his endeavour to do what he could for the prosperity of the club, and if they wished to show their appreciation of his efforts they would induce young members to come forward, and, by doing their level best, assist those who had long been playing mem- bers. (Applause.)—Mr. Speakman submitted "The vice-presidents and patrons," and Mr. Robinson, in res- ponding, hoped the club might gain the honoured dis- tinction, namely, that they could not be equalled in the broad acres of Cheshire. (Applause )—Mr. D. Kirkham gave "The officers of the club," and Mr. Somerville res. ponded.—Mr. S. Dodd proposed "The committee," and Messrs. Fraser and Bull acknowledged the compliment. —Mr. Speakman proposed "The host and hostess" in felicitous terms.—Mr. Vose replied, saying he was pleased that their efforts had given satisfaction.—Dur- ing the evening a number of songs were interpreted by Messrs J. E. Tudor, Hope, C. Pendlebury, Joseph Ball, A. Tudor, Fythe, D. Kirkham, and James Tudor. Mr. SHOCKING MACHINERY FATALITY AT Holt acted efficiently as accompanist. NEWTON,

Bro. J. Walker, P.P.G.M., responded, and said it was a toast which they ought to be proud of. Forty years ago he was made a member of the lodge with 19 others, and at that time it was worth £ll5, now they were worth shout, £2.000. (Applause.) The other toasts included " Host and hostess," " Visiting officers and brothers," and" Lodge Surgeon." A lengthy programme of songs was gone through, Bro. J. Howard giving a couple of whistling solos in his liquidly clever style, and a most enjoyable evening was spent.

On Friday morning an old man named John Kay. 83 veers nf age, employed at the Paper Mill of Afessrs. Gil- lespie and mason, Newton met with a shocking death whilst following his employment of machine man. The cleceased,who had been engag4 d at the same work shout 25 years, is supposed to have been removing the felt off the roller. He had gone into the pit to do so, and un- fortunately had been caught by the belting and flung out of the pit. Re had not been seen by his assistant for abnut a quarter of an hour. and on a search being made hp was found lying near the machine quite dead, his skull being smashed and legs and ribs broken. _

An engoiry into the cirenmstances WRA held et the Millatone Inn, Newton.on Monday, bv Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner. Mr. R. Tinkor, Her Majesty's Inspector nf Factories, was present, and Mr. R. Barton represented the firm. Previous tn the enquiry, the Coroner and jury visited the scene of the accident. Flannah Kay, widow of thet deceased gave evidence of identification, and said her husband WAR 83 years of a.re and had worked at the Mills considerably over 20 years. _

Robert Wilson stated that he worked at the Paper Mills and sa w deceased at 25 minutes past 10 in the machine room. Witness had worked there four years. and had seen deceased put lagging and felt on the pulley. When doing so be stood in the pit, close to the pulley and a revolving shaft. The lagging was taken off with a bar,and the process of both nutting on and taking off had to be done whilst the machinery was running. He had never seen it done whilst it was at a standstill.

William Broom, who had been employed at the works over 13 years as reeler-man, paid on Friday morning an assistant of deceased asked him if ha had seen Bay. He said he had not,and learning that he had been missing a quarter of an hour he went in search of him and found him dead in the pit lying on his face. He had seen lag- ging put on and taken off the pully when the machine Was running at high speed. It could net he done when the machinery was at a standstill, because they would not then know how much to put on or take off. It was also necessary that the man doing the work should stand in the pit,as he had more power there than when on the platform. The distance from the edge of the belting to the edge of the plat'orrn, within which space the de- ceased had to stand wan about 12 inches, and he had to stand sidcwaya.—Questioned by Mr. Tinker, witnesa considered it was dangerous work, and would not do it himself.

Ja meg Brodie,fereman at the works,gave corrohnrative pvidenen. He said the pulley was revolving at the rate of 53 per minute. All paper making machines WPM alike, and he admitted the work was dangernus.--By Mr. Tinker: He had often done the work himself. There would he more room if the platform was cut away. div.p: FROD-§HAM.

Pasant COUNCIL MERTING.—A meeting of the Counci acting as the Parochial Committee was held on Friday, under the rresidency of Mr. Heywood.—The Clerk of the Rural District Council reported thatthe plans for the erection of a slaughter-house at Frodsnam Bridge had been referred back to the co mmittee for re-censideration. fie pointed out the difficulties which might accrue with the agreement with the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany if the drain from the slaughter-house were con- nected with the Authority's sewer instead of being turned direct into the river.—lt was resolved that providing Mr. Rigby would enter into an agreement embodying the terms of the resolution with reference thereto passed at the last meeting of the Committea such plans be passed.—A letter was read from Mr. Mason of the Bir- kenhead Joint Railways with reference to the alleged nuisance at Frcdsham station, stating that he hoped to communicate further with the Clerk on the matter in the course if a few days.—The minutes were confirmed at the meeting of the Rural Council on Tuesday.

div.head: FRODSRAM POLICE COURT.
div.p: FRODSRAM POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.—Before Mr. A. Thomas and Dr. Steele. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Joseph Gardner, brick- layer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Chester Main-road, Helsby. P.C. Breeze pr wed the case, and the defendant having been previously con- victed, was fined 20s. and costs or one month's im- prisonment. He went to prison. Mom:wt.—Before Mr. Thomas. BEGGING..—John Smith was charged with begging on Saturday .—Sergeant Clays stated that the prisoner was begging from doer to door in Main-street, Frodsham. The prisoner was committed to prison for fourteen days. _

WERNESDAT.—Before Mr. A. Thomas. A SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A. WARRINGTON YOUTH.— George Robinson, 19 years of age, of Mill-lane, Warring- ton, wire-drawer's apprentice, was charged with a criminal offence on Sarah Ellams, 16 years of age, of Frodsharn, on the 19th inst.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, Warrington appeared on benalf of the accused. Evi- dence was given by the girl in question and a lad, from which it appeared that Robinson had been playing with the Warrington Loco's second team versus the Frodsham Wanderers Football Club,at Frodsham Bridge on Saturday afternoon. About 5.20 p.m. two young men, one of whom, it was alleged was the accused, dragged the girl down Ellis-lane, and committed the assault complained of,upon her. Information was given to the police. In cross-examination by Mr. Browne, the prosecutrix admitted that she bad failed to identify the prisoner when asked to do so before the commencement of the court. Mr. Browne submitted that there was no case, and added that he had five witnesses who were prepared to prove that the prisoner was innocent of the charge.—The magistrate was of opinion that no jury would convict on the evidence given,and discharged the accused.

BOOKFOR MARRIED WOMEN The information contained in this book ought to be known by every married woman, aud it will not harm the unmarriep to read. The book is conveniently divided into la chapters The first chapter treats of the changes at puberty, or when a girl becomes a woman. The second chapter treats of marriage from a doctor's standpoint ; points out thu best age for marriage, and who should have children and who not, and furnishes useful information that one can ordinarily get only from an intelligent doctor. The third chapter treats of the marriage of blood relations; and condemns such marriages as a rule. Chapter four treats of the signs of pregnancy. The fifth chapter tells how a woman should live during the pregnant state. Tne sixth chapter treats t mishaps and how to avoid them. The seventh chapter treats of maternal impressions and shows that birthmarks are not due to longings on the part of the mother, but rather to her poor health. The eighth chapter teaches how to have easy confinements. Certain people believe that women shoal d bring forth in pain and trouble, but the hygienic physician says that confinements can be made comptratively easy if certain rules are obeyed ; these rules are given. The ninth chapter treats of the proper management of confinement until the baby is born. The tenth chapter tells how to treat he mother till she is up and about again. The eleventh Chapter treats of sterility ; gives the main causes of it, how these may be overcome and children result The last chapter treats of the "change," a most important article for all women over forty. The book is full of useful information and no book is written which goes so thoroughly into matters elating to married women. Some may think too much is told ; such can scarcely be the case, for knowledge is power and the means of attaining happiness. The book can be ha 1 from Dr. T. R.
